Kinsey is widely regarded as the first major figure in American [sexology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexology "Sexology"); his research helped pave the way for a deeper exploration into sexuality among sexologists and the general public, as well as liberating [female sexuality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_female_sexuality "Human female sexuality").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-Irvine-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-Zastrow-18) For example, Kinsey's work disputed the notions that women generally are not sexual and that female [orgasms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orgasm "Orgasm") experienced [vaginally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vagina "Vagina") are superior to [clitoral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clitoris "Clitoris") orgasms.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-Irvine-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-Zastrow-18) He initially became interested in different forms of sexual practices in 1933, after discussing the topic extensively with a colleague, Robert Kroc. Kinsey had been studying the variations in mating practices among [gall wasps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gall_wasp "Gall wasp"). During this time, he developed a scale measuring sexual orientation, now known as the [Kinsey scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_scale "Kinsey scale"), which ranges from 0 to 6, where 0 is exclusively [heterosexual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heterosexuality "Heterosexuality") and 6 is exclusively [homosexual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homosexuality "Homosexuality"); a rating of X for "no socio-sexual contacts or reactions" was later added.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-19)

In 1935, Kinsey delivered a lecture to a faculty discussion group at Indiana University, his first public discussion of the topic, wherein he attacked the "widespread ignorance of sexual structure and physiology" and promoted his view that "delayed marriage" (that is, delayed sexual experience) was psychologically harmful. Kinsey obtained research funding from the [Rockefeller Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockefeller_Foundation "Rockefeller Foundation"), which enabled him to further study human sexual behavior.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-20) He published _Sexual Behavior in the Human Male_ in 1948, followed in 1953 by _Sexual Behavior in the Human Female_, both of which reached the top of the bestseller lists and turned Kinsey into a celebrity. These publications later became known as the Kinsey Reports. Articles about him appeared in magazines such as _[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time\_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")_, _[Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life\_(magazine) "Life (magazine)")_, _[Look](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Look\_(American\_magazine) "Look (American magazine)")_, and _[McCall's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCall's "McCall's")_. The Kinsey Reports, which led to a storm of controversy, are regarded by many as a precursor to the [sexual revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_revolution "Sexual revolution") of the 1960s and 1970s.

### Controversies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alfred_Kinsey&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Controversies")]

Kinsey's research went beyond theory and interview to include observation of and participation in sexual activity, sometimes involving co-workers. Kinsey justified this sexual experimentation as being necessary to gain the confidence of his research subjects. He encouraged his staff to do likewise, and to engage in a wide range of sexual activity, to the extent that they felt comfortable; he argued that this would help his interviewers understand the participants' responses.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-Vern1-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-Vern2-22) Kinsey filmed sexual acts which included co-workers in the attic of his home as part of his research;[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-pbs-23) Biographer [Jonathan Gathorne-Hardy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Gathorne-Hardy "Jonathan Gathorne-Hardy") explains that this was done to ensure the films' secrecy, which would have caused a scandal had it become public knowledge.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-25) James H. Jones, author of _Alfred C. Kinsey: A Public/Private Life_, and British conservative cultural critic and psychiatrist [Anthony Malcolm Daniels aka Theodore Dalrymple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Dalrymple "Theodore Dalrymple"), among others, have speculated that Kinsey was driven by his own sexual needs.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-26)

Some of the data published in the two _Kinsey Reports_ books is controversial in the scientific and psychiatric communities, owing to Kinsey's decision to interview volunteers who may not have been representative of the general population.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-Boothe-27) University of Chicago sociology professor [Edward Laumann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Laumann "Edward Laumann") also argued that Kinsey's work was focused on the biology of sex and lacked psychological and clinical information and analysis.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-Boothe-27)

Kinsey collected sexual material from around the world, which brought him to the attention of the U.S. Customs Service when they seized some pornographic films in 1956; he died before this matter was resolved legally.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-pbs-23) Kinsey wrote about pre-adolescent orgasms using data in tables 30 to 34 of the male volume, which report observations of orgasms in over 300 children aged from two months up to fifteen years.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-kinsey-tables-28) This information was said to have come from adults' childhood memories, or from parent or teacher observation.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-kinsey-inst-29) Kinsey said he also interviewed nine men who had sexual experiences with children and who told him about the children's responses and reactions. Little attention was paid to this part of Kinsey's research at the time, but where Kinsey had gained this information began to be questioned nearly 40 years later.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-BeyondBed-30) It was later revealed that Kinsey used data from a single pedophile and presented it as being from various sources. Kinsey knew the abuse would continue but had seen the need for participant confidentiality and anonymity as necessary to gain "honest answers on such taboo subjects".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-Pool-32) Years later, the Kinsey Institute said that the data on children in tables 31–34 came from one man's journal (started in 1917) and that the events concerned predated the Kinsey Reports.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-Pool-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-33) According to Mikella Procopio, "the lure of otherwise unattainable data was difficult to resist".[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-34) But "Kinsey was fiercely against any use of force or compulsion in sex".[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-35)

These allegations were revived by a dispute inside the [Indiana State Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_State_Senate "Indiana State Senate"). The opposition protested that these were "warmed over Internet memes that keep coming back."[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-Indiana_Capital_Chronicle_2023-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-AP_NEWS_2023-37)[IndyStar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IndyStar "IndyStar") asserted that opponents of Kinsey "cited long-held but largely debunked allegations".[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-IndyStar_2023_w873-38)

Jones wrote that Kinsey's sexual activity influenced his work, that he over-represented prisoners and prostitutes, classified some single people as "married",[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-Jones-39) and that he included a disproportionate number of homosexual men, which may have distorted his studies.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-Vern1-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-Vern2-22) While he has been criticized for omitting African Americans from his research,[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-Reumann0-40) his report on the human male includes numerous references to African-American participants.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReumann200524-41) Historian [Vern Bullough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vern_Bullough "Vern Bullough") writes that the data was later reinterpreted, excluding prisoners and data derived from an exclusively gay sample, and the results indicate that it does not appear to have skewed the data. Kinsey may have over-represented homosexuals, but Bullough considers that this may have been because homosexual behavior was stigmatized and needed to be better understood.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-Vern1-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-Vern2-22)[Paul Gebhard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Gebhard "Paul Gebhard"), who was Kinsey's colleague from 1946 to 1956 and who also succeeded Kinsey as Director of the Kinsey Institute following his death,[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-gebhardrelia-42) attempted to justify Kinsey's work in the 1970s by removing some of the suspect data where Kinsey allegedly showed a bias towards homosexuality.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-gebhardrelia-42) After Gebhard recalculated the findings in Kinsey's work, he found only slight differences between the original and updated figures.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-43)

Bailey et al., in their 2016 review of the sexual orientation literature, stated that Kinsey's survey likely overestimated the frequencies of nonheterosexual attractions and expressions, because his statistics show a higher percentage of the American population as homosexual or bisexual than more modern studies do.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-44) However Kinsey biographer Jonathan Gathorne-Hardy states that Kinsey's interview style was quite different from the methodologies of modern studies, something he attributes as a reason for difference of answers.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-Gathorne-Hardy-2000-45) Kinsey focused on in-depth interviews with subjects carried out by himself or highly trained members of his team, and emphasized creating rapport with the interviewee and making them feel comfortable and secure.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-46) Modern interviewers tend to be less thoroughly trained and emphasize scientific detachment, which may make respondents less likely to share sensitive personal details.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-Gathorne-Hardy-2000-45)

A [postmodern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postmodernism "Postmodernism") take on Kinsey is that sexuality should not be made an object of science,[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-Janssen2012-47)_i.e._, postmodernism heavily rejects a study of sexuality based upon naturalistic assumptions.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-p833-48)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alfred_Kinsey&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Personal life")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/35/First_Street_1320%2C_Kinsey_House%2C_Vinegar_Hill_HD.jpg/250px-First_Street_1320%2C_Kinsey_House%2C_Vinegar_Hill_HD.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:First_Street_1320,_Kinsey_House,_Vinegar_Hill_HD.jpg)

Kinsey's home in [Bloomington, Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomington,_Indiana "Bloomington, Indiana")

Kinsey was raised as a [Methodist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodist "Methodist"), and for a time converted to a much less fundamentalist [Congregationalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregationalism "Congregationalism").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-Jones_2004_p._116-49) During his studies at Harvard he apparently became agnostic or atheist, replacing religious fervor with fervor for science.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-Jones_2004_p._154-50) He married [Clara McMillen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clara_McMillen "Clara McMillen") in 1921. Their marriage ceremony, like his college graduation, was avoided by Alfred Sr. The couple had four children. Their first son, Donald, born in 1922, died from complications of [juvenile diabetes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juvenile_diabetes "Juvenile diabetes") in 1927, just before his fifth birthday. Their first daughter, Anne, was born in 1924, followed by Joan in 1925, and then by their second son Bruce in 1928.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Kinsey was [bisexual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bisexual "Bisexual"),[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-51) and one biographer believes that as a young man he would punish himself for having homoerotic feelings.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-Jones6-52) He and his wife agreed that both could have sex with other people as well as with each other. Kinsey had sex with other men, including his student [Clyde Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clyde_Martin "Clyde Martin").[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-53)

Kinsey was a friend of the [occult](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occult "Occult") filmmaker [Kenneth Anger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Anger "Kenneth Anger"). In 1955, both visited the [Abbey of Thelema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbey_of_Thelema "Abbey of Thelema") in [Cefalù](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cefal%C3%B9 "Cefalù"), [Sicily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sicily "Sicily"), where [Aleister Crowley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleister_Crowley "Aleister Crowley") had established a commune.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-the_Guardian-2023-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-anger1-55)

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e9/Clara_McMillen_yearbook_photo.jpg/250px-Clara_McMillen_yearbook_photo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Clara_McMillen_yearbook_photo.jpg)

Clara McMillen in the [Indiana University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_University "Indiana University") yearbook, 1921

Kinsey and Anger were interested in the [Thelema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thelema "Thelema") religion that Crowley had created.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-the_Guardian-2023-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-anger1-55) According to Anger, "Kinsey was an agnostic. He wasn't a believer in anything, really, except science."[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-anger1-55)

Kinsey designed his own house, which was built in the [Vinegar Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinegar_Hill_Historic_District "Vinegar Hill Historic District") neighborhood of Bloomington, Indiana, at 1320 First Street. There he practiced his deep interest in [gardening](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gardening "Gardening").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-56)

Kinsey died on August 25, 1956, in Bloomington Hospital at the age of 62. The cause of his death was reported to be a heart ailment and [pneumonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pneumonia "Pneumonia").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-APobit-57) The _New York Times_ ran the following editorial on August 27, 1956:

> The untimely death of Dr. Alfred C. Kinsey takes from the American scene an important and valuable, as well as controversial, figure. Whatever may have been the reaction to his findings—and to the unscrupulous use of some of them—the fact remains that he was first, last, and always a scientist. In the long run, it is probable that the values of his contribution to contemporary thought will lie much less in what he found out than in the method he used and his way of applying it. Any sort of scientific approach to the problems of sex is difficult because the field is so deeply overlaid with such things as moral precept, taboo, individual and group training, and long-established behavior patterns. Some of these may be good in themselves, but they are no help to the scientific and empirical method of getting at the truth. Dr. Kinsey cut through this overlay with detachment and precision. His work was conscientious and comprehensive. Naturally, it will receive a serious setback with his death. Let us earnestly hope that the scientific spirit that inspired it will not be similarly impaired.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-New_York_Times_editorial-59)

Kinsey was buried at Rose Hill Cemetery in [Bloomington, Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomington,_Indiana "Bloomington, Indiana").[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-61)

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alfred_Kinsey&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Legacy")]

The popularity of _Sexual Behavior in the Human Male_ prompted widespread media interest in 1948. _[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time\_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")_ magazine declared, "Not since _[Gone With the Wind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gone\_with\_the\_Wind\_(novel) "Gone with the Wind (novel)")_ had booksellers seen anything like it."[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-Time1-62) The first pop culture references to Kinsey appeared not long after the book's publication; "[Martha Raye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Raye "Martha Raye") [sold] a half-million copies of 'Ooh, Dr. Kinsey!'"[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-63)[Cole Porter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cole_Porter "Cole Porter")'s song "[Too Darn Hot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Too_Darn_Hot "Too Darn Hot")", from the Tony Award-winning Broadway musical _[Kiss Me, Kate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiss\_Me,\_Kate "Kiss Me, Kate")_, devoted its [bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridge_(music) "Bridge (music)") to "the Kinsey report / Every average man you know / Much prefers to play his favorite sport".[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-64) In 1949 [Mae West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mae_West "Mae West"), reminiscing on the days when the word "sex" was rarely uttered, said of Kinsey, "That guy merely makes it easy for me. Now I don't have to draw 'em any blueprints... We are both in the same business[...] Except I saw it first."[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-Time2-65)

The publication of _Sexual Behavior in the Human Female_ prompted even more intensive news coverage. Kinsey appeared on the cover of the August 24, 1953, issue of _Time_.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-66) The national news magazine featured two articles on the scientist, one focusing on his research, career and new book,[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-Time3-67) the other on his background, personality, and lifestyle.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-68) In the magazine's cover portrait, "Flowers, birds, and a bee surround Kinsey; the mirror-of-Venus female symbol decorates his bow tie."[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-69) The lead article concluded: "'Kinsey[...] has done for sex what Columbus did for geography,' declared a pair of enthusiasts[...] forgetting that Columbus did not know where he was when he got there.[...] Kinsey's work contains much that is valuable, but it must not be mistaken for the last word."[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-Time3-67) A character called "Dr. Kinsey" appeared on the September 15, 1953, television episode of _[The Jack Benny Program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Jack\_Benny\_Program "The Jack Benny Program")_ as a bow-tied man interviewing a young woman on board a [cruise ship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cruise_ship "Cruise ship") that has left [Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii "Hawaii"). When "Dr. Kinsey" identifies himself to [Jack Benny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Benny "Jack Benny"), Benny steps away in embarrassment.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-Jack_Benny-70) The "Dr. Kinsey" character was also written into another sketch in the same episode, commenting on a fantasy Benny is having about [Marilyn Monroe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marilyn_Monroe "Marilyn Monroe") (a guest on the episode).[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-Jack_Benny-70)

The early 2000s saw a renewed interest in Kinsey. In 2003 [Theatre of NOTE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_of_NOTE "Theatre of NOTE") produced the Steve Morgan Haskell play titled _Fucking Wasps_ which followed Kinsey's life from childhood until death. Written and directed by Steve Morgan Haskell, _Fucking Wasps_ received many accolades, including a Playwriting of the Year nomination from Backstage West. Premiering in 2003, the musical _Dr. Sex_ focuses on the relationship between Kinsey, his wife, and their shared lover Wally Matthews (based on [Clyde Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clyde_Martin "Clyde Martin")). The play had a score by Larry Bortniker, a book by Bortniker and Sally Deering, and won seven [Jeff Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Jefferson_Awards "Joseph Jefferson Awards"). It was produced off-Broadway in 2005. The 2004 [biographical film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biographical_film "Biographical film")_[Kinsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey\_(film) "Kinsey (film)")_, written and directed by [Bill Condon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Condon "Bill Condon"), stars [Liam Neeson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liam_Neeson "Liam Neeson") as the scientist and [Laura Linney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laura_Linney "Laura Linney") as his wife. In 2004 [T. Coraghessan Boyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._Coraghessan_Boyle "T. Coraghessan Boyle")'s novel about Kinsey, _[The Inner Circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Inner\_Circle\_(T.\_C.\_Boyle\_novel) "The Inner Circle (T. C. Boyle novel)")_, was published. The following year, [PBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Broadcasting_Service "Public Broadcasting Service") produced the documentary _Kinsey_ in cooperation with the [Kinsey Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute_for_Research_in_Sex,_Gender_and_Reproduction "Kinsey Institute for Research in Sex, Gender and Reproduction"), which allowed access to many of its files. _Mr. Sex_, a [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC") radio play by Steve Coombes concerning Kinsey and his work, won the 2005 Imison Award.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-71)

In 2012, Kinsey was inducted into the [Legacy Walk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legacy_Walk "Legacy Walk") in Chicago, an outdoor public display which celebrates [LGBT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBT "LGBT") history and people.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-72)

In June 2019, Kinsey was one of the inaugural fifty American "pioneers, trailblazers, and heroes" inducted on the [National LGBTQ Wall of Honor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_LGBTQ_Wall_of_Honor "National LGBTQ Wall of Honor") within the [Stonewall National Monument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stonewall_National_Monument "Stonewall National Monument") (SNM) in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City")'s [Stonewall Inn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stonewall_Inn "Stonewall Inn").[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-SDGLN-74) The SNM is the first [U.S. national monument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_monument_(United_States) "National monument (United States)") dedicated to [LGBTQ rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBT_rights_in_the_United_States "LGBT rights in the United States") and [history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_LGBT_people "History of LGBT people"),[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-75) and the wall's unveiling was timed to take place during the [50th anniversary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stonewall_50_%E2%80%93_WorldPride_NYC_2019 "Stonewall 50 – WorldPride NYC 2019") of the [Stonewall riots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stonewall_riots "Stonewall riots").[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-76)

William Condon(born October 22, 1955) is an American director and screenwriter. Condon is known for writing and/or directing numerous successful and acclaimed films, including Gods and Monsters,Chicago,Kinsey,Dreamgirls,The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn – Part 1,The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn – Part 2, and Beauty and the Beast.He has received two nominations for the Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay,Gods and Monsters and Chicago, winning for the former. ×

#### Your Privacy

When you visit any website, it may store or retrieve information on your browser, mostly in the form of cookies. This information might be about you, your preferences, or your device, and is mostly used to make the site work as you expect. The information does not usually identify you directly, but it can give you a more personalized web experience. Because we respect your right to privacy, you can choose not to allow some types of cookies. Click on the different category headings to learn more and change our default settings. Blocking some types of cookies may impact your experience of the site and the services we are able to offer. 

[More information](https://cookiepedia.co.uk/giving-consent-to-cookies)

#### Strictly Necessary Cookies

Always Active

These cookies are necessary for the website to function and cannot be switched off in our systems. They also help us to remember prior selections you have made, such as setting your privacy preferences, such as setting your privacy preferences, logging in or filling in forms. You can set your browser to block or alert you about these cookies, but some parts of the site will not then work.

- [x] Performance Cookies

If you do not allow these cookies, we will have less information to help us improve the site’s functionality.

#### Functional Cookies

- [x] Functional Cookies 

These cookies enable the website to provide enhanced functionality and personalization, such as remembering language settings and customer service chat history. If you do not allow these cookies, then some or all of these services may not function properly.

#### Social Media Cookies

- [x] Social Media Cookies 

These cookies are set by a range of social media services that we have added to the site to enable you to share our content with your friends and networks. They are capable of tracking your browser across other sites and building up a profile of your interests. This may impact the content and messages you see on other websites you visit. If you do not allow these cookies you may not be able to use or see these sharing tools.

#### Targeting Cookies

- [x] Targeting Cookies 

These cookies may be set through our site by our advertising partners. They may be used by those companies to build a profile of your interests and show you relevant adverts on this and other sites. If you do not allow these cookies, you will still see advertising, but it will not be targeted to your specific interests.

They also acted in a 2013 dramatic thriller directed by someone best known for directing and writing the critically acclaimed Kinsey. Can you tell me what it is based on the above details available as of December 2023?

**Alfred Charles Kinsey** ([/ˈ k ɪ n z i/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); June 23, 1894 – August 25, 1956) was an American [sexologist](link_19), [biologist](link_20), and professor of [entomology](link_21) and [zoology](link_22) who, in 1947, founded the Institute for Sex Research at [Indiana University](link_18),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey#cite_note-1) now known as the [Kinsey Institute for Research in Sex, Gender, and Reproduction](link_23). He is best known for writing _Sexual Behavior in the Human Male_ (1948) and _Sexual Behavior in the Human Female_ (1953), also known as the [Kinsey Reports](link_13), as well as for the [Kinsey scale](link_14). From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

American screenwriter and director

This article is about the director and screenwriter. For the Australian footballer, see [Bill Condon (footballer)](link_2).

**William Condon** (born October 22, 1955) is an American director and screenwriter. Condon is known for writing and/or directing numerous successful and acclaimed films including _[Gods and Monsters](link_6)_, _[Chicago](link_7)_, _[Kinsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey\_(film) "Kinsey (film)")_, _[Dreamgirls](link_8)_, _[The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn – Part 1](link_9)_, _[Part 2](link_10)_, and _[Beauty and the Beast](link_11)_.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Condon#cite_note-CondonDisneylive-actionBeautyandtheBeast-1) He has received two nominations for the [Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay](link_12), _Gods and Monsters_ and _Chicago_, winning for the former.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bill_Condon&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Condon was born in [New York City](link_4) on October 22, 1955,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Condon#cite_note-ibdb-2) the son of a police [detective](link_13),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Condon#cite_note-3) and was raised in an [Irish Catholic](link_14) family.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Condon#cite_note-columbiacollege-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Condon#cite_note-5) He attended [Regis High School](link_15) and [Columbia College of Columbia University](link_16), graduating in 1976 with a degree in philosophy.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Condon#cite_note-columbiacollege-4)

Two films had a significant impact of Condon's early life. At the age of twelve, he found himself drawn to screenplay writing with his first viewing of [_Bonnie and Clyde_](link_17).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Condon#cite_note-6) In college he saw _[Sweet Charity](link_18)_ (1969), which led to "a lifelong love affair with movies that are reviled and rejected in their time."[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Condon#cite_note-columbiacollege-4)

After completing college, Condon worked as a journalist for film magazines, including _[American Film](link_19)_ and _Millimeter_. In 1981, he won "the world's most difficult film trivia quiz" sponsored by _[The Village Voice](link_20)_.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Condon#cite_note-7)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bill_Condon&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

His career as a filmmaker began with screenplays for the [independent feature](link_21)_[Strange Behavior](link_22)_ (1981), an homage to the pulp horror films of the 1950s,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Condon#cite_note-sb-8) and the [science-fiction](link_23) feature _[Strange Invaders](link_24)_ (1983), which starred [Nancy Allen](link_25) and [Wallace Shawn](link_26).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Condon#cite_note-9)

_**Gods and Monsters**_ is a 1998 [period drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_drama "Historical drama") film written and directed by [Bill Condon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Condon "Bill Condon"), based on [Christopher Bram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Bram "Christopher Bram")'s 1995 novel _[Father of Frankenstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Father\_of\_Frankenstein "Father of Frankenstein")_. The film stars [Ian McKellen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_McKellen "Ian McKellen"), [Brendan Fraser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brendan_Fraser "Brendan Fraser"), [Lynn Redgrave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynn_Redgrave "Lynn Redgrave"), [Lolita Davidovich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lolita_Davidovich "Lolita Davidovich"), and [David Dukes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Dukes "David Dukes"). Its plot is a partly fictionalized account of the last days of the life of film director [James Whale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Whale "James Whale") (McKellen), known for directing _[Frankenstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frankenstein\_(1931\_film) "Frankenstein (1931 film)")_ (1931) and _[Bride of Frankenstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bride\_of\_Frankenstein "Bride of Frankenstein")_ (1935). A veteran of [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"), the aged Whale develops a complicated relationship with his gardener, Clayton Boone (Fraser), a fictitious character originally created by Bram for the source novel.

An international co-production between the United Kingdom and the United States, _Gods and Monsters_ is produced by [Paul Colichman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Colichman "Paul Colichman"), [Gregg Fienberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregg_Fienberg "Gregg Fienberg"), and Mark R. Harris; [Clive Barker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_Barker "Clive Barker") served as executive producer.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gods_and_Monsters_(film)#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gods_and_Monsters_(film)#cite_note-5) As well as featuring reconstructions of the production of the _Bride of Frankenstein_, the film's title is derived from a scene in _Bride of Frankenstein_, in which the character [Dr. Pretorius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dr._Pretorius "Dr. Pretorius") toasts [Dr. Frankenstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dr._Frankenstein "Dr. Frankenstein"), "To a new world of gods and monsters!"

_Gods and Monsters_ was nominated for three [Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards"), including [Best Actor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Actor "Academy Award for Best Actor") for McKellen and [Best Supporting Actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Supporting_Actress "Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress") for Redgrave, and won for [Best Adapted Screenplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Adapted_Screenplay "Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gods_and_Monsters_(film)#cite_note-Oscars1999-6) Despite receiving positive reviews, the film was a [box office failure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box-office_bomb "Box-office bomb"). It was later adapted as a play of the same name which premiered in London at the [Southwark Playhouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwark_Playhouse "Southwark Playhouse") in February 2015.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gods_and_Monsters_(film)#cite_note-7)

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gods_and_Monsters_(film)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

In the 1950s, [James Whale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Whale "James Whale"), the director of _[Frankenstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frankenstein\_(1931\_film) "Frankenstein (1931 film)")_ and _[Bride of Frankenstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bride\_of\_Frankenstein "Bride of Frankenstein")_, has retired. Whale lives with his long-time housemaid, Hanna, who loyally cares for him but disapproves of his [homosexuality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homosexuality "Homosexuality"). He has suffered a series of [strokes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stroke "Stroke") that have left him fragile and tormented by memories: growing up as a poor outcast, his tragic [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") service, and the filming of _Bride of Frankenstein_. Whale slips into his past and indulges in his fantasies, reminiscing about gay pool parties and sexually teasing a slightly embarrassed, starstruck fan. He battles [depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Depression_(mood) "Depression (mood)"), and at times contemplates [suicide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suicide "Suicide"), as he realizes his life, his attractiveness, and his health are slipping away.

Whale befriends his young, handsome gardener, Clayton Boone, and the two begin a sometimes uneasy friendship as Boone poses for Whale's sketches. The two men bond while discussing their lives and dealing with Whale's spells of disorientation and weakness from the strokes. Boone, impressed with Whale's fame, watches _Bride of Frankenstein_ on television as his friends mock the movie, his friendship with Whale, and Whale's intentions.

Boone assures Whale that he is straight and receives Whale's assurance that there is no sexual interest, but Boone storms out when Whale graphically discusses his sexual history. Boone later returns with the agreement that no such "locker room" discussions occur again. Boone is invited to escort Whale to a party hosted by [George Cukor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Cukor "George Cukor") for [Princess Margaret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princess_Margaret,_Countess_of_Snowdon "Princess Margaret, Countess of Snowdon"). There, a photo op has been arranged for Whale with "his Monsters": [Boris Karloff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Karloff "Boris Karloff") and [Elsa Lanchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elsa_Lanchester "Elsa Lanchester") from "ancient" movie fame. This event exacerbates Whale's depression. A sudden rainstorm becomes an excuse to leave.

Back at Whale's home, Boone needs a dry change of clothes. Whale can only find a sweater, so Boone wears a towel wrapped around his waist. Whale decides to try to sketch Boone one more time. After some minutes, he shows his sketches to Boone, disclosing that he has lost his ability to draw. To cheer him up, Boone drops his towel to pose nude. Whale makes him wear a [World War I gas mask](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I_gas_mask "World War I gas mask") and then uses the opportunity to make a sexual advance on Boone, kissing his shoulder and neck, and forcefully reaches for his genitals. An enraged Boone fights off Whale, who confesses he had planned this because he wanted Boone to kill him and relieve him of his suffering. Boone refuses, puts Whale to bed, then sleeps downstairs. The next morning, Hanna is alarmed when she cannot find Whale, prompting a search by Boone and Hanna. Boone finds Whale floating dead in the pool as a distraught Hanna runs out, clutching a [suicide note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suicide_note "Suicide note"). Boone and Hanna agree that he should disappear from the scene to avoid a scandal.

A decade later, Boone and his son, Michael, watch _Bride of Frankenstein_ on television. Michael is skeptical of his father's claim that he knew Whale, but Boone produces a sketch of the Frankenstein monster drawn by Whale, and signed, "To Clayton. Friend?". Boone later walks down a street at night in the rain, miming the movements of Frankenstein's monster.

## Reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gods_and_Monsters_(film)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Reception")]

_Gods and Monsters_ received positive reviews from critics, with McKellen's, Fraser's and Redgrave's performances singled out for particular praise. _[Time Out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time\_Out\_(company) "Time Out (company)")_ called it "not a complicated film, but warm and clever".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gods_and_Monsters_(film)#cite_note-8)

The film has a 96% rating on [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes"), based on 67 reviews, with an average rating of 8.4/10. The site's critical consensus states: "_Gods and Monsters_ is a spellbinding, confusing piece of semi-fiction, featuring fine performances; McKellen leads the way, but Redgrave and Fraser don't lag far behind."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gods_and_Monsters_(film)#cite_note-9) On [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), the film has a score of 74 out of 100, based on reviews from 32 critics, indicating "generally favorable" reviews.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gods_and_Monsters_(film)#cite_note-10)

## Real life basis

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gods_and_Monsters_(film)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Real life basis")]

James Whale had several men (and women) pose nude for him, and some of these are shown in the making-of featurette. Several of his paintings were bought by a collector and loaned to the studio for the making of this film.

Whale suffered from strokes towards the end of his life, which affected his mental abilities, and he was found dead in his pool.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gods_and_Monsters_(film)#cite_note-35) There were rumours that this was a homicide, but the evidence only pointed at suicide.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gods_and_Monsters_(film)#cite_note-36)

In the documentary included on the DVD and in interviews, novelist Christopher Bram explains that the character of Clayton Boone is completely fictitious.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gods_and_Monsters_(film)#cite_note-37)

The **Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay** (formerly known as the **Academy Award for Best Screenplay – Based on Material from Another Medium**) is the [Academy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards") for the best [screenplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screenplay "Screenplay")[adapted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_adaptation "Film adaptation") from previously established material. The most frequently adapted media are novels, but other adapted narrative formats include stage plays, musicals, short stories, TV series, and other films and film characters. All sequels are also considered adaptations by this standard, being based on the story and characters of the original film.

Prior to its current name, the award was known as the **Academy Award for Best Screenplay Based On Material From Another Medium**.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Adapted_Screenplay#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Adapted_Screenplay#cite_note-2) The Best Adapted Screenplay category has been a part of the Academy Awards since their inception.

## Superlatives

The first person to win twice in this category was [Joseph L. Mankiewicz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_L._Mankiewicz "Joseph L. Mankiewicz"), who won the award in two consecutive years, 1949 and 1950. Others to win twice in this category include [George Seaton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Seaton "George Seaton"), [Robert Bolt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Bolt "Robert Bolt") (who also won in consecutive years), [Francis Ford Coppola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Ford_Coppola "Francis Ford Coppola"), [Mario Puzo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Puzo "Mario Puzo"), [Alvin Sargent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alvin_Sargent "Alvin Sargent"), [Ruth Prawer Jhabvala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Prawer_Jhabvala "Ruth Prawer Jhabvala"), [Michael Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Wilson_(writer) "Michael Wilson (writer)"), [Alexander Payne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Payne "Alexander Payne") and [Christopher Hampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Hampton "Christopher Hampton"). Payne won both awards as part of a writing team, with [Jim Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Taylor_(writer) "Jim Taylor (writer)") for _[Sideways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sideways "Sideways")_ and [Jim Rash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Rash "Jim Rash") and [Nat Faxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nat_Faxon "Nat Faxon") for _[The Descendants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Descendants "The Descendants")_. [Michael Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Wilson_(writer) "Michael Wilson (writer)") was [blacklisted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood_blacklist "Hollywood blacklist") at the time of his second Oscar, so the award was given to a front (novelist [Pierre Boulle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Boulle "Pierre Boulle")). However, the Academy officially recognized him as the winner several years later.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Adapted_Screenplay#cite_note-oscars1-3)

[Billy Wilder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Wilder "Billy Wilder"), [Charles Brackett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Brackett "Charles Brackett"), [Paddy Chayefsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paddy_Chayefsky "Paddy Chayefsky"), [Francis Ford Coppola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Ford_Coppola "Francis Ford Coppola"), [Horton Foote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horton_Foote "Horton Foote"), [William Goldman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Goldman "William Goldman"), [Robert Benton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Benton "Robert Benton"), [Bo Goldman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bo_Goldman "Bo Goldman"), [Waldo Salt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waldo_Salt "Waldo Salt"), and the [Coen brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coen_brothers "Coen brothers") have won Oscars for both original and adapted screenplays.

[Frances Marion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frances_Marion "Frances Marion") (_[The Big House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Big\_House\_(1930\_film) "The Big House (1930 film)")_) was the first woman to win in any screenplay category, although she won for her original script for Best Writing, which then included both original and adapted screenplays before a separate award for Best Original Screenplay was introduced. [Sarah Y. Mason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Y._Mason "Sarah Y. Mason") (_[Little Women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little\_Women\_(1933\_film) "Little Women (1933 film)")_) was the first woman to win for adaptation from previously established material; she shared the award with her husband, [Victor Heerman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Heerman "Victor Heerman"). They are also the first of two married couples to win in this category;[Peter Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Jackson "Peter Jackson") and [Fran Walsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran_Walsh "Fran Walsh") (_[The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Lord\_of\_the\_Rings:\_The\_Return\_of\_the\_King "The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King")_) are the others.

[Pierre Collings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Collings "Pierre Collings") and [Sheridan Gibney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheridan_Gibney "Sheridan Gibney") (_[The Story of Louis Pasteur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Story\_of\_Louis\_Pasteur "The Story of Louis Pasteur")_) were the first to win for adapting their own work.

[Philip G. Epstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_G._Epstein "Philip G. Epstein") and [Julius J. Epstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_J._Epstein "Julius J. Epstein") (_[Casablanca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casablanca\_(film) "Casablanca (film)")_) are the first siblings to win in this category. [James Goldman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Goldman "James Goldman") (_[The Lion in Winter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Lion\_in\_Winter\_(1968\_film) "The Lion in Winter (1968 film)")_) and [William Goldman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Goldman "William Goldman") (_[All the President's Men](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All\_the\_President's\_Men\_(film) "All the President's Men (film)")_) are the first siblings to win for separate films. [Joel Coen and Ethan Coen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coen_brothers "Coen brothers") (_[No Country for Old Men](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No\_Country\_for\_Old\_Men\_(film) "No Country for Old Men (film)")_) are the third winning siblings.

[Mario Puzo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Puzo "Mario Puzo") is the one of two writers whose work has been adapted and resulted in two wins. Puzo's novel _The Godfather_ resulted in wins in 1972 and 1974 for himself and [Francis Ford Coppola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Ford_Coppola "Francis Ford Coppola"). The other is [E. M. Forster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E._M._Forster "E. M. Forster"), whose novels _[A Room with a View](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Room\_with\_a\_View "A Room with a View")_ and _[Howards End](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howards\_End "Howards End")_ resulted in wins for [Ruth Prawer Jhabvala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Prawer_Jhabvala "Ruth Prawer Jhabvala").

[Larry McMurtry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_McMurtry "Larry McMurtry") is the only person who has won for adapting someone else's work (_[Brokeback Mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brokeback\_Mountain "Brokeback Mountain")_), and whose own work has been adapted by someone else, resulting in a win (_[Terms of Endearment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terms\_of\_Endearment "Terms of Endearment")_).

[William Monahan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Monahan "William Monahan") (_[The Departed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Departed "The Departed")_) and [Sian Heder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sian_Heder "Sian Heder") (_[CODA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CODA\_(2021\_film) "CODA (2021 film)")_) are the only people who have won this award by using another full-length feature film as the credited source of the adaptation.

[Geoffrey S. Fletcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffrey_S._Fletcher "Geoffrey S. Fletcher") (_[Precious](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precious\_(film) "Precious (film)")_), [John Ridley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Ridley "John Ridley") (_[12 Years a Slave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/12\_Years\_a\_Slave\_(film) "12 Years a Slave (film)")_) and [Cord Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cord_Jefferson "Cord Jefferson") (_[American Fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American\_Fiction\_(film) "American Fiction (film)")_) are the only African-Americans to win solo in this category; Fletcher is also the first African-American to win in any writing category. [Barry Jenkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_Jenkins "Barry Jenkins") and [Tarell Alvin McCraney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarell_Alvin_McCraney "Tarell Alvin McCraney") (_[Moonlight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moonlight\_(2016\_film) "Moonlight (2016 film)")_) are the first African-American writing duo to win; [Spike Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spike_Lee "Spike Lee") and [Kevin Willmott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Willmott "Kevin Willmott") (_[BlacKkKlansman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BlacKkKlansman "BlacKkKlansman")_) are the second, although their co-writers, David Rabinowitz and [Charlie Wachtel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Wachtel "Charlie Wachtel"), are both white.

[James Ivory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Ivory "James Ivory") (_[Call Me by Your Name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Call\_Me\_by\_Your\_Name\_(film) "Call Me by Your Name (film)")_) is the oldest person to receive the award at age 89.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Adapted_Screenplay#cite_note-4) Charlie Wachtel (_[BlacKkKlansman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BlacKkKlansman "BlacKkKlansman")_) is the youngest at age 32.

[Taika Waititi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taika_Waititi "Taika Waititi") (_[Jojo Rabbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jojo\_Rabbit "Jojo Rabbit")_) is the first person of [Māori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C4%81ori_people "Māori people") descent to receive the award.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Adapted_Screenplay#cite_note-5)

[Emma Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Thompson "Emma Thompson") (_[Sense and Sensibility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sense\_and\_Sensibility\_(1995\_film) "Sense and Sensibility (1995 film)")_) is the only winner who has also won for acting.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Adapted_Screenplay#cite_note-6) Winners [Billy Bob Thornton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Bob_Thornton "Billy Bob Thornton") (_[Sling Blade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sling\_Blade\_(film) "Sling Blade (film)")_) and [John Huston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Huston "John Huston") (_[The Treasure of the Sierra Madre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Treasure\_of\_the\_Sierra\_Madre\_(film) "The Treasure of the Sierra Madre (film)")_) have been nominated for acting but not won.

[Charles Schnee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Schnee "Charles Schnee") (_[The Bad and the Beautiful](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Bad\_and\_the\_Beautiful "The Bad and the Beautiful")_), [Billy Bob Thornton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Bob_Thornton "Billy Bob Thornton") (_[Sling Blade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sling\_Blade\_(film) "Sling Blade (film)")_), and [Bill Condon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Condon "Bill Condon") (_[Gods and Monsters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gods\_and\_Monsters\_(film) "Gods and Monsters (film)")_) are the only winners whose respective films were not nominated for [Best Picture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Picture "Academy Award for Best Picture").

## Notable nominees

7.   [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Adapted_Screenplay#cite_ref-captainblood_17-0)_[Captain Blood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain\_Blood\_(1935\_film) "Captain Blood (1935 film)")_, written by [Casey Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_Robinson "Casey Robinson") from the novel _[Captain Blood: His Odyssey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain\_Blood\_(novel) "Captain Blood (novel)")_ by [Rafael Sabatini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rafael_Sabatini "Rafael Sabatini"), was not officially nominated for this award, but appears in Academy records because it placed third in voting as a write-in candidate in 1935.
8.   [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Adapted_Screenplay#cite_ref-18)The Academy also announced that Talbot Jennings, Jules Furthman, and Carey Wilson came in second and Casey Robinson third. This means Waldemar Young, John L. Balderston, Achmed Abdullah, Grover Jones, and William Slavens McNutt came in fourth.
9.   [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Adapted_Screenplay#cite_ref-nichols_19-0)[Dudley Nichols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dudley_Nichols "Dudley Nichols") refused to accept the award, but was in possession of it by 1949 according to Academy records.
10.   [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Adapted_Screenplay#cite_ref-maltz_22-0)[Michael Blankfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Blankfort "Michael Blankfort") was originally nominated as the screenwriter of _[Broken Arrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broken\_Arrow\_(1950\_film) "Broken Arrow (1950 film)")_. In 1991, research proved blacklisted [Albert Maltz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Maltz "Albert Maltz") was the screenwriter and his credit was restored. Blankfort was removed from the nomination and it was given to Maltz.
11.   [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Adapted_Screenplay#cite_ref-wilson_23-0)[Michael Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Wilson_(writer) "Michael Wilson (writer)") was originally credited as the screenwriter of _[Friendly Persuasion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friendly\_Persuasion\_(1956\_film) "Friendly Persuasion (1956 film)")_, but [Allied Artists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monogram_Pictures "Monogram Pictures"), acting in agreement with the [Screen Writers Guild](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screen_Writers_Guild "Screen Writers Guild"), removed his credit because he was blacklisted. Early in 1957, the Academy revised its bylaws so the film would be eligible for a writing nomination without naming Wilson as a nominee. _Friendly Persuasion_ was initially announced a nominee without a writer's name attached. The Academy's Board of Governors voted to strike the nomination altogether and it was not included on the final ballot. The Board of Governors, however, reinstated the nomination with Wilson's name attached in 2002.
12.   [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Adapted_Screenplay#cite_ref-kwai_24-0)[Pierre Boulle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Boulle "Pierre Boulle") was credited as the screenwriter of _[The Bridge on the River Kwai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Bridge\_on\_the\_River\_Kwai "The Bridge on the River Kwai")_ and ultimately won the award. Blacklisted writers [Michael Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Wilson_(writer) "Michael Wilson (writer)") and [Carl Foreman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Foreman "Carl Foreman"), who actually wrote the screenplay, were awarded [posthumous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_posthumous_Academy_Award_winners_and_nominees "List of posthumous Academy Award winners and nominees") Oscars by the Academy's Board of Governors in 1984.
13.   [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Adapted_Screenplay#cite_ref-young_25-0)Due to blacklisting, Young wrote under the pseudonym Nathan E. Douglas.
14.   [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Adapted_Screenplay#cite_ref-wilson2_26-0)In 1995, research proved blacklisted [Michael Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Wilson_(writer) "Michael Wilson (writer)") was also a screenwriter of _[Lawrence of Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence\_of\_Arabia\_(film) "Lawrence of Arabia (film)")_. He was added as a nominee by the Academy's Board of Governors.
15.   [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Adapted_Screenplay#cite_ref-vazak_27-0)_[Greystoke: The Legend of Tarzan, Lord of the Apes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greystoke:\_The\_Legend\_of\_Tarzan,\_Lord\_of\_the\_Apes "Greystoke: The Legend of Tarzan, Lord of the Apes")_ was initially adapted by screenwriter [Robert Towne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Towne "Robert Towne"), but he removed his name from the credits because he was unhappy with co-writer Michael Austin's alterations and the finished film itself. He instead used the pseudonym P.H. Vazak, the name of his late Hungarian sheepdog.
16.   [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Adapted_Screenplay#cite_ref-kaufman_29-0)Screenwriter [Charlie Kaufman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Kaufman "Charlie Kaufman") is a character in his own script for _[Adaptation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adaptation\_(film) "Adaptation (film)")_, as is his fictional twin brother Donald. The nonexistent Donald was credited as a screenwriter and was nominated for an Academy Award. The film's end credits claimed he had died during pre-production.

_**The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn – Part 2**_ is a 2012 American [romantic fantasy film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romantic_fantasy_film "Romantic fantasy film"), directed by [Bill Condon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Condon "Bill Condon"), and written by [Melissa Rosenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melissa_Rosenberg "Melissa Rosenberg"), based on [the 2008 novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breaking_Dawn "Breaking Dawn"). It is the fifth and final installment in [_The Twilight Saga_ film series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga_(film_series)#Films "The Twilight Saga (film series)"). The film features [Kristen Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kristen_Stewart "Kristen Stewart"), [Robert Pattinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Pattinson "Robert Pattinson"), and [Taylor Lautner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Lautner "Taylor Lautner") reprising their roles from the previous films, with the [ensemble cast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ensemble_cast "Ensemble cast") also including [Billy Burke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Burke_(actor) "Billy Burke (actor)"), [Peter Facinelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Facinelli "Peter Facinelli"), [Elizabeth Reaser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Reaser "Elizabeth Reaser"), [Kellan Lutz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kellan_Lutz "Kellan Lutz"), [Nikki Reed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikki_Reed "Nikki Reed"), [Jackson Rathbone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_Rathbone "Jackson Rathbone"), [Ashley Greene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashley_Greene "Ashley Greene"), [Michael Sheen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Sheen "Michael Sheen"), and [Dakota Fanning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dakota_Fanning "Dakota Fanning"). In the film, Bella, now a vampire, aligns with the Cullens, the werewolves, and other allies to face [the Volturi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Volturi "The Volturi"), who view her half-human, half-vampire child as a possible threat.

[Summit Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summit_Entertainment "Summit Entertainment") announced that _Breaking Dawn_ would be adapted into a two-part film on June 10, 2010. [Principal photography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_photography "Principal photography") for both parts began on November 1, 2010, and wrapped on April 22, 2011. The second part was shot in [Baton Rouge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baton_Rouge "Baton Rouge"), [New Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans "New Orleans") and [Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vancouver "Vancouver").

_The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn – Part 2_ premiered at the [Nokia Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peacock_Theater "Peacock Theater") in Los Angeles on November 12, 2012, and was theatrically released in the United States on November 16, by Summit Entertainment. The film received mixed reviews from critics and grossed $868 million, becoming the [sixth-highest-grossing film of 2012](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_in_film#Highest-grossing_films "2012 in film") and the highest-grossing of the series. The film received eleven nominations at the [33rd Golden Raspberry Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/33rd_Golden_Raspberry_Awards "33rd Golden Raspberry Awards") and won seven, including [Worst Picture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Raspberry_Award_for_Worst_Picture "Golden Raspberry Award for Worst Picture").

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

The film continues from the events of the [previous film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_1# "The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn – Part 1"), as [Bella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bella_Swan "Bella Swan"), who has just given birth, awakens from her human-to-vampire transformation. After her vampire husband Edward Cullen helps her tame her initial thirst for blood, Bella is introduced to their daughter [Renesmee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renesmee_Cullen "Renesmee Cullen"). The rest of the Cullens and Bella's werewolf friend [Jacob](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Black "Jacob Black") stay nearby, and when Jacob acts possessively towards Renesmee, Bella learns he has "imprinted" on her, a werewolf phenomenon that makes Jacob and Renesmee soul-mates.

Meanwhile, Bella's father, [Charlie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Swan_(Twilight) "Charlie Swan (Twilight)"), has been trying to contact the Cullens for updates on Bella's health. [Carlisle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlisle_Cullen "Carlisle Cullen"), the Cullen patriarch and a medical doctor, announces that they have to leave [Forks, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forks,_Washington "Forks, Washington"), to protect their identities.

Jacob, desperate not to lose Renesmee, visits Charlie and tells him that Bella is alive and vaguely describes that she has transformed, revealing his wolf form to Charlie to persuade him to stop asking further questions. Charlie goes to the Cullen house to see Bella and meet Renesmee. He accepts that Bella is now recovered but somehow different, though he does not know what has changed or where Renesmee came from, instead accepting she is "adopted".

Several months pass with Carlisle monitoring Renesmee's rapid growth. The vampire Irina spots Renesmee in the forest and mistakenly assumes she is an "[immortal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immortality "Immortality") child": a type of vampire transformed in childhood who, because it cannot be reasoned with or trained, sucks the blood out of humans uncontrollably. The creation of such children is outlawed by the vampire leadership, [the Volturi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Volturi "The Volturi"), and anyone caught with one is executed on the spot. Irina reports the supposed crime to the Volturi.

After Edward's sister [Alice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Cullen_(Character) "Alice Cullen (Character)"), who can see glimpses of the future, experiences a vision of the Volturi and Irina coming to kill the Cullens, she instructs the others to gather as many witnesses as they can to testify that Renesmee is not an immortal child.

As the Volturi serve punishments swiftly, the Cullens and their werewolf allies prepare for a possible battle. Bella soon realizes she has a special ability: a powerful mental shield that had protected her from [Edward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Cullen "Edward Cullen")'s mind-reading even when she was human, which she is taught to extend to protect others from vampire superpowers.

The army of the Volturi arrives in Forks, led by Aro, who can read people's minds by touching them. Seeing the Cullens alongside their witnesses and allies, the Volturi hesitate. The Cullens are able to prove to Aro that Renesmee is not an immortal child.

However, the Volturi are eager to subdue the Cullens to [forcibly enlist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impressment "Impressment") their talented members, so they [summarily execute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summary_execution "Summary execution") Irina for her mistake to provoke the Cullens into battle. But before an all-out fight breaks out, Alice appears in time to give Aro her vision of the future if fighting ensues.

In Alice's vision, Carlisle, Jasper, Aro, and several others on all sides are killed in a violent battle while Jacob and Renesmee escape. Aro, despite being afraid of the vision, still wants to execute Renesmee as she might be a threat to the vampires' secrecy.

Alice reveals their final witness, a [Mapuche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mapuche "Mapuche") man from South America, who is a half-human half-vampire, just like Renesmee. He proves that he is not a threat, supporting the notion that Renesmee is not one either. The Volturi unhappily leave, Aro concluding that there will be no battle today.

Back at the Cullen home, Alice glimpses the future, seeing Edward and Bella greeting Jacob and a fully matured Renesmee, also a couple, on a sun-dappled beach. Edward reads Alice's mind and feels relieved that Renesmee has Jacob to protect her.

Alone in their favorite meadow, Bella pushes her mental shield away and finally allows Edward to see into her mind, showing him every moment they have shared together in a [montage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montage_(filmmaking) "Montage (filmmaking)"). They kiss after Bella tells him, "nobody has ever loved anybody as much as I love you", and he romantically responds "There’s one exception".

## Production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Production")]

See also: [The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn – Part 1 §Production](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_1#Production "The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn – Part 1")

### Development

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Development")]

On June 10, 2010, [Summit Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summit_Entertainment "Summit Entertainment") announced that a two-part adaptation of the novel _[Breaking Dawn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breaking\_Dawn "Breaking Dawn")_ would start filming in November and made clear that all major actors would return for both parts.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-BD2-5)

### Pre-production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Pre-production")]

By August 2010, screenwriter [Melissa Rosenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melissa_Rosenberg "Melissa Rosenberg") said that the scripts for _Part 1_ and _2_ were 75 to 85 percent completed. She found the greatest challenge in writing the scripts to be the final sequence of _Part 2_, explaining, "The final battle sequence is a big challenge because it lasts 25 pages. It's almost an entire three-act story in and of itself. You have to track [keep it all in one setting] hundreds of characters. It's an enormous challenge to choreograph on the page and for [Bill [Condon]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Condon "Bill Condon") to choreograph on the stage." She had written various drafts of the scene but, at the time, hadn't revised or discussed them with Condon yet. She said, "That's the next big hurdle to sit down with the stunt coordinator and create the ballet. It's a lot of work. I'm exhausted, but we're intent on making them the best scripts yet."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-6) Producer [Wyck Godfrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyck_Godfrey "Wyck Godfrey") called _Part 2_ "an [action film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_film "Action film") in terms of life-and-death stakes" and said that in _Part 1_ "there are the pangs of newlywed tension that occur that are relatable even in a [fantasy film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fantasy_film "Fantasy film"). Marriage is not quite the experience that they thought it was."[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-7)

Godfrey considered releasing the second film in [3D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3-D_film "3-D film") to differentiate between the time before and after Bella becomes a vampire, an idea originally proposed for _[The Twilight Saga: Eclipse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Twilight\_Saga:\_Eclipse "The Twilight Saga: Eclipse")_, but said that the decision was up to Condon. However, he said that if the second film were to be released in 3D, he would like to shoot it with the proper equipment in "real" 3D as was done with _[Avatar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avatar\_(2009\_film) "Avatar (2009 film)")_ (2009), not convert it into 3D in post-production as was done with _[Clash of the Titans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash\_of\_the\_Titans\_(2010\_film) "Clash of the Titans (2010 film)")_ (2010).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-Yamato-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-9)

### Filming

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Filming")]

Principal photography started on November 1, 2010, and wrapped on April 22, 2011, ending [the franchise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga_(film_series) "The Twilight Saga (film series)")'s three years of production since March 2008. Filming was shot on location in [Baton Rouge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baton_Rouge,_Louisiana "Baton Rouge, Louisiana") and [New Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans "New Orleans"), [Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana "Louisiana"); and [Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vancouver "Vancouver"), Canada. Filming also occurred at [Raleigh Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Famous_Players_Film_Company "Famous Players Film Company") in Baton Rouge.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-10)

On the subject of the final day and her final moment as Bella, Stewart stated, "After that scene, my true final scene, I felt like I could shoot up into the night sky and every pore of my body would shoot light. I felt lighter than I've ever felt in my life."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-11)

In April 2012, the crew and some of the cast, including Pattinson and Stewart, returned for reshoots to pick up some additional shots for technical work. These re-shoots did not include any new scenes or dialogue.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-12)

### Special effects

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Special effects")]

[Tippett Studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tippett_Studio "Tippett Studio") first began working on the CGI ([computer-generated imagery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer-generated_imagery "Computer-generated imagery")) wolves in February 2009 for _[The Twilight Saga: New Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Twilight\_Saga:\_New\_Moon "The Twilight Saga: New Moon")_, and the look of the creatures has evolved, becoming more photo-real over the course of the saga, with the input of three different directors. "It's a subtle balance of just how anthropomorphic these wolves are," says Eric Leven. "Bill [Condon] wanted to make sure that we had a sense of the human or the shapeshifter in there. Finding that balance of how much of a human performance versus an animal performance was important for Bill."

Leven adds, "Bill has always treated the wolves as characters and never as computer-generated things, and directs them in the same way he'd direct any actor. He would always give us direction like Sam should be angrier. It's the best way to work. His treating these creatures as characters, instead of just computer bits, was really great."

"Because we've been working on this franchise for such a prolonged period of time, we've been able to improve the look from show to show," comments [Phil Tippett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Tippett "Phil Tippett"). "Wolves generally are pretty darn clean and since Bill wanted the wolves rangier, that means a lot more fur matting and clumping, like they've lived out in the woods. We edged towards something a bit more feral."

"However, there is also a balance between look and technology," adds Tippett. "The body count of the wolves escalates and because we're adding a great deal more hair to get the right texture, that fur really ups the rendering time. We've gone from four wolves to eight to twelve, to sixteen in _Part 2_. So we have to be very careful about that balance because it takes hundreds of hours to render each wolf."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-13)
