It was revealed in January 2012 that the soundtrack for _Part 2_ had already started production.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-Breaking_Dawn_Part_2_Soundtrack-14) Confirmed for the soundtrack in advance were "Heart of Stone" by [Iko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iko_(band) "Iko (band)"), which plays when Edward and Bella are talking in the cottage after finding Alice's note and "Where I Come From" by [Passion Pit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passion_Pit "Passion Pit"), which will play when Bella wakes up from her transformation.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-15) The lead single from the soundtrack is "[The Forgotten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Forgotten_(Green_Day_song) "The Forgotten (Green Day song)")", performed by the American rock band [Green Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Day "Green Day"). "A Thousand Years, Pt. 2" by the American singer [Christina Perri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christina_Perri "Christina Perri") is also featured on the soundtrack album.

[Carter Burwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carter_Burwell "Carter Burwell"), the composer of _[Twilight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twilight\_(soundtrack)#Twilight:\_The\_Score "Twilight (soundtrack)")_ and _[Breaking Dawn: Part 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Twilight\_Saga:\_Breaking\_Dawn\_%E2%80%93\_Part\_1\_(soundtrack)#The\_Twilight\_Saga:\_Breaking\_Dawn\_%E2%80%93\_Part\_1\_(The\_Score) "The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn – Part 1 (soundtrack)")_, returned to score the final installment of the series.

## Release

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Release")]

Fans registered online for a chance and circa 1,500 people spent the weekend at a temporary tent city on Friday ahead of Monday's premiere screening, in the street in front of [Staples Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staples_Center "Staples Center") and across [L.A. Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L.A._Live "L.A. Live") plaza, outside of _Nokia Theatre L.A. Live_, now [Peacock Theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peacock_Theater "Peacock Theater") in Los Angeles.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-thr/388546-16)

### Box office

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Box office")]

_The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn – Part 2_ earned $293 million in North America and $575 million in other territories, for a worldwide total of $868 million.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-bom-4) The film is the [sixth-highest-grossing film of 2012](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_in_film "2012 in film"), and the highest-grossing film of the _Twilight_ series. It had a $340.9 million worldwide opening, which was the eighth-largest ever, the largest for the _Twilight_ franchise, and the largest for a film released outside the summer period.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-17)

In North America, the film grossed $30.4 million in Thursday night and midnight showings, achieving the third-highest midnight gross[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-19) and the highest midnight gross of the franchise.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-21)_Breaking Dawn – Part 2_ made $71.2 million on its opening day, which is the sixth-highest opening- and single-day gross as well as the third-highest of the franchise.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-22) For its opening weekend, the movie earned $141.1 million,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-23) which is the 13th-highest-grossing opening weekend of all time,[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-25) the second-highest-grossing of the franchise,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-26) the third-largest November opening,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-27) and the fourth-largest opening of 2012.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-28) It retained first place in its second weekend by dropping 69.1% with a gross of $43.6 million over the three-day weekend and made a total of $64.4 million over the five-day Thanksgiving holiday weekend.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-29) In its third weekend, _Breaking Dawn Part – 2_ held onto the number one spot again by dropping 60.1% and grossing $17.4 million.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-30) It became the third-highest-grossing film of the franchise behind _Eclipse_ and _New Moon_.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-31)

Outside North America, the film opened on Wednesday, November 14, 2012, in six countries earning $13.8 million. By Thursday, it had opened in 37 territories, earning $38.8 million. In all territories, it opened with similar or higher earnings than its immediate predecessor.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-32) Through its first Friday, it earned $91.0 million, after expanding to 61 territories.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-34) By the end of its opening weekend (Wednesday–Sunday), it scored a series-best $199.5 million opening from 61 territories on 12,812 screens. This is the eighth-largest opening outside North America and the largest 2012 opening.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-35)[IMAX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMAX "IMAX") showings generated $3 million from 82 locations.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-36) The film's largest openings were recorded in the UK, Ireland, and Malta ($25.2 million), Russia and the [CIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Independent_States "Commonwealth of Independent States") ($22.0 million), and France and the [Maghreb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maghreb "Maghreb") region ($17.9 million).[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-BOM-ovrs-37) In Spain, it set a three-day opening-weekend record with $11.9 million.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-38) In total earnings, its three highest-grossing markets after North America are the UK, Ireland, and Malta ($57.9 million), Brazil ($54.2 million), and Russia and the CIS ($42.8 million).[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-BOM-ovrs-37)

## Reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Reception")]

On [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes"), the film has a 49% approval rating and an average score of 5.3/10 based on 197 reviews. The consensus states: "It's the most entertaining _Twilight_, but that's not enough to make _Breaking Dawn Part 2_ worth watching for filmgoers who don't already count themselves among the franchise converts."[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-rottentomatoes.com-39) On [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), it has a weighted average score of 52 out of 100 based on reviews from 31 critics.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-40) Audiences polled by [CinemaScore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CinemaScore "CinemaScore") gave it an average rating of "A".[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-41)

Todd McCarthy of _[The Hollywood Reporter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Hollywood\_Reporter "The Hollywood Reporter")_ wrote, "The final installment of the immortal Bella/Edward romance will give its breathlessly awaiting international audience just what it wants".[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-42)[Owen Gleiberman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen_Gleiberman "Owen Gleiberman") of _[Entertainment Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment\_Weekly "Entertainment Weekly")_ said, "_Breaking Dawn: Part 2_ starts off slow but gathers momentum, and that's because, with Bella and Edward united against the Volturi, the picture has a real threat".[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-43) Sara Stewart of the _[New York Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_York\_Post "New York Post")_ wrote, "Finally, someone took the source material at its terribly written word and stopped treating the whole affair so seriously".[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-44) Justin Chang of _[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety\_(magazine) "Variety (magazine)")_ praised the performance of Stewart by saying, "No longer a mopey, lower-lip-biting [emo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emo "Emo") girl, this Bella is twitchy, feral, formidable and fully energized, a goddess even among her exalted bloodsucker brethren".[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-45) Manohla Dargis of _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ said, "Despite the slow start Mr. Condon closes the series in fine, smooth style. He gives fans all the lovely flowers, conditioned hair and lightly erotic, dreamy kisses they deserve".[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-46)

[Roger Ebert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Ebert "Roger Ebert") of the _[Chicago Sun-Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago\_Sun-Times "Chicago Sun-Times")_ gave the film two-and-a-half stars out of four, saying "its audience, which takes these films very seriously indeed, will drink deeply of its blood. The sensational closing sequence cannot be accused of leaving a single loophole, not even some of those we didn't know were there". He concluded by saying, "_Breaking Dawn, Part 2_ must be one of the more serious entries in any major movie franchise... it bit the bullet, and I imagine fans will be pleased."[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-rogerebert.com-47) Helen O'Hara of _[Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire\_(film\_magazine) "Empire (film magazine)")_ gave the film a mixed review and said, "Fans will be left on a high; other viewers will be confused but generally entertained by a saga whose romance is matched only by its weirdness".[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-48)

## Home media

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Home media")]

_The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn – Part 2_ was released on [DVD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DVD "DVD") and [Blu-ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blu-ray "Blu-ray") on March 2, 2013.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-49) As of June 1, 2014, _Breaking Dawn: Part 2_ has sold 4,810,249 DVDs along with 1,224,869 Blu-ray Discs for $71,418,469 and $24,472,107, respectively, totaling $99,195,325.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-50)

## Spin-offs

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Spin-offs")]

In September 2016, [Lionsgate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionsgate_Films "Lionsgate Films") co-chairman Patrick Wachsberger stated that a sequel was "a possibility", but would only go ahead if Stephenie Meyer wanted to do one.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-51) On August 8, 2017, _[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety\_(magazine) "Variety (magazine)")_ reported that Lionsgate CEO [Jon Feltheimer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Feltheimer "Jon Feltheimer") has interest in having spinoffs made for _The Twilight Saga_, and wants to create a writers' room to explore the idea.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_Breaking_Dawn_%E2%80%93_Part_2#cite_note-52)

## From today's featured article

[![Image 4: Sarah Goodridge](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/Miniature_Painting%2C_Sarah_Goodridge_Self_Portrait.jpg/120px-Miniature_Painting%2C_Sarah_Goodridge_Self_Portrait.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Miniature_Painting,_Sarah_Goodridge_Self_Portrait.jpg "Sarah Goodridge")

Sarah Goodridge

_**[Beauty Revealed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty\_Revealed "Beauty Revealed")**_ is an 1828 [self-portrait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-portrait "Self-portrait") watercolor by the American artist [Sarah Goodridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Goodridge "Sarah Goodridge")_(pictured)_. Depicting Goodridge's bared breasts surrounded by white cloth, the [portrait miniature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portrait_miniature "Portrait miniature") is painted on a piece of [ivory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivory "Ivory"). It was originally backed with paper and is now in a modern frame. Goodridge presented the breasts as youthful and individualized, employing a frontal view that showed the area from the collarbone to just underneath the breasts. She gave the portrait to statesman [Daniel Webster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Webster "Daniel Webster"), who was a frequent subject and possible lover, following the death of his wife; she may have intended to provoke him into marrying her. Although Webster married someone else, his family held onto the portrait until the 1980s, when it was auctioned at [Christie's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christie's "Christie's") and purchased by Gloria and Richard Manney. The painting was acquired by the [Metropolitan Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Museum_of_Art "Metropolitan Museum of Art") in 2006. It has been read as a work of [erotica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erotica "Erotica"), as well as an expression of Goodridge's confident sexuality. _(**[Full article...](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty\_Revealed "Beauty Revealed")**)_

## Today's featured picture

[![Image 8: Humpback whale](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Humpback_whale_%28Megaptera_novaeangliae%29_with_calf_Moorea_2.jpg/500px-Humpback_whale_%28Megaptera_novaeangliae%29_with_calf_Moorea_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Humpback_whale_(Megaptera_novaeangliae)_with_calf_Moorea_2.jpg "Humpback whale")
The **[humpback whale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humpback_whale "Humpback whale")** (_Megaptera novaeangliae_) is a species of [baleen whale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baleen_whale "Baleen whale") in the [rorqual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rorqual "Rorqual") family, Balaenopteridae. It is found in oceans worldwide and migrates thousands of kilometres between polar feeding grounds and tropical breeding areas. The adult humpback can weigh up to 40 tonnes and typically measures 14–15 metres (46–49 ft) in length, with longer individuals up to 17 metres (56 ft) recorded. Distinguished by its unusually long [pectoral fins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fish_fin#AnchPectoral "Fish fin") and [tubercles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tubercle "Tubercle") on its head, the humpback is known for [breaching and other distinctive surface behaviors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cetacean_surfacing_behaviour "Cetacean surfacing behaviour"), as well as the complex songs produced by males, lasting up to 33 minutes. It feeds mainly on krill and small fish, sometimes using cooperative [bubble-net feeding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubble-net_feeding "Bubble-net feeding") techniques. Driven close to extinction by commercial whaling, the species has recovered substantially since the 1960s, although entanglement in fishing gear and ship collisions remain significant threats. This humpback whale with calf was photographed off [Moʼorea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mo%CA%BCorea "Moʼorea"), an island in French Polynesia.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Two books on human sexual behavior by Alfred Kinsey and others

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/7/72/Kinsey-Male.jpg/250px-Kinsey-Male.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kinsey-Male.jpg)

The 1948 first edition of _Sexual Behavior in the Human Male_, the first of the two Kinsey Reports

The **Kinsey Reports** are two scholarly books on [human sexual behavior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_sexual_behavior "Human sexual behavior"), _**Sexual Behavior in the Human Male**_[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-1) (1948) and _**Sexual Behavior in the Human Female**_[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-2) (1953), written by [Alfred Kinsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey "Alfred Kinsey"), [Wardell Pomeroy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wardell_Pomeroy "Wardell Pomeroy"), [Clyde Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clyde_Martin "Clyde Martin"), and (for _Sexual Behavior in the Human Female_) [Paul Gebhard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Gebhard "Paul Gebhard") and published by [W.B. Saunders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saunders_(publisher) "Saunders (publisher)"). Kinsey was a [zoologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoologist "Zoologist") at [Indiana University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_University_(Bloomington) "Indiana University (Bloomington)") and the founder of the [Kinsey Institute for Research in Sex, Gender, and Reproduction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute_for_Research_in_Sex,_Gender,_and_Reproduction "Kinsey Institute for Research in Sex, Gender, and Reproduction") (more widely known as the Kinsey Institute). Jean Brown, Cornelia Christenson, Dorothy Collins, Hedwig Leser, and Eleanor Roehr were all acknowledged as research assistants on the book's title page. Alice Field was a sex researcher, [criminologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criminologist "Criminologist"), and [social scientist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_scientist "Social scientist") in New York; as a research associate for _Sexual Behavior in the Human Female_, she provided assistance with legal questions.

The sociological data underlying the analysis and conclusions found in _Sexual Behavior in the Human Male_ was collected from approximately 5,300 men over a fifteen-year period. _Sexual Behavior in the Human Female_ was based on personal interviews with approximately 6,000 women. In the latter, Kinsey analyzed data for the frequency with which women participate in various types of sexual activity and looked at how factors such as age, social-economic status, and religious adherence influence sexual behavior.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-3)

The two best-selling books were immediately controversial, both within the scientific community and the general public, because they challenged conventional beliefs about [sexuality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_sexuality "Human sexuality") and discussed subjects that had previously been [taboo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taboo "Taboo").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-4) The validity of Kinsey's methods were sometimes called into question. Despite this, Kinsey's work is considered pioneering and some of the best-known sex research of all time.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-Lehmiller-5):29

## Background and method

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kinsey_Reports&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background and method")]

Surveys of sexual behavior were unprecedented in American society, although [Clelia Duel Mosher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clelia_Duel_Mosher "Clelia Duel Mosher") had conducted a survey of Victorian women. Qualitative studies had been done by [Havelock Ellis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Havelock_Ellis "Havelock Ellis") and [Magnus Hirschfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnus_Hirschfeld "Magnus Hirschfeld"), but these researchers did not attempt to gather quantitative data. Kinsey built up academic prestige over decades of study and gained the support of [Rockefeller family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockefeller_family "Rockefeller family")-backed philanthropists for a large-scale analysis. His research was unprecedented in scale, involving 18,000 interviews.

Data was gathered primarily by means of [subjective report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subjective_report "Subjective report") interviews, conducted according to a structured questionnaire memorized by the experimenters (but not marked on the response sheet in any way).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-Ericksen1998-6) The response sheets were encoded in a way to maintain the confidentiality of the respondents, being entered on a blank grid using response symbols defined in advance.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-Ericksen1998-6) The data were later computerized for processing. All of this material, including the original researchers' notes, remains available from the [Kinsey Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute_for_Research_in_Sex,_Gender_and_Reproduction "Kinsey Institute for Research in Sex, Gender and Reproduction") to qualified researchers who demonstrate a need to view such materials. The institute also allows researchers to use statistical software in order to analyze the data.

Parts of the Kinsey Reports regarding diversity in [sexual orientations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_orientation "Sexual orientation") are frequently used to support the common estimate of 10% for [homosexuality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homosexuality "Homosexuality") in the general population. Instead of three categories ([heterosexual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heterosexuality "Heterosexuality"), [bisexual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bisexuality "Bisexuality") and [homosexual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homosexuality "Homosexuality")), a seven-point [Kinsey scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_scale "Kinsey scale") system was used.

The reports also state that nearly 46% of the male subjects had "reacted" sexually to persons of both sexes in the course of their adult lives, and 37% had at least one homosexual experience.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-7) 11.6% of white men (ages 20–35) were given a rating of 3 (about equal heterosexual and homosexual experience/response) throughout their adult lives.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-8) The study also reported that 10% of American men surveyed were "more or less exclusively homosexual for at least three years between the ages of 16 and 55" (in the 5 to 6 range on the Kinsey scale).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-9)

7% of single women (ages 20–35) and 4% of previously married women (ages 20–35) were given a rating of 3 (about equal heterosexual and homosexual experience/response) on Kinsey Heterosexual-Homosexual Rating Scale for this period of their lives.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-10) 2 to 6% of women, aged 20–35, were more or less exclusively homosexual in experience/response,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-11) and 1 to 3% of unmarried women aged 20–35 were exclusively homosexual in experience/response.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-12)

### Kinsey scale

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kinsey_Reports&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Kinsey scale")]

Main article: [Kinsey scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_scale "Kinsey scale")

The Kinsey scale, ranging from 0 to 6, represents a person's sexuality, with 0 being completely heterosexual and 6 completely homosexual. An additional category, X, was mentioned to describe those who had "no socio-sexual contacts or reactions,"[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-13) which has been cited by scholars to mean [asexuality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asexuality "Asexuality").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-Stange-14) The scale was first published in _Sexual Behavior in the Human Male_ (1948) by Kinsey, [Wardell Pomeroy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wardell_Pomeroy "Wardell Pomeroy") and others, and was also prominent in the complementary work _Sexual Behavior in the Human Female_ (1953). Introducing the scale, Kinsey wrote:

> Males do not represent two discrete populations, heterosexual and homosexual. The world is not to be divided into sheep and goats. It is a fundamental of taxonomy that nature rarely deals with discrete categories [...] The living world is a continuum in each and every one of its aspects. While emphasising the continuity of the gradations between exclusively heterosexual and exclusively homosexual histories, it has seemed desirable to develop some sort of classification which could be based on the relative amounts of heterosexual and homosexual experience or response in each history... An individual may be assigned a position on this scale, for each period in his life. [...] A seven-point scale comes nearer to showing the many gradations that actually exist.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-15)

The scale is as follows:

| Rating | Description |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | Exclusively heterosexual |
| 1 | Predominantly heterosexual, only incidentally homosexual |
| 2 | Predominantly heterosexual, but more than incidentally homosexual |
| 3 | Equally heterosexual and homosexual |
| 4 | Predominantly homosexual, but more than incidentally heterosexual |
| 5 | Predominantly homosexual, only incidentally heterosexual |
| 6 | Exclusively homosexual |
| X | No socio-sexual contacts or reactions |

*   **Men**: 11.6% of white men aged 20–35 were given a rating of 3 for this period of their lives.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-16)
*   **Women**: 7% of single women aged 20–35 and 4% of previously married women aged 20–35 were given a rating of 3 for this period of their lives.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-17) 2 to 6% of women, aged 20–35, were given a rating of 5[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-18) and 1 to 3% of unmarried women aged 20–35 were rated as 6.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-19)

### Marital coitus

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kinsey_Reports&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Marital coitus")]

The average frequency of marital sex reported by women was 2.8 times a week in the late teens, 2.2 times a week by age 30, and 1.0 times a week by age 50.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-20) Kinsey estimated that approximately 50% of all married men had [extramarital sex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extramarital_sex "Extramarital sex") at some time during their married lives.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-21) Among the sample, 26% of women had extramarital sex by their forties. Between 1 in 6 and 1 in 10 women from age 26 to 50 were engaged in extramarital sex.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-22) However, Kinsey classified couples who have lived together for at least a year as "married", inflating the statistics for extra-marital sex.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-Kinsey,_Alfred_p._53-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-Jones,_James_H._1997-24)

## Criticism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kinsey_Reports&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Criticism")]

Kinsey's statistics in his Reports have been criticized both at the time he published and today. Although Kinsey sought to work on a more complete report involving 100,000 interviews and considered the initial 1948 publication to be a sample progress report, academics have criticized the sample selection and [sample bias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sample_bias "Sample bias") in the reports' [methodology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodology "Methodology").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-27) The main issues cited by researchers are that Kinsey did not use random sampling procedures when collecting his data, that significant portions of his samples come from prison populations and male prostitutes, and that people who volunteer to be interviewed about [taboo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taboo "Taboo") subjects are likely to create a [self-selection bias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-selection_bias "Self-selection bias"). These issues would undermine the usefulness of the sample in terms of determining the tendencies of the overall population.

### Statistics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kinsey_Reports&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Statistics")]

In 1948, the same year as the original publication, a committee of the [American Statistical Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Statistical_Association "American Statistical Association"), including notable [statisticians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistician "Statistician") such as [John Tukey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Tukey "John Tukey"), condemned the sampling procedure. In a tense meeting with Kinsey, Tukey supposedly declared that even a sample as small as three to five, chosen randomly, would be preferable to hundreds in Kinsey's sample.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-28) In 1954, leading statisticians, including [William Gemmell Cochran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Gemmell_Cochran "William Gemmell Cochran"), [Frederick Mosteller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Mosteller "Frederick Mosteller"), John Tukey, and [W. O. Jenkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._O._Jenkins?action=edit&redlink=1 "W. O. Jenkins (page does not exist)") issued for the [American Statistical Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Statistical_Association "American Statistical Association") a critique of Kinsey's 1948 _Male_ report, stating:

> Critics are justified in their objections that many of the most interesting and provocative statements in the [Kinsey 1948] book are not based on the data presented therein, and it is not made clear to the reader on what evidence the statements are based. Further, the conclusions drawn from data presented in the book are often stated by KPM [Kinsey, Pomeroy, and Martin] in much too bold and confident a manner. Taken cumulatively, these objections amount to saying that much of the writing in the book falls below the level of good scientific writing.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-29)

In response, [Paul Gebhard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Gebhard "Paul Gebhard"), Kinsey's close colleague, "Sexual Behavior in the Human Female" co-author, and successor as director of the [Kinsey Institute for Sex Research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute_for_Sex_Research "Kinsey Institute for Sex Research"),[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-nygebhard-30) cleaned the Kinsey data of purported contaminants, removing, for example, all material derived from prison populations in the basic sample.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-gebhardrelia-31) (Gebhard had, while working with Kinsey, raised serious concerns about the use of prison populations especially, but had been shot down by Kinsey at the time.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-32)) In 1979, Gebhard (with Alan B. Johnson) published _The Kinsey Data: Marginal Tabulations of the 1938–1963 Interviews Conducted by the Institute for Sex Research_. Their conclusion, to Gebhard's surprise, was that none of Kinsey's original estimates were significantly affected by this bias: that is, the prison population and male prostitutes had the same statistical tendencies as the rest of the men Kinsey interviewed. The results were summarized by historian, playwright, and gay-rights activist [Martin Duberman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Duberman "Martin Duberman"): "Instead of Kinsey's 37% (men who had at least one homosexual experience), Gebhard and Johnson came up with 36.4%; the 10% figure (men who were "more or less exclusively homosexual for at least three years between the ages of 16 and 55"), with prison inmates excluded, came to 9.9% for white, college-educated men and 12.7% for those with less education.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-MDOG-33)

Kinsey himself was extremely frustrated by the criticisms of his sampling procedures, because he maintained that there was no way to do a successful study about sex using random probability sampling.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-Gathorne-Hardy-2000a-34) As Kinsey biographer Jonathan Gathorne-Hardy points out, because of the sensitive nature of a sex study, contacting a truly random sample will garner a very high refusal rate—as modern sex studies using random sampling have shown.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-Gathorne-Hardy-2000a-34) If the study is trying to gather information about any sort of population subgroups, as Kinsey was, the small percentages of the population plus the high rates of refusal may make these subgroups effectively disappear, despite their importance to the study.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-Gathorne-Hardy-2000a-34)

> For some forty years, scientists of all persuasions have scrutinized and analyzed the two Kinsey reports. Some conclusions are close to unanimous. According to Edward Brecher, author of _The Sex Researchers_, 'Whatever their shortcomings, the Kinsey data remain today the fullest and most reliable sampling of human sexual behavior in a large population...' (Francoeur Part III 52)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-35)

### Volunteer bias

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kinsey_Reports&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Volunteer bias")]

In the 1950s, [psychologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychologist "Psychologist")[Abraham Maslow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Maslow "Abraham Maslow") stated that Kinsey did not consider "[volunteer bias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volunteer_bias "Volunteer bias")." The data represented only those volunteering to participate in discussion of taboo topics. Most Americans were reluctant to discuss the intimate details of their sex lives even with their spouses and close friends. Before the publication of Kinsey's reports, Maslow tested Kinsey's volunteers for bias. He concluded that Kinsey's sample was unrepresentative of the general population.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-36)

The charge of an over-reliance on volunteers is also critiqued in the Gathorne-Hardy biography. All surveys rely on volunteers.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-Gathorne-Hardy-2000a-34) Kinsey attempted to correct for this by gathering as many "100 percent groups" as he could—that is, collecting all (or nearly all) of the sex histories of a given group that had gathered together for reasons other than sex, such as law societies, sororities, or even a small group of hikers.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-Gathorne-Hardy-2000b-37) Kinsey would ask the president or leader of the group to agree to an interview, and then that leader's influence would get him an initial batch of volunteers from the group, a second batch who did not want to be seen volunteering but would agree to be interviewed, and then a third batch brought in by, essentially, peer pressure.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-Gathorne-Hardy-2000b-37) While all the participants were still volunteers, he got interviews and thus samples he would not have otherwise gotten. In addition, the groups themselves, though any one was not representative of the population as a whole, provided a random element while encouraging greater participation.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-Gathorne-Hardy-2000b-37) These "100 percent groups" made up about a quarter of Kinsey's overall data.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-Gathorne-Hardy-2000b-37)

### Other criticisms

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kinsey_Reports&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Other criticisms")]

More recent researchers have also criticized Kinsey's sampling methods and believe that he overestimated the frequency of nonheterosexual behaviors and attractions, because the Kinsey Reports show higher frequencies of homosexuality than more modern studies do.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-Lehmiller-5):147[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-Bailey16-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-Balthazart-39):9 This may be explained in part by Kinsey's interview style, which focused on in-depth conversations with subjects carried out by himself or highly trained members of his team; they emphasized creating rapport with the interviewee and making them feel comfortable and secure.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-Gathorne-Hardy-2000c-40) Modern interviewers tend to be less thoroughly trained and emphasize scientific detachment, which may make respondents less likely to share sensitive personal details.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-Gathorne-Hardy-2000c-40)

It has been suggested that some data in the reports could not have been obtained without collaborations with pedophiles.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-41) The Kinsey Institute denies this charge, though it acknowledges that men who have had sexual experiences with children were interviewed, with Kinsey balancing what he saw as the need for their anonymity to solicit "honest answers on such taboo subjects" against the likelihood that their crimes would continue.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-kinsey-inst-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-Welsh-Huggins-43)

Sociologist Edward Laumann stated that the Kinsey Reports were limited to the biology of sex and lacked psychological and clinical information and analysis and that this "meant that sex research did not move into the mainstream of academic credibility. People took their reputations in their hands if they attempted to pursue it."[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-www.cbsnews.com-2003-44) Laumann also acknowledged that "The Kinsey report was a cultural event of enormous consequence."[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-www.cbsnews.com-2003-44)

American literary critic [Lionel Trilling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionel_Trilling "Lionel Trilling"), besides criticizing the methodology for the interviews, and the lack of cultural perspective of Kinsey's approach, made the following comment on the public for the reports: "With this public, science is authority. It has been trained to accept heedlessly 'what science says', which it conceives to be a unitary utterance."[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-45)

## Context and significance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kinsey_Reports&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Context and significance")]

Only 5,000 copies of _Sexual Behavior in the Human Male_ were initially printed in 1948, and its success surprised the publisher. The popular late-1948 [Cole Porter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cole_Porter "Cole Porter") song "[Too Darn Hot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Too_Darn_Hot "Too Darn Hot")" makes reference to it.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-46) Prior to the release of the second report in 1953, the first book had sold over 265,000 copies in the United States.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-47) Together, the Kinsey Reports sold three-quarters of a million copies, were translated into thirteen languages and may be considered as belonging to the most successful and influential scientific books of the 20th century.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-Irvine-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-Zastrow-49) They were associated with a change in the [public perception of sexuality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_revolution "Sexual revolution"), in conjunction with [Masters and Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masters_and_Johnson "Masters and Johnson")'s texts about their 1960s investigations into the [physiology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physiology "Physiology") of sex, breaking taboos and misapprehensions.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-Irvine-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports#cite_note-Zastrow-49)

**The Kinsey Institute for Research in Sex, Gender, and Reproduction** (often shortened to **The Kinsey Institute**) is a research institute at [Indiana University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_University "Indiana University"). Established in [Bloomington, Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomington,_Indiana "Bloomington, Indiana"), in 1947 as a nonprofit, the institute merged with Indiana University in 2016, "abolishing the 1947 independent incorporation absolutely and completely."[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-2)

The institute's mission is "To foster and promote a greater understanding of human sexuality and relationships through research, outreach, education, and historical preservation." Research, graduate training, information services, and the collection and preservation of library, art, and archival materials are main activities carried out by The Kinsey Institute.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-3) The institute and [Alfred Kinsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey "Alfred Kinsey") himself have been the subject of much controversy. As of July 1,2019,[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kinsey_Institute&action=edit) evolutionary biologist and sex researcher Justin Garcia holds the title of executive director of The Kinsey Institute, previously noted as the institute's research director.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-news.iu.edu-4) Garcia is the institute's eighth executive director and their youngest in history at 34 years old when appointed as executive director.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-5)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kinsey_Institute&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Formation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kinsey_Institute&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Formation")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/Front_row_%28left_to_right%29-_Cornelia_V._Christenson%3B_Mrs._Leser%3B_Clyde_E._Martin._Arranged_on_steps_%28left_to_right%29-_Mrs._Brown%3B_Paul_H._Gebhard%3B_William_Dellenback%3B_Alfred_E._Kinsey%3B_Wardell_B._%285493916199%29.jpg/250px-thumbnail.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Front_row_(left_to_right)-_Cornelia_V._Christenson;_Mrs._Leser;_Clyde_E._Martin._Arranged_on_steps_(left_to_right)-_Mrs._Brown;_Paul_H._Gebhard;_William_Dellenback;_Alfred_E._Kinsey;_Wardell_B._(5493916199).jpg)

The staff of the institute in 1953. Second director [Paul Gebhard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Gebhard "Paul Gebhard") is seated on the upper steps, second from left.

The origins of the Kinsey Institute lie in the scientific research of [Indiana University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_University "Indiana University") professor and entomologist turned sexuality researcher, [Alfred Kinsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Kinsey "Alfred Kinsey"). The 1947 creation of the nonprofit institute, originally named the Institute for Sex Research (ISR), was supported by both Indiana University president [Herman B Wells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herman_B_Wells "Herman B Wells") and the [Rockefeller Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockefeller_Foundation "Rockefeller Foundation"), a major financial backer of Kinsey's research. The ISR was established to protect and preserve the [confidentiality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confidentiality "Confidentiality") of Kinsey's data and research materials by creating a secure, permanent repository for them.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-6)

Alfred Kinsey was director of the institute from 1947 until his death in 1956. Since then, the institute has had six directors: [Paul Gebhard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Gebhard "Paul Gebhard") PhD (1956–1982), June Reinisch PhD (1982–1993), Stephanie Sanders PhD (interim director, 1993–1995), [John Bancroft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bancroft_(sexologist) "John Bancroft (sexologist)") MD (1994–2004), [Julia Heiman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julia_Heiman "Julia Heiman") PhD (2004–2014), [C. Sue Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._Sue_Carter "C. Sue Carter") PhD (2014–2019), and Justin Garcia PhD (2019–present).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-7)[_[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_]

### Kinsey's directorship (1947–1956)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kinsey_Institute&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Kinsey's directorship (1947–1956)")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/73/Alfred_Kinsey_%285493900781%29.jpg/250px-Alfred_Kinsey_%285493900781%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alfred_Kinsey_(5493900781).jpg)

Translation of German and French sources underway in the institute's library, 1953

Shortly after the ISR's establishment, Kinsey's interview based research was published in the 1948 bestselling[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-8) book, _Sexual Behavior in the Human Male_.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-9) Its companion _Sexual Behavior in the Human Female_ was published five years later.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-10) These books were popularly known as the "[Kinsey Reports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Reports "Kinsey Reports")".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-11) Also, in 1950, research materials being shipped to the ISR were seized by [U.S. Customs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Customs_Service "United States Customs Service") thereby resulting in the federal court case _U.S. v. 31 Photographs_. This case continued on after Kinsey's death, until it was finally settled in the institute's favor in 1957. The ruling granted ISR permission to import erotic materials for "research purposes".[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-12)

### Gebhard's directorship (1956–1982)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kinsey_Institute&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Gebhard's directorship (1956–1982)")]

Under Paul Gebhard's leadership, the interview based research project continued, resulting in the publication of _[Pregnancy, Birth and Abortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pregnancy,\_Birth\_and\_Abortion?action=edit&redlink=1 "Pregnancy, Birth and Abortion (page does not exist)")_[[wd](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Special:EntityPage/Q126599075#sitelinks-wikipedia "d:Special:EntityPage/Q126599075")][[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-13) and _[Sex Offenders: An Analysis of Types](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex\_Offenders\_(1965\_book) "Sex Offenders (1965 book)")_.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-14) Other significant publications included JoAnn Brook's _Sexual Nomenclature: A Thesaurus_[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-15) and Alan Bell and Martin Weinberg's _[Homosexualities: A Study of Diversity Among Men and Women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homosexualities:\_A\_Study\_of\_Diversity\_Among\_Men\_and\_Women "Homosexualities: A Study of Diversity Among Men and Women")_.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-Rice-16) Additionally, in response to criticism that Kinsey's original data was biased and not well defined, Gebhard and Johnson wrote _The Kinsey Data: Marginal Tabulations of the 1938-1963 Interviews_.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-17) To honor its founder, the Institute for Sex Research was renamed The Kinsey Institute for Sex Research in 1981.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-kinseyinstitute1-18)

### June Reinisch's directorship (1982–1993)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kinsey_Institute&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: June Reinisch's directorship (1982–1993)")]

When [June Machover Reinisch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/June_Machover_Reinisch "June Machover Reinisch") became the new director, the name of the institute changed to The Kinsey Institute for Research in Sex, Gender, and Reproduction, in order to better reflect its expanded mission.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-kinseyinstitute1-18) During her first years as director, as part of her contract with the university, the institute was completely renovated and expanded adding a new full floor for the library including temperature and humidity controlled stacks, a scholars' reading room, additional staff offices, and The John Money Visiting Scholars Study, an art gallery and new archives for the art and artifacts collections and additional research offices and laboratory space. Reinisch's directorship also saw the creation of a five-volume monographic series, The Kinsey Institute Series, beginning with the publication of _Masculinity/Femininity_[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-19) resulting from institute-sponsored multidisciplinary seminars. Research focused on at-risk sexual behavior and the effects of prenatal exposure to medications on sexual and psychosexual development. Additionally, in 1990 the establishment of the institute's art gallery led to exhibitions featuring its art collection.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-20)

From 1984 to 1993, with direction from Indiana University to play an active role in public education, the institute produced "The Kinsey Report", an internationally syndicated newspaper column.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-21) Although "The Kinsey Report" is no longer a syndicated column, the Kinsey Institute continues to maintain a sex and sexuality FAQ and statistics page on their website.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-22) Additionally, a trade book aimed at popular audiences, _The Kinsey Institute New Report on Sex: What you must know to be Sexually Literate_, was released in 1991.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-23)

### Stephanie Sanders's interim directorship (1993–1995)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kinsey_Institute&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Stephanie Sanders's interim directorship (1993–1995)")]

Following June Reinisch's retirement, Stephanie Sanders held the institute's research and curriculum programs together as the Board reorganized its internal structure amid drastic budget cuts from Indiana University.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-25)

### John Bancroft's directorship (1995–2004)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kinsey_Institute&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: John Bancroft's directorship (1995–2004)")]

From 1995 to 2001, The Kinsey Institute operated a clinic for sexual health and menstrual problems under the directorship of John Bancroft.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-26) Research focus was placed upon the psychology of sexual behavior, hormonal effects on sex, and sexuality and well-being. Bancroft and Erick Janssen developed the Dual-control model of sexual arousal, a theory of sexual arousal involving inhibitory and excitation processes.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-27) In 1999, the website Kinsey Confidential (originally called Kinsey Institute Sexuality Information Service for Students) was started to provide research-based information regarding sexuality to college-aged adults. It includes sex questions and answers provided by sex researcher and columnist [Debby Herbenick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debby_Herbenick "Debby Herbenick") in both column-format and podcast-format.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-28) During the following year, the institute began regularly rotating exhibitions of artwork and archival materials in addition to offering public tours.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-29)

### Julia Heiman's directorship (2004–2013)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kinsey_Institute&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Julia Heiman's directorship (2004–2013)")]

In 2006, the institute began hosting an annual juried art show.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-newsinfo1-30) In 2007, The Kinsey Institute also hosted the inaugural conference of The University Consortium for Sexuality Research and Training.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-newsinfo1-30) Also, a question and answer column from the Kinsey Confidential runs in university newspapers including Indiana University's _[Indiana Daily Student](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana\_Daily\_Student "Indiana Daily Student")_.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-31) Ongoing research themes include such topics as [condom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Condom "Condom") usage,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-32) sex in long-term relationships,[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-33) and hormones and reproduction.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-34)

### Sue Carter's directorship (2014–2019)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kinsey_Institute&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Sue Carter's directorship (2014–2019)")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a9/Sue_Carter.jpg/250px-Sue_Carter.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sue_Carter.jpg)

Director [C. Sue Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._Sue_Carter "C. Sue Carter") (pictured 2008)

[Sue Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._Sue_Carter "C. Sue Carter"), a pioneer in examining mechanisms underlying love, bonding and other emotions, was named director in October 2014.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-35) Carter said her directorship will emphasize love, sexuality and well-being. "I want to take Kinsey into directions that are unequivocally important" including sexual trauma, the [transgender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transgender "Transgender") movement, and medical interventions that can affect a person's sexuality and relationships. Reflecting this broadened scope, the institute changed its tagline from "advancing sexual health and knowledge worldwide" to "explore love, sexuality, and well-being" and introduced a new red logo, a circle inscribed with a hexagonal arrangement of circular arcs.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-36) The prior logo, a stylised K designed by Enock, Inc.,[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-37) had been phased out around 2010–11.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-38) For most of her life, Carter has studied [prairie voles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prairie_vole "Prairie vole"). Unlike most other mammals, these voles [pair-bond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pair_bond "Pair bond").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-39)

### Justin Garcia's directorship (2019–present)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kinsey_Institute&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Justin Garcia's directorship (2019–present)")]

On July 1, 2019, evolutionary biologist and sex researcher Justin Garcia became the institute's youngest executive director at 34 years old, replacing director Sue Carter.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-news.iu.edu-4)

In 2023, the [Indiana House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_House_of_Representatives "Indiana House of Representatives") passed legislation banning any state funds from going to the Kinsey Institute.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-41)

In 2026, [Indiana Public Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WFIU "WFIU") reported that Garcia and fellow Kinsey researcher [Helen Fisher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helen_Fisher_(anthropologist) "Helen Fisher (anthropologist)") appeared in documents related to the activities of [Jeffrey Epstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeffrey_Epstein "Jeffrey Epstein") released in January 2026.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-:0-42) Garcia had emailed Epstein in 2012 in response to an interaction with him on LinkedIn.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-:0-42) Garcia clarified his appearance in the documents, stating, "I only later learned of his criminal background, antithetical to all of my work. I never met or spoke with him, and I did not receive any funding. I totally condemn what he did."[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-:0-42) Fisher, a Senior Research Fellow with The Kinsey Institute, met with Epstein on several occasions, dining with him and other guests, including [Woody Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woody_Allen "Woody Allen"), [Kathy Ruemmler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathy_Ruemmler "Kathy Ruemmler"), and [Ehud Barak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ehud_Barak "Ehud Barak").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-:0-42)

## Library, archive, and art gallery

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kinsey_Institute&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Library, archive, and art gallery")]

### Library, archive, and art collection

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kinsey_Institute&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Library, archive, and art collection")]

The Kinsey Institute is considered to have one of the largest collections of library, archival, and art materials pertaining to sex, gender, and reproduction.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-43) The current collection began as Alfred Kinsey's private research collection. To ensure its protection, Kinsey [sold it to the institute for one dollar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peppercorn_(legal) "Peppercorn (legal)").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-44) Over the years, neither state nor grant money have been used to build collections. Instead the institute uses funds obtained from book royalties and fees in addition to donations. A sampling of the broad range of items housed at the institute includes scientific and popular books, pulp magazines, publications from both sexual and anti-sexual organizations, data from Kinsey's original interview project, films, photos, erotic objects, and artwork by both professionals and amateurs. Items from all over the world are represented in the collection and some objects even date back to the [pre-Columbian era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Columbian_era "Pre-Columbian era").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-45) However, materials do not circulate and must be studied within the reading room which is open to scholars, professionals, university faculty, and students over eighteen who are researching topics pertaining to sexuality, gender, and reproduction.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-46) Due to the highly specialized nature of the collection, holdings are described using subject headings created by The Kinsey Institute and organized using a modified version of the [Dewey Decimal System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dewey_Decimal_Classification "Dewey Decimal Classification").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-47)

### Art gallery

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kinsey_Institute&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Art gallery")]

The Kinsey Institute's art gallery[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-48) is accessible to the public and hosts a variety of exhibitions each year. Some titles of past exhibitions have included Nature & Nurture: Exploring Human Reproduction from Pregnancy through Early Childhood, Private Eyes: Amateur Art from The Kinsey Institute Collections, Eros in Asia: Erotic Art from Iran to Japan, and Sex and Presidential Politics.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-49) Exhibits featuring the institute's collection have also traveled around both the state of Indiana[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-50) and country.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-51) Each year since 2006, The Kinsey Institute's annual juried art show features art work that explores themes of sexuality, gender, romance, reproduction, gender and sexual politics, the human figure, and the relation between illness and sexuality. Due to the large size of the show, it is hosted at Indiana University's SoFa gallery.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinsey_Institute#cite_note-52)

## [Bill Condon](https://www.themoviedb.org/person/15557-bill-condon)

### Biography

William Condon(born October 22, 1955) is an American director and screenwriter. Condon is known for writing and/or directing numerous successful and acclaimed films, including Gods and Monsters,Chicago,Kinsey,Dreamgirls,The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn – Part 1,The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn – Part 2, and Beauty and the Beast.He has received two nominations for the Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay,Gods and Monsters and Chicago, winning for the former.

#### Your Privacy

When you visit any website, it may store or retrieve information on your browser, mostly in the form of cookies. This information might be about you, your preferences, or your device, and is mostly used to make the site work as you expect. The information does not usually identify you directly, but it can give you a more personalized web experience. Because we respect your right to privacy, you can choose not to allow some types of cookies. Click on the different category headings to learn more and change our default settings. Blocking some types of cookies may impact your experience of the site and the services we are able to offer. 

[More information](https://cookiepedia.co.uk/giving-consent-to-cookies)

#### Strictly Necessary Cookies

Always Active

These cookies are necessary for the website to function and cannot be switched off in our systems. They also help us to remember prior selections you have made, such as setting your privacy preferences, such as setting your privacy preferences, logging in or filling in forms. You can set your browser to block or alert you about these cookies, but some parts of the site will not then work.

#### Performance Cookies

- [x] Performance Cookies 

These cookies allow us to count visits and traffic sources so we can measure and improve the performance of our site. They help us to know which pages are the most and least popular and see how visitors move around the site. If you do not allow these cookies, we will have less information to help us improve the site’s functionality.

#### Functional Cookies

- [x] Functional Cookies 

These cookies enable the website to provide enhanced functionality and personalization, such as remembering language settings and customer service chat history. If you do not allow these cookies, then some or all of these services may not function properly.

#### Social Media Cookies

- [x] Social Media Cookies 

These cookies are set by a range of social media services that we have added to the site to enable you to share our content with your friends and networks. They are capable of tracking your browser across other sites and building up a profile of your interests. This may impact the content and messages you see on other websites you visit. If you do not allow these cookies you may not be able to use or see these sharing tools.

#### Targeting Cookies

- [x] Targeting Cookies 

These cookies may be set through our site by our advertising partners. They may be used by those companies to build a profile of your interests and show you relevant adverts on this and other sites. If you do not allow these cookies, you will still see advertising, but it will not be targeted to your specific interests.

Of the two films made in the last half decade about internet-based social evolution/revolution, it is a sad statement about current zeitgeist that the film regarding the social network was more solidly made and much better received than the film about exposing corruption in world governments. It is easy to see what "The Fifth Estate," the film about WikiLeaks founder, Julian Assange, is trying to do. Like "The Social Network," it wants to be a slick expose on a man and his pioneering creation. Unlike Fincher's film, "The Fifth Estate" can not muster the narrative balance and interesting characters to cement it as a better-than-above average experience.

[1998](https://letterboxd.com/films/year/1998/)
Directed by [Bill Condon](https://letterboxd.com/director/bill-condon/)

### Synopsis

#### A portrait of an outrageous friendship.

It’s 1957, and James Whale’s heyday as the director of “Frankenstein,” “Bride of Frankenstein” and “The Invisible Man” is long behind him. Retired and a semi-recluse, he lives his days accompanied only by images from his past. When his dour housekeeper, Hannah, hires a handsome young gardener, the flamboyant director and simple yard man develop an unlikely friendship, which will change them forever.

Acts as both a critique of the Hollywood system and a study of the trauma and danger that lies within open homosexuality. It’s incredibly rare - hell, I can’t think of another American queer film - that is written, directed, and stars an actual gay person, so it’s surprisingly refreshing that there’s one from the 90s. Ian McKellen delivers his finest performance as the retired classic director James Whale, showcasing a stunning amalgamation of the emotional intensities and delicacies that come with age and sexuality. While this may seem like a shock, and it could be a personal matter, but I doubt I’ve ever seen homosexuality portrayed this well on film with regard to the mentality and mannerisms of this character, making _Gods and Monsters_ as special as it is.

## [Bill Condon](https://www.themoviedb.org/person/15557-bill-condon)

### Biography

William Condon(born October 22, 1955) is an American director and screenwriter. Condon is known for writing and/or directing numerous successful and acclaimed films, including Gods and Monsters,Chicago,Kinsey,Dreamgirls,The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn – Part 1,The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn – Part 2, and Beauty and the Beast.He has received two nominations for the Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay,Gods and Monsters and Chicago, winning for the former.

Because we respect your right to privacy, you can choose not to allow some types of cookies. Click on the different category headings to learn more and change our default settings. Blocking some types of cookies may impact your experience of the site and the services we are able to offer.

Always Active

## [Discover your next favorite video with Ask YouTube, available on web, mobile, and TVs](https://blog.youtube/news-and-events/ask-youtube-web-mobile-tv/)

By **Emily Moxley****,**_VP, Product Management, Viewer AI_

Oct 12, 2026 First announced at [Google I/O](https://blog.youtube/news-and-events/youtube-news-google-io-2026/), we launched Ask YouTube on search to help viewers get to the right video faster. Now, we’re bringing this feature to mobile devices, making Ask YouTube available to U.S. viewers [across web, mobile and TVs](https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/16943763).

This reimagined, conversational search tool allows users to ask complex queries, refine with follow up questions, and receive results in an interactive format, whether they’re on the go or using voice commands from the couch.

We’ve already seen users ask how to DIY their Halloween costumes, dive into video essays, and debate cutting their own bangs.

Ask YouTube on the watch page, which launched last year, is also expanding to help viewers connect even more deeply with the content and creators they love.

Earlier this year, [we added the feature to TVs](https://blog.youtube/news-and-events/youtube-conversational-ai-tool-available-smart-tvs/), and viewers will soon be able to use Ask YouTube directly from the watch page while watching Shorts and live streams, receiving instant context as the action unfolds. ## [Dr. Garth talks healthy digital habits with Mummy & Daddy Pig from Peppa Pig](https://blog.youtube/news-and-events/healthy-habits-screen-time-kids-dr-garth-graham-peppa-pig/)

Sep 03, 2026 As families dive headfirst into the back-to-school routine, many parents are asking a familiar question: how do we build healthy screen habits that actually stick?

Whether you’re trying to transition from a favorite show to the dinner table without causing a _muddy puddle_ of tears, or just trying to find good quality content, getting the right balance can feel like a whole operation.

To help families navigate those moments, [Dr. Garth Graham](https://blog.youtube/author/dr-garth-graham/) — a practicing physician, public health expert, father of four, and Head of YouTube Health — sat down for a very special video call with two of the world’s most recognisable parents: Mummy Pig and Daddy Pig.

Debuting on the [Peppa Pig: Muddy Puddle Parenting YouTube channel](https://www.youtube.com/@MuddyPuddleParentingOfficial), this lighthearted sit-down unpacks practical, clinician-tested tips for managing screen time at home … no snorting required. ## [Why millions of viewers tune into bento box meal prep on YouTube](https://blog.youtube/culture-and-trends/youtube-bento-box-meal-prep-trend/)

By **The YouTube Culture & Trends team**

Sep 04, 2026 From [weekly prep](https://youtu.be/Gj9IvRIore8?si=ImGQF89MPGqMF_af) to [beautifully arranged lunches](https://youtu.be/U0yyESb38fw?si=YZqhh-LMvi-tA7Fa), creators are turning meal preparation into a comforting art form. Through satisfying tutorials, they offer a calming visual experience of tidiness, uniform chopping, and culinary control.

The hunger for this organized aesthetic is massive: In the first six months of 2026, there were more than 250M views of videos with "bento box" or "#bentobox" in the title.*

In preparation for the back-to-school season, don’t miss our unique YouTube logo (also known as the Yoodle) celebrating the meal prep community. Ready to pack your perfect lunch? Dive into our [playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLCYvO0_kPn2g).

### Thank you for your interest

[[edit](https://donate.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?title=Template:CountryNope&action=edit&section=T-1 "Edit section: Thank you for your interest")]

Thank you for your interest in supporting the Wikimedia Foundation. We are not fundraising in your country at this time, but monetary contributions are not your only option for donating to and supporting Wikipedia.

Wikipedia is a "wiki", which means that everyone can edit pages. You don't need to apply or get special permission to join us. At the top of each page is an "edit" label. Try it, for example, at [the Wikipedia sandbox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Sandbox "w:Wikipedia:Sandbox"). You don't even need to log in to edit, although [creating an account](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:UserLogin/signup "w:Special:UserLogin/signup") gives you more options and helps you keep track of your contributions. There is no central editorial board; all edits are made by individual members of the Wikipedia community. For more information, please see the [introduction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Introduction "w:Help:Introduction").

If you have any further questions regarding Wikipedia or editing, please contact info![Image 1: @](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/88/At_sign.svg/20px-At_sign.svg.png?utm_source=donate.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)wikimedia.org. This email address is answered by longtime project participants who have vast experience in Wikipedia-related issues.

Thanks again for your interest, and we hope you join us!

_**Gods and Monsters**_ is a 1998 [period drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_drama "Historical drama") film written and directed by [Bill Condon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Condon "Bill Condon"), based on [Christopher Bram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Bram "Christopher Bram")'s 1995 novel _[Father of Frankenstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Father\_of\_Frankenstein "Father of Frankenstein")_. The film stars [Ian McKellen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_McKellen "Ian McKellen"), [Brendan Fraser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brendan_Fraser "Brendan Fraser"), [Lynn Redgrave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynn_Redgrave "Lynn Redgrave"), [Lolita Davidovich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lolita_Davidovich "Lolita Davidovich"), and [David Dukes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Dukes "David Dukes"). Its plot is a partly fictionalized account of the last days of the life of film director [James Whale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Whale "James Whale") (McKellen), known for directing _[Frankenstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frankenstein\_(1931\_film) "Frankenstein (1931 film)")_ (1931) and _[Bride of Frankenstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bride\_of\_Frankenstein "Bride of Frankenstein")_ (1935). A veteran of [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"), the aged Whale develops a complicated relationship with his gardener, Clayton Boone (Fraser), a fictitious character originally created by Bram for the source novel.

An international co-production between the United Kingdom and the United States, _Gods and Monsters_ is produced by [Paul Colichman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Colichman "Paul Colichman"), [Gregg Fienberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregg_Fienberg "Gregg Fienberg"), and Mark R. Harris; [Clive Barker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_Barker "Clive Barker") served as executive producer.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gods_and_Monsters_(film)#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gods_and_Monsters_(film)#cite_note-5) As well as featuring reconstructions of the production of the _Bride of Frankenstein_, the film's title is derived from a scene in _Bride of Frankenstein_, in which the character [Dr. Pretorius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dr._Pretorius "Dr. Pretorius") toasts [Dr. Frankenstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dr._Frankenstein "Dr. Frankenstein"), "To a new world of gods and monsters!"

_Gods and Monsters_ was nominated for three [Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards"), including [Best Actor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Actor "Academy Award for Best Actor") for McKellen and [Best Supporting Actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Supporting_Actress "Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress") for Redgrave, and won for [Best Adapted Screenplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Adapted_Screenplay "Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gods_and_Monsters_(film)#cite_note-Oscars1999-6) Despite receiving positive reviews, the film was a [box office failure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box-office_bomb "Box-office bomb"). It was later adapted as a play of the same name which premiered in London at the [Southwark Playhouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwark_Playhouse "Southwark Playhouse") in February 2015.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gods_and_Monsters_(film)#cite_note-7)
