# Ferrara, Abel

[Florian Zappe](https://www.sensesofcinema.com/author/florian-zappe/ "Posts by Florian Zappe")

July 2026

[Great Directors](https://www.sensesofcinema.com/category/great-directors/ "View all posts in Great Directors")

[Issue 118](https://www.sensesofcinema.com/issues/issue-118)

### **b. 19 July 1951, New York City, United States**

> _“I do think that filmmaking is sacred.“_
> 
> 
> – Abel Ferrara[1](https://www.sensesofcinema.com/2026/great-directors/ferrara-abel/#fn-52234-1)

Discussions of Abel Ferrara – who celebrates his 75th birthday this year – have long been shaped by a popular mythology that has proved remarkably persistent: “the folk hero of New York independent film,”[2](https://www.sensesofcinema.com/2026/great-directors/ferrara-abel/#fn-52234-2) the eccentric solitary, the Dionysian/Orphean maverick filmmaker[3](https://www.sensesofcinema.com/2026/great-directors/ferrara-abel/#fn-52234-3) who has survived (both metaphorically and literally) in the film industry for more than five decades without ever fully belonging to it, the liminal figure moving between seemingly incompatible cultural and industrial spaces, the gritty street poet with a camera, venerated by audiences and critics with something approaching cultic devotion or punished with emphatic rejection. Such attributes are certainly somewhat clichéd, but they also testify to the difficulty – to invoke yet another cliché – of categorising Ferrara’s extensive and multifaceted body of work.

His films do in fact move restlessly between genres, cultural registers and production contexts, and have never quite settled into the taxonomies by which film histories tend to organise careers in retrospect. As a director, Ferrara has shed his skin more than once: from his beginnings in the cinematic underground of late 1970s New York, through exploitation cinema and the indie film wave of the 1980s and 1990s, to his later status as an arthouse darling and regular presence at A-list festivals of the European circuit.

These transformations may have altered the outward shape, but not the essence of his rough yet deeply philosophical filmmaking. One critic once attributed a “tabloid sensibility”[4](https://www.sensesofcinema.com/2026/great-directors/ferrara-abel/#fn-52234-4) to Sam Fuller, and the same label can doubtlessly be applied to Ferrara, who combines it, however, with the ethos of an auteur and an almost avantgardistic spirit of disruption and refusal to please his audiences all too easily. The result is a stylistically and generically eclectic body of work held together by a series of recurring motifs and topoi – questions of guilt and redemption, often negotiated through Catholic iconography; the immediacy of violence, bodily degradation and addiction; urban alienation and social displacement; debt, dependency and personal betrayal – all of which return, in different forms, to what I would argue is the central question of Ferrara’s cinema: whether an authentic, unalienated and autonomous self, still capable of at least some form of ethical judgement, remains possible in a world fundamentally hostile to it.

## **Setting the Scene: Ferrara’s Beginnings**

Born in 1951 to Italian and Irish-American parents and raised in a lower-middle-class milieu in the Bronx, Ferrara was a film enthusiast from an early age and began shooting his first 8mm films at 16. As far as his filmmaking education beyond these first autodidactic attempts is concerned, the literature is not entirely consistent. Depending on the account, he attended practical film courses at Rockland Community College in New York State[5](https://www.sensesofcinema.com/2026/great-directors/ferrara-abel/#fn-52234-5) and/or spent a brief period studying film in England in 1970 as part of the college’s exchange programme.[6](https://www.sensesofcinema.com/2026/great-directors/ferrara-abel/#fn-52234-6) Ferrara’s recently published autobiography does little to shed light on the matter, apart from adding the anecdote that he sneaked, without being officially enrolled, into film classes at the San Francisco Art Institute, including some transgressive-performative lessons taught by the iconic German _enfant terrible_ Rosa von Praunheim in the early 1970s.[7](https://www.sensesofcinema.com/2026/great-directors/ferrara-abel/#fn-52234-7)

Like many young filmmakers of his generation, Ferrara first tested the possibilities of the artform in the short-film format. _Nicky’s Film_ (1971), _The Hold Up_ (1972) and _Could This Be Love_ (1973) are significant above all because they mark the beginning of one of the decisive creative relationships in his career, as they were partly (co-)written by Nicodemo Oliverio, who would become – usually under the pseudonym Nicholas St. John – Ferrara’s most important collaborator during the first phase of his oeuvre. Between 1976 and 1996, Oliverio contributed the scripts to ten of Ferrara’s films before fundamental disagreements arose during the preparation of the William Gibson adaptation _New Rose Hotel_ (1998). Differing opinions on the ethos of filmmaking (and on Ferrara’s drug issues at the time) brought this artistic symbiosis to an end.[8](https://www.sensesofcinema.com/2026/great-directors/ferrara-abel/#fn-52234-8)

The move towards feature-length filmmaking took Ferrara into a cinematic territory of comparatively low cultural prestige: the (s)exploitation market of the 1970s, a niche of the industry that offered young directors still without credentials access to (admittedly modest) means of film production. His first feature, _9 Lives of a Wet Pussy_ (1976), emerged from the brief historical moment in which hardcore pornography had acquired a certain fashionable visibility beyond its usual audiences. This relative cultural permissiveness did not, however, translate into a climate of open authorial acknowledgement. Ferrara appeared in the credits as “Jimmy Boy L.”, Oliverio/St. John as “Nicholas George”. As this long-obscure[9](https://www.sensesofcinema.com/2026/great-directors/ferrara-abel/#fn-52234-9) film was only retrospectively acknowledged as part of Ferrara’s filmography, _The Driller Killer_ (1979) has therefore often been misidentified as his ‘actual’ debut, which established a form of notoriety of its own that would haunt the director for decades. The film was a hyperbolic low-budget hybrid of horror film, art-world grotesque, black comedy and downtown music culture; its afterlife as a cult film was decisively shaped by its prominent role in the context of the British “video nasties” moral panic of the early 1980s.

[![Image 53](http://www.sensesofcinema.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Fig.-2.jpg)](http://www.sensesofcinema.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Fig.-2.jpg)
_The Driller Killer_

The film is only at the most superficial level the blood-soaked splatter film its title promises, although it certainly exploits the gory attractions of the genre. Beyond this, it is also the first film in which Ferrara presents us with the archetype of what might be called the Ferrarian protagonist who will reappear in many of the films to follow, like a revenant in various guises: a figure torn between an intrinsic drive to do something good, true and meaningful and circumstances that make this impossible, and who ultimately breaks under this dilemma. Ferrara himself plays Reno Miller, a struggling painter in the Lower East Side whose precarious existence is defined by unpaid bills, pressure from his landlord, the scorn of the institutionalised art world, the emotional instability of his domestic arrangement with the two women he lives with, Carol (Carolyn Marz) and Pamela (Baybi Day), and the intrusive rehearsals of a No Wave band in the neighbouring loft. As Reno tries to finish a painting that is meant to secure him both money and artistic recognition, his mental state steadily deteriorates. On nocturnal wanderings through the city, he starts to murder homeless men with a power drill, before his violence turns against the figures he associates more directly with his humiliation and failure. While gory and committed to a sensationalism that follows the conventions of the genre (pushing them slightly towards the grotesque), Ferrara stages the film’s graphic violence as the expression of a specific crisis rooted in profound alienation. Reno’s rampage marks the collapse of a creative individual caught between the demand for authentic artistic existence and the social and material conditions that make such authenticity almost impossible. In this sense, _The Driller Killer_ is not only Ferrara’s first major work of notoriety but also an early treatment of one of his central themes: the often irresolvable tension between individual self-realisation and socially induced alienation which, in his cinema, often seeks release in acts of violent catharsis, however doomed such attempts may be.[10](https://www.sensesofcinema.com/2026/great-directors/ferrara-abel/#fn-52234-10) At the same time, it is a contemporary document of the late-1970s New York Downtown scene, a milieu that later cultural memory has often converted into an object of nostalgic fascination, but which Ferrara presents as a space of existential struggle in a material and above all metaphysical sense.

Excessive violence as revenge against a hostile world also structures Ferrara’s next film, the rape-revenge drama _Ms .45_ (1981), which, like _The Driller Killer_, acquired the somewhat problematic status of a cult film, problematic because such a label tends to reduce the disturbance of the work to the pleasures of subcultural recognition. Zoë Lund plays Thana, a mute seamstress in New York’s garment district who is raped twice on the same day, first in the street and then in her apartment, where she kills the second attacker and takes possession of his calibre .45 pistol. After dismembering his body and disposing of it across the city, she begins to shoot men whose gestures, looks or advances appear as extensions of the violence already done to her. The film culminates in a Halloween party, where Thana, dressed as a nun, turns her revenge into a grotesque ritual of purification. In _Ms .45_, the violence that had erupted in _The Driller Killer_ from a profoundly masculine wounded artistic ego, denied recognition and subjected to economic humiliation, is displaced onto another terrain. Here it emerges from a different manifestation of a socially determined denial of self-determination: the female experience of patriarchal humiliation, which escalates into extreme sexual violence and is met with no less extreme counter-violence.[11](https://www.sensesofcinema.com/2026/great-directors/ferrara-abel/#fn-52234-11)

[![Image 54](http://www.sensesofcinema.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Fig.-3.jpg)](http://www.sensesofcinema.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Fig.-3.jpg)
_Ms .45_

With _Fear City_ (1984), Ferrara expanded his spectrum of genres. The film, his first sustained engagement with mafia material, already points away from the semi-underground conditions of the earlier work and towards a brief period in which he moved through more conventional industrial formats. During the second half of the 1980s, this included _China Girl_ (1987), the Elmore Leonard adaptation _Cat Chaser_ (1989), two episodes of _Miami Vice_, the pilot for the short-lived series _Crime Story_(like _Miami Vice_, produced by Michael Mann), and two largely (and quite rightfully) forgotten television films – _The Gladiator_ (1986), _The Loner_ (1988). Undoubtedly, this period can be understood as an interlude of commercial compromise as these works remain, in many respects, closer to the aesthetic and narrative expectations of their respective industrial formats than to the more disturbing energies of Ferrara’s strongest films.

## **Of Good and Bad Lieutenants**

The rise of American “indie” cinema in the late 1980s and early 1990s resulted from an interaction between changing viewing habits among at least parts of the audience and a set of transformations within the film industry itself. The commercial success of comparatively low-budget films with complex themes and recognisable stylistic ambitions contributed to an – at least nominal – erosion of the opposition between capital-driven mainstream studio production and marginal filmmaking. A cultural space emerged in which the label “independent” increasingly functioned as a marketing category for artistically mature and demanding works that appeared sufficiently distant from the blockbuster logic of mainstream cinema in the 1970s and 1980s, even when their financing, distribution and promotion remained tied to the commercial structures of the industry, partially obscured by the use of imprints promising a higher degree of cultural capital. It was in this ambivalent context of “Indiewood” that Ferrara’s cinema entered its first broadly visible phase. _King of New York_ (1990) and _Bad Lieutenant_ (1992) are certainly the most significant, critically acclaimed and most prominent films of this period.

_King of New York_, written by Oliverio/St. John, begins with gangster Frank White’s (Christopher Walken) release from prison and his return to a city he regards as lost territory he wants to reclaim. Walken plays Frank as a drug lord with an almost aristocratic allure, an urban dandy of unsettling politeness, whose calm and elegance obscure the ruthlessness with which he pursues his business interests; this also makes him an allegory of the yuppie-capitalist _zeitgeist_ predominant in the coke- and money-infused Manhattan of the 1980s. Once back in New York, he gathers his old crew, most prominently Jimmy Jump (Laurence Fishburne), and sets about eliminating rival dealers, Asian gangsters, mafia figures and other obstacles to his control of the cocaine trade. At the same time, he surrounds himself with the white-collar crooks of New York’s high society and presents himself as a civic benefactor, as he wants to secure the funding of a hospital in the Bronx, whose survival the official city seems unable or unwilling to guarantee. Ferrara does not allow this mixture of criminal power and social gesture to settle into a simple Robin Hood fantasy. It is more ambiguous: Frank wants to be the drug kingpin, criminal entrepreneur, violent avenger and – the film makes quite clear that he is sincere about this – a benevolent saviour at the same time because he needs to maintain some kind of moral compass in the nihilistic world he operates in. Yet, as in a classic tragedy, he seems predestined to fail in all these roles.

[![Image 55](http://www.sensesofcinema.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Fig.-4.jpg)](http://www.sensesofcinema.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Fig.-4.jpg)
_The King of New York_

His antagonists are a group of street-level policemen, above all Roy Bishop (Victor Argo), a lieutenant whose weary sense of morality gives the film its clearest, if increasingly fragile, counterweight to Frank’s criminal sovereignty. On Bishop’s team are Dennis Gilley (David Caruso) and Thomas Flanigan (Wesley Snipes), two younger and more impulsive officers whose pursuit of Frank gradually assumes the form of a private vendetta as they are frustrated by a legal system that cannot keep Frank contained, enraged by the deaths of colleagues and drawn towards the temptation to answer his violence with their own. The conflict of the film therefore does not run only between criminality and law enforcement, but also through the police themselves, where institutional duty, personal revenge and masculine humiliation begin to contaminate one another. The ensuing escalation leads to a spiral of violence on both sides during which both Flanigan and Gilley are killed. At the end, the film moves towards a duel-like confrontation in the New York subway between Bishop – the good lieutenant who has preserved a modicum of ethical restraint and belief in institutional justice that his disillusioned and cynical colleagues, increasingly drawn into a vigilante logic, have long abandoned – and Frank. The latter is wounded in the shootout, flees, and finally dies in a taxi stuck in traffic (his journey quite literally brought to a standstill) in the realisation of his failure.

_Bad Lieutenant_, made two years later, was co-written by _Ms .45_ star Zoë Lund and centres on an unnamed New York police lieutenant (Harvey Keitel), who is corrupt, addicted to drugs, consumed by gambling debts and caught in a routine of theft, intimidation, sexual coercion and self-degradation. He is assigned to investigate the rape of two Catholic nuns in a church. One of the nuns knows the perpetrators and refuses to identify or condemn them and forgives them based on her Christian ethic. As his gambling losses and drug use intensify, the Lieutenant roams through the city in a downward spiral towards utter physical and psychic devastation, abusing his badge, stealing, hallucinating and trying to impose his own need for redemption onto the crime he is supposed to investigate. After a breakdown in the church, he tracks down the two rapists, but instead of arresting or killing them, he gives them money and puts them on a bus out of New York. After sending the two rapists out of the city, the Lieutenant returns to his car near Penn Station, where men connected to his unpaid gambling debts pull up beside him and shoot him. The film closes on the immediate aftermath of this killing, with the dead Lieutenant left in the car.

[![Image 56](http://www.sensesofcinema.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Fig.-5.webp)](http://www.sensesofcinema.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Fig.-5.webp)
_Bad Lieutenant_

These two films have often been discussed as complementary works, and to a certain degree they are. Both move within a genre framework – the gangster film and the post-noir cop drama respectively – in order to tell twisted morality tales. Frank White and the Bad Lieutenant are two deeply morally degraded figures, both products of a profoundly dysfunctional society, who nevertheless try, helplessly and in full knowledge of the futility of these attempts, to resist this degradation.

During the following years, Ferrara remained committed to innovative genre cinema and displayed a considerable range within it, with varying degrees of recognition from audiences and critics. The gangster film remained a staple within his repertoire, though not always in the contemporary setting of _King of New York_. With _The Funeral_ (1996), set in 1939, he made an excursion into the historical gangster saga, supported by an illustrious cast including, among others, Christopher Walken (by then a regular member of what one might call the Ferrara ensemble), Chris Penn, Isabella Rossellini, Vincent Gallo and Benicio del Toro, before returning thematically to the narcotic underworld of contemporary New York City with _’R Xmas_ (2001). He also contributed two films to the then-current trend of meta-films on the social and creative impact of the film industry on its protagonists that had gained a certain popularity in the 1990s after the success of Robert Altman’s _The Player_(1992). The first of these, _Dangerous Game_ (also released under the title _Snake Eyes_, 1993), is a drama starring Madonna and Harvey Keitel, (the latter as a director clearly modelled on Ferrara himself) that explores the unhealthy dynamics within the creative process of filmmaking. It was followed by _The Blackout_ (1997), a drama about a burned-out film star that, despite an illustrious cast including Matthew Modine, Dennis Hopper, Claudia Schiffer and Béatrice Dalle, failed at the box office. He also adapted William Gibson’s 1984 short story _New Rose Hotel_ (1998), starring Walken, Willem Dafoe and Asia Argento. With the often-underrated _Body Snatchers_ (1993) – the third screen adaptation of Jack Finney’s timeless parable of social conformity – and _The Addiction_ (1995), Ferrara also entered the terrain of horror film. These two films are especially significant in his career as they brought him his first major recognition at A-list festivals, with the former screening in competition at Cannes and the latter in competition at Berlin.

_The Addiction_ is one of Ferrara’s most complex and interesting genre pieces, and not only because the director here deals, in sublimated form, with his own personal problems with addiction. Again written by Oliverio/St. John and realised by Ferrara’s regular cinematographer Ken Kelsh in elegiac-expressionist black-and-white images, the film centres on Kathleen Conklin (Lili Taylor), a philosophy graduate student in New York whose work is concerned with questions of evil, responsibility and historical violence. One night she is attacked in the street by Casanova (Annabella Sciorra), a vampire who bites her and leaves her with a hunger for blood that quickly begins to structure her movements through the city. Kathleen’s transformation manifests itself as an increasingly compulsive condition. She becomes physically weakened, avoids daylight, and begins to prey on people around her, including strangers, but also acquaintances, especially her fellow student Jean (Edie Falco). Her academic reflections on guilt, human cruelty and free will increasingly turn into a self-reflexive discourse on her new bodily and psychic state of dependency. Kathleen later encounters Peina (Christopher Walken), a kind of elder statesman among vampires who has learned to control his appetite through discipline and abstinence. His example gives her a possible model of restraint, but it does not release her from the hunger that has taken hold of her. After completing her dissertation, Kathleen hosts a graduation party attended by friends and colleagues. The gathering turns into an outbreak of vampiric violence, in which the façade of social and academic distinction collapses and the party essentially breaks down into two groups: vampires and their victims who, once ‘infected’, follow the implacable logic of addiction and become driven by the same hunger. After the party, Kathleen is taken to hospital, where she tries to end her existence by exposing herself to daylight, but Casanova returns and prevents the attempt. A priest is then called to her bedside and administers the last rites; the film’s final image shows Kathleen in daylight at her own grave.

[![Image 57](http://www.sensesofcinema.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Fig.-6.1.jpeg)](http://www.sensesofcinema.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Fig.-6.1.jpeg)
_The Addiction_

In the figure of the doctoral student, the film intellectualises – quite uncommon for a genre film – the perennial Ferrarian theme of autonomous, ethically-oriented selfhood being made impossible by circumstance. This intradiegetic explication of these questions and their framing within a deeply Catholic mysticism of guilt and atonement are doubtless indebted to the script by St. John/Oliverio, who, unlike his by-then Buddhist director, never renounced Catholicism and, according to Ferrara’s account, also holds a master’s degree in philosophy from the University of Würzburg in Germany.[12](https://www.sensesofcinema.com/2026/great-directors/ferrara-abel/#fn-52234-12)

## **Towards New Shores**

In the early 2000s, Ferrara made Italy the centre of his life and became a sort of expat filmmaker in Rome. With this geographical relocation, the production conditions under which he worked inevitably also changed, as did the character of his films. He himself has repeatedly stated that he receives greater appreciation in Europe than in the United States and that it is, at least in part, easier for him to get his projects financed there, even if this meant gathering money from various financiers, often – as is, after all, quite common in European cinema – from different countries. With this move, Ferrara left his ‘American’ phase of renegotiating classic genre conventions behind. His feature films now moved closer to the European arthouse cinema for which he had always felt an affinity, even if he remained faithful to his fascination with the sensational and the spectacular. And he discovered a new field for himself: documentary film.

Ferrara’s documentaries are often neglected in the reception of his work, partly because many of them have had only limited circulation. They are nevertheless interesting, since several have a strongly personal, autobiographical character, with Ferrara often integrating himself into the films as a gonzo-style documentarist in search of (sometimes vanished) authentic cultural niches that can serve as refuge in a capitalistically alienated world. His documentary work begins with _Chelsea on the Rocks_ (2008), a return to the legendary Chelsea Hotel and to a bygone mythological bohemian New York. _Napoli Napoli Napoli_ (2009) shifts his filmic exploration to Southern Italy, closer to his familial roots, which had always remained partly present in his Italian American cinema. _Mulberry St._ (2010) brings him back to Little Italy and the festival of the quarter’s patron saint San Gennaro, but the neighbourhood film also becomes a film about Ferrara himself: walking, talking, singing, working, drifting through a place already marked by gentrification, population shifts and the unease of belonging to something that is disappearing while one is filming it. With _Alive in France_ (2017), a film about Ferrara’s activities as a musician, he puts himself literally centre stage. _Piazza Vittorio_ (2017) explores the eponymous square in Rome and portrays the various migrant communities that gather there. _The Projectionist_(2019) returns to New York to portray Nicolas “Nick” Nicolaou, the Cypriot-born cinema owner whose life in exhibition also becomes a history of disappearing independent theatres, changed viewing habits and the erosion of the city’s older film culture. _Sportin’ Life_ (2020) then folds Ferrara’s working life, his collaborators, the Berlin presentation of _Siberia_ (2020) and the beginning of Covid-era confinement into a video diary. With _Turn in the Wound_ (2024), his documentary practice moves to the experience of the war in Ukraine, where interviews with soldiers, civilians and Volodymyr Zelenskyy (alongside a spoken-word performance by Patti Smith) form a rough mosaic that, it has to be said, remains strangely underdeveloped. Nevertheless, these documentary works would deserve a larger audience; in their subjective and often dissociative-essayistic form, they give insights into Ferrara’s worldview, in large as well as small matters, that could enrich the reception of his feature films.

The first of his international features was _Mary_ (2005), a French-American co-production starring Juliette Binoche, Forest Whitaker, Marion Cotillard, Matthew Modine and Heather Graham that approaches religious crisis as a spiritual drama of faith, while the dark comedy _Go Go Tales_ (2007) was funded by American and Italian producers. Although both films had financial backing from the US, they were never commercially released in America. In 2011 came _4:44 Last Day on Earth_, an apocalyptic film that entered the competition at the Venice Film Festival, which did not prevent it from failing with critics and at the box office.

After these less successful films, 2014 proved to be a better year for Ferrara with two films that received broader resonance and also belong among the strongest works of his second career phase. _Welcome to New York_ is a fictionalised version of the sexual assault allegations against Dominique Strauss-Kahn, the former director of the International Monetary Fund and prospective candidate for the office of French president. For several reasons, the film had the potential for scandal and generated considerable controversy, especially in France. The casting of Gérard Depardieu as George Devereaux (the Strauss-Kahn figure) was itself highly contentious, since Depardieu brought with him his own long history of sexual abuse charges.

[![Image 58](http://www.sensesofcinema.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Fig.-7.jpg)](http://www.sensesofcinema.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Fig.-7.jpg)
_Welcome to New York_

The film also provoked legal threats from Strauss-Kahn’s side and, because of the prominence and explosive character of the case, was rejected by the Cannes Film Festival and moved to the film market. The film again takes up the question of an unalienated selfhood no longer stifled by social convention, but here, unlike even in the gangster films, this selfhood has no emancipatory dimension and becomes purely predatory. It is an unsparing portrait of a fusion of hubris, power and misogyny, allegorically condensed in Depardieu’s massive body: the portrayal of a figure permeated by entitlement and a feeling of superiority, but no longer capable of even asking the question of ethical coordinates and, unlike earlier criminal figures in Ferrara’s cinema, no longer showing even a trace of ambivalence.

_Pasolini_, Ferrara’s second film released in 2014, deals with an artist for whom he expressed his deepest appreciation and whom he has repeatedly named as an artistic role model. Based on a cleverly constructed and knowledgeably written screenplay by Maurizio Braucci, Ferrara’s first venture into the biopic breaks with the conventions of the genre from the outset. The film is a highly experimental homage that interweaves the historical facts of Pasolini’s last day and his murder on 2 November 1975 in Ostia with adapted passages from two texts Pasolini left unfinished: the novel _Petrolio_ and the script for the never-realised film _Porno-teo-kolossal_. _Pasolini_, too, negotiates alienation and authenticity on the level of plot as well as on the theoretical level.

[![Image 59](http://www.sensesofcinema.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Fig.-8.1.jpg)](http://www.sensesofcinema.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Fig.-8.1.jpg)
_Pasolini_

Willem Dafoe – who almost literally slips into the skin of Pasolini[13](https://www.sensesofcinema.com/2026/great-directors/ferrara-abel/#fn-52234-13) – presents him as a tired figure, worn down by Sisyphean activist and artistic struggles, yet still repeatedly articulating his sharp diagnosis of society and capitalism in conversations with other characters. That the historical Pasolini, with his preference for hustlers from the subproletarian _borgate_, also has a history as a sexual exploiter is not judged by the film in the same way as in the case of Depardieu/Devereaux. His nocturnal cruising is staged instead as part of an anti-bourgeois quest for authenticity, understood alongside art and politics as an equally integral element of an ethos of liberation. At the same time, the film also shows Pasolini – as history itself leaves it little choice – as a failing figure whose restless searching culminates in an act of brutal violence, staged with the graphic directness typical of Ferrara.

The next two films were again made in close collaboration with Dafoe, who by then was also living in Italy. _Tommaso_ (2019) places an American expatriate artist in Rome at the centre of a loose narrative whose autobiographical undertones are difficult to miss, with Ferrara’s own domestic and creative surroundings being unusually close to the fictional material. Dafoe plays Ferrara’s quasi alter ego in recovery, living with a young wife and child, played by Cristina Chiriac and Anna Ferrara, the director’s actual wife and daughter. He teaches, works, moves through cafés, AA meetings and the Roman streets, while the fragile stability of this life is repeatedly disturbed by jealousy, memory and fantasy. _Siberia_ (2020) is more introspective, moving into the unstable terrain of surreal psychological drama, and brought Ferrara again to the Berlin Film Festival competition. Dafoe plays a man withdrawn to an unnamed, cold and remote place, where isolation does not bring peace but sets in motion a complex spiral of introspection and recurring traumatic memory.

_Zeros and Ones_ (2021) quite visibly came out of the pandemic conditions. Ethan Hawke moves through a Rome of soldiers, checkpoints, night streets and political rumours, and Ferrara lets the film remain jagged, thin and feverish instead of hiding the restrictions under which it was made. With _Padre Pio_ (2022), he returned to Catholic material in a more literal sense, though the film’s public reception was soon tied to Shia LaBeouf as much as to the saint. LaBeouf played Pio after spending time with Capuchin friars and later described the preparation as decisive for his turn to Catholicism. His confirmation in 2023 gave that story a second life around the film.

Abel Ferrara is a filmmaker who, despite often adverse production circumstances, has created a body of work marked by audacity, independence and a self-conscious disregard for the cultural registers of high and low, though not always consistent in quality (but whose is?). His present reception remains divided. In the United States, he is still valued above all for the genre films of the 1990s, while his more recent works, though highly present on the European festival circuit, unfortunately do not receive the attention and distribution they would deserve there. But regardless of the stage in his career, and whoever his collaborators are, Ferrara’s cinema has the unique signature of an auteur. It is spiritual, somatic and visceral in equal measure, and addresses deeply philosophical questions in cinematic forms where one would not necessarily expect them.

Patrick F. Campos is a Philippine film scholar, critic, curator, and professor at the University of the Philippines Film Institute. He is the author of _The End of National Cinema_ and editor-in-chief of _Pelikula._

### [Salvador Carrasco](https://www.sensesofcinema.com/author/salvador-carrasco/)

Salvador Carrasco is a Mexican film director based in Santa Monica, California. He is the writer, director, and editor of the highly acclaimed and influential feature film _La otra conquista_ (_The Other Conquest,_ 1999), which explores the multifaceted Aztec resistance to Spanish colonisation. The film was a cultural breakthrough, becoming the highest-grossing historical drama in Mexican cinema at the time of its release. It was selected by The _Los Angeles Times_ and _The New York Times_ as one of the Top Ten Films of 2000, and was re-released theatrically by Alliance Atlantis in 2008, earning a 90% rating from Rotten Tomatoes' top film critics. Committed to both cinema and education, Carrasco has received numerous film and academic awards. He taught directing at USC and the LA Film School and, as the Moseley Fellow in Creative Writing, screenwriting at Pomona College. Carrasco is a tenured professor at Santa Monica College, where he founded and now heads the Film Production Program, which has been featured in _Variety_ and _The Hollywood Reporter_ and repeatedly ranked by _MovieMaker_ magazine as one of the top film schools in North America. He has also been a guest film director at CinemadaMare in Italy, alongside directors Margarethe von Trotta, Paolo Sorrentino and Krzysztof Zanussi. Carrasco’s critical essays have been published by the _Los Angeles Times,_ the Latin American Studies Association (LASA), and _The Nation Books,_ among others. A regular contributor to _Senses of Cinema,_ he is currently preparing a new feature film, _Lovers,_ based on a short story by the Colombian writer Juan Gabriel Vásquez. More information can be found at [www.salvadorcarrasco.me](http://www.salvadorcarrasco.me/)

# Sodankylän elokuvajuhlien ohjaaja­vieraiksi Susan Seidelman ja Abderrahmane Sissako

Seidelmanin läpimurto­elokuva oli Madonnan tähdittämä ja 1980-luvun kultti­elokuvaksi kuvattu ”Missä olet, Susan?”.

![Image 6: Ilmakuva, jossa ihmisjono jonottaa suureen telttaan.](https://img.img-cdn.yle.fi/crop_extract,w_5271,h_2954,x_0,y_0/crop_fill,w_767,h_431,ar_16:9,dpr_1/f_auto/39-147969768498088e2d70/1749647811)

Avaa kuvien katselu

Sodankylän elokuvajuhlat järjestetään jälleen kesäkuussa. Anssi Mänttäri sekä Aki ja Mika Kaurismäki perustivat tapahtuman vuonna 1986.Kuva: Juuso Stoor / Yle

*   [Annu Passoja](https://yle.fi/p/56-74-429/fi)

15.5. 15:12

Kuuntele juttu 1:54

Sodankylän elokuvajuhlien nimekkäimpiä ohjaajavieraita ovat yhdysvaltalainen **Susan Seidelman** ja mauritanialais-malilainen **Abderrahmane Sissako**.

Seidelmanin tunnetuimpia elokuvia on 80-luvulla valmistunut komedia ”Missä olet, Susan?”, jonka toista pääosaa esitti pop-ikoni Madonna. Seidelmanilta nähdään Sodankylässä myös kolme muuta elokuvaa.

Sissakon tunnetuimpia elokuvia on monia palkintoja saanut, jihadismista kertova ”Timbuktu” sekä ”Bamako”, jossa käydään taistelua Maailmanpankkia ja Kansainvälistä valuuttarahastoa kohtaan. Sodankylässä esitetään neljä Sissakon elokuvaa. Hänen käsittelemiinsä teemoihin kuuluu esimerkiksi kolonialismi, siirtolaisuus ja uskonto.

Elokuvajuhlilla saa myös ensi-iltansa saksalaisen **İlker Çatakin** poliittinen jännäri ”Yellow letters”, joka palkittiin Berliinin elokuvajuhlien pääpalkinnolla.

Kotimaisista elokuvista esitetään muiden muassa **Tuomari Nurmion** konserttielokuva ”13 kylmää laulua”. Nurmio myös esiintyy Festivaaliklubilla.

Sodankylän elokuvajuhlien perustajiin kuuluvien **Aki** ja **Mika Kaurismäen** tuotannosta nähdään ”Le Havre” sekä ”Zombie ja kummitusjuna”. Molempia voi pitää muistonäytöksenä, sillä sekä ”Le Havressa” näyttelevä **Elina Salo** että ”Zombie ja kummitusjunan” miespääosan esittäjä **Silu Seppälä** kuolivat viime vuonna.

Le Havren leikkaaja, Jussi-patsaalla palkittu **Timo Linnasalo** menehtyi tämän vuoden alussa.

Sodankylän elokuvajuhlat järjestetään 10-14. kesäkuuta. Lipunmyynti alkaa toukokuun viimeisellä viikolla.

Abderrahmane Sissako ![Image 2](https://msfilmfestival.fi/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Abderrahmane_Sissako_at_Berlinale_2024-700x858.jpg) Subsaharan Africa has thus far been sadly, even shamefully underrepresented at our festival. But now, director Abderrahmane Sissako’s visit to our festival signifies another eminent addition to our already illustrious roster of Subsaharan guests, which so far has included the likes of Burkinabè director Idrissa Ouédraogo (who attended our festival in 1989), Malian director Souleymane Cissé (2011), and Chadian director Mahamat-Saleh Haroun (2018). Sissako, who was born in Mauritania but raised in Mali, is perhaps the most renowned African director of the 2000’s. Sissako directed his first short film, the student work _The Game_ (1989) in Moscow, and has since then been able to make only four feature-length African films (one of which is only an hour long), in addition to a Taiwanese co-production, _Black Tea_ (2024). But the quartet screened at our festival is the real deal, from [_Life on Earth_](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/movies/life-on-earth/) (1998), an originally made-for-TV film centered around the turn of the millennium, to the acclaimed [_Timbuktu_](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/movies/timbuktu/) (2014), which tackles the jihadism that plagues Western and Central Africa. The latter is a truly unique case in African cinema: the film not only earned Sissako an Oscar nomination for Best Foreign Language Film, but an astonishing seven wins at the Césars (France’s answer to the Oscars) – including Best Film and Best Director, making Sissako the first Black African filmmaker to win either award. The morning discussion with Sissako will surely be exceptionally fascinating to hear: How was he born in his mother’s homeland of Mauritania, but raised in his father’s homeland of Mali? How did he, following the example of his mother’s eldest son, end up studying film directing, thus spending around ten years in the USSR as the Union was circling the drain, before later moving to Paris? In 2002, Sissako won the International Federation of Film Critics (FIPRESCI) award for the film [_Waiting for Happiness_](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/movies/waiting-for-happiness/), after which the film was asked to be screened at the New York Film Festival. But the film was never screened there: like Finnish director Aki Kaurismäki, Sissako was boycotting the United States at the time due to the visa denial of Iranian filmmaker Abbas Kiarostami (who attended our festival in 2007). The conflicts of French West Africa as well as those between North and South play a prominent part in Sissako’s work, but he is no didactic preacher on a soapbox. Instead, with a loving and humane hand, Sissako places his focus on his characters, amid the wealth of African customs and traditions. On the other hand, even a Western viewer needs no special background knowledge in order to enjoy his films, in which the plot and dialogue are not central. Sissako places his trust in his painterly imagery and the poetic quality of his narration, as well as in music and humor. When I first saw Abderrahmane Sissako’s feature-length debut [_Life on Earth_](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/movies/life-on-earth/) nearly 30 years ago, I was distantly reminded of the films of Jacques Tati and Georgian-French director Otar Iosseliani. But Sissako’s influences are surely diverse, and in most of his films, closer to Africa. _Timo Malmi_ #### Festival * [Home](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/) * [News](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/ajankohtaista/) * [Partners](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/contact/partners/) * [Photo gallery](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/photo-gallery/) * [Contact](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/contact/) * [Volunteers 2026](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/volunteers/) * [History](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/history/) * [Travel & Stay](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/travel-stay/) * [Visitor Services](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/visitor-services/) * [Privacy Policy](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/privacy-policy/) #### Press * [Press](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/press/) * [News](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/ajankohtaista/) * [Photo gallery](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/photo-gallery/) #### Program * [Elokuvat](https://msfilmfestival.fi/elokuvat/) * [Vieraat](https://msfilmfestival.fi/vieraat/) * [Muu ohjelmisto](https://msfilmfestival.fi/muu-ohjelmisto/) ![Image 3: footer-logo](https://msfilmfestival.fi/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/footer-logo.png) © 2026 [Midnight Sun Film Festival.](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/)Made with ❤ by [Web-veistämö](http://web-veistamo.fi/ "Web-veistämön kotisivulle") [](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/guests/abderrahmane-sissako/)[](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/guests/abderrahmane-sissako/)[](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/guests/abderrahmane-sissako/)[](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/guests/abderrahmane-sissako/)

FEEDBACK](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/audience-feedback/ "AUDIENCE FEEDBACK") [Etusivu](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/) / [Guests](https://msfilmfestival.fi/vieraat/) / Marina Person # Marina Person ![Image 2](https://msfilmfestival.fi/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Marina-Person-700x933.jpeg) An actress, filmmaker and TV personality, Marina Person became known as a VJ on Brazilian MTV from 1995 to 2011. During those years of near-daily television reporting, she sculpted an on-screen persona that was effervescent and glamourous without losing depth and relatability. Marina rose to become a key interlocutor of pop-cultural life in Brazil, but as her auspicious run at MTV wound down, she plotted her next move. Following the footsteps of her filmmaker parents Luis Sérgio Person and Regina Jehá, she directed the theatrical features _Person_ (2004), which dealt with her father’s personal and historical legacy, and [_Califórnia_](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/movies/california/) (2015), her narrative debut reflecting on her youth in the tumultuous Brazil of the 1980s. Directing film and television is now Person’s primary activity, and so it came as a suprise to her when I offered her the lead in [_Isabel_](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/movies/isabel/)(2026). Why the choice? Marina Person embodies qualities of our shared city of São Paulo: she is scrappy, fast-moving, determined… You want to be her friend, you want to root for her. And for someone who has been so versatile and succesful in her career, I was interested in exploring the idea of failure and frustration with her, to find her more vulnerable side. I’m grateful to her for accepting the challenge, for going deep into the wine cellar with me. _Gabe Klinger_ #### Festival * [Home](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/) * [News](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/ajankohtaista/) * [Partners](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/contact/partners/) * [Photo gallery](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/photo-gallery/) * [Contact](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/contact/) * [Volunteers 2026](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/volunteers/) * [History](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/history/) * [Travel & Stay](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/travel-stay/) * [Visitor Services](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/visitor-services/) * [Privacy Policy](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/privacy-policy/) #### Press * [Press](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/press/) * [News](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/ajankohtaista/) * [Photo gallery](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/photo-gallery/) #### Program * [Elokuvat](https://msfilmfestival.fi/elokuvat/) * [Vieraat](https://msfilmfestival.fi/vieraat/) * [Muu ohjelmisto](https://msfilmfestival.fi/muu-ohjelmisto/) ![Image 3: footer-logo](https://msfilmfestival.fi/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/footer-logo.png) © 2026 [Midnight Sun Film Festival.](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/)Made with ❤ by [Web-veistämö](http://web-veistamo.fi/ "Web-veistämön kotisivulle") [](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/guests/marina-person/)[](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/guests/marina-person/)[](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/guests/marina-person/)[](https://msfilmfestival.fi/en/guests/marina-person/)

2](https://msfilmfestival.fi/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/juholiukkonen3-1-700x466.jpg) On the Saturday morning discussion, Brazilian director **Fernando Meirelles** told about his versatile career, which has included various works from video art to successful international films and from experimental TV series to opera. Meirelles remembers his first film experiences are related to his father’s movie clips which were shot on 16mm film. However, the career as a director was not Meirelles’s original plan. He grew up in São Paulo and after discontinuing his biology studies Meirelles studied architecture. He decided to become a filmmaker after seeing **Jorge Bodanzky** and **Orlando Senna**’s _Iracema_ (1975). It was a film that combined fiction and documentary such an exceptional way and was so impressive for Meirelles that he decided to make a short film as his final project and, as a result, made his introduction to the film industry. At the beginning of his career, Meirelles and his colleagues made experimental short films and video art. He also directed several years fun and experimental series and worked in advertising. However, the ads were not enough for Meirelles – instead, he dreamed of directing a feature film. He practiced directing a feature film with his first film _Maids_ (2001). “I always want to get involved in projects that make me feel insecure. The topics I don’t know much about and I usually even regret, that I agreed to take on such an impossible idea. For some reason, these work the best in the end.” Meirelles wanted to film **José Saramago**‘s novel _Blindness_, but because of the copyrights, the plan was almost canceled. One of the luckiest coincidences on Meirelles’s career was when the publisher of Saramago asked if Meirelles would be interested in directing **Paulo Lins**‘s novel _The City of God_. After a short moment of hesitation, Meirelles grasped this opportunity and chose a completely different topic. Meirelles’s The City of God was screened at the Cannes Film Festival and was a great success. The film was followed by another success, _The Constant Gardener_ (2005), after which Meirelles announced that he would stop making movies. However, he went back on his decision, as he finally got the opportunity to direct a film adaption of Blindness (2008). The film was followed by _360_ (2011) and then Meirelles returned to TV series. Even after that the director has still broken new ground. Trying something new has always inspired Meirelles. He has directed, for example, the opera _Les Pêcheurs de Perles_ in 2015 and the opening ceremony of the Olympic Games in Rio de Janeiro in 2016. Currently, the director has many projects in progress, including a climate crisis series for the BBC, a science documentary and the feature film _The Pope_ produced by Netflix. Meirelles would bring the film Iracema with him to a deserted island. Aamukeskustelussa Fernando Meirelles ![Image 2](https://msfilmfestival.fi/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/juholiukkonen3-1-700x466.jpg) Lauantain aamukeskustelussa brasilialainen ohjaaja **Fernando Meirelles**kertoi monipuolisesta urastaan, johon on mahtunut monenlaista videotaiteesta kansainvälisiin menestyselokuviin ja kokeellisista tv-sarjoista oopperaan. Meirellesin ensimmäiset elokuvakokemukset liittyvät hänen isänsä kuvaamiin, 16 millimetrisiin filmipätkiin. Ohjaajan ura ei ollut Sao Paulossa varttuneen Meirellesin alkuperäinen suunnitelma. Biologian opinnot keskeytettyään hän opiskeli arkkitehdiksi. Hän päätti ryhtyä elokuvantekijäksi katsottuaan **Jorge Bodanzkyn** ja **Orlando Sennan** elokuvan _Iraceman_ (1975). Ennennäkemättömällä tavalla fiktiota ja dokumenttia yhdistelevä elokuva teki Meirellesiin niin suuren vaikutuksen, että hän teki opintojensa lopputyöksi lyhytelokuvan ja sai sen myötä ensikosketuksen elokuva-alalle. Uransa alussa Meirelles kuvasi ystäviensä kanssa kokeellisia lyhytelokuvia ja videotaidetta. Hän myös ohjasi useita vuosia hauskoja ja kokeellisia sarjoja sekä työskenteli mainosmaailmassa. Mainokset eivät kuitenkaan riittäneet Meirellesille, vaan hän haaveili kokoillan elokuvan ohjaamisesta. Hän harjoitteli pitkän el okuvan ohjaamista esikoisellaan _Maids_ (2001). “Haluan aina olla mukana projekteissa, jotka saavat tuntemaan oloni epävarmaksi. Sellaisia, joiden aiheista en tiedä paljon ja yleensä kadun, että ylipäänsä suostuin ottamaan niin mahdottoman idean vastaan. Jostain syystä nämä toimivat lopulta kaikista parhaiten.” Meirel les olisi halunnut filmatisoida José Saramagon romaanin _Kertomus sokeudesta_, mutta oikeuksien takia suunnitelma oli jäädä haaveeksi. Yksi Meirellesin uran onnekkaimmista sattumista oli, kun Saramagon kustantaja kysyi, olisiko Meirelles kiinnostunut ohjaamaan **Paulo Linsin** romaanin _Jumalan kaupunki._ Alun epäröinnin jälkeen Meirelles tarttui tähän täysin erilaiseen aiheeseen. Meirellesin ohjaama _Jumalan kaupunki_ -elokuva esitettiin Cannesin elokuvajuhlilla, ja se saavutti suuren suosion. _Jumalan kaupunkia_ seurasi toinen menestyselokuva _Uskollinen puutarhuri_ (2005), jonka jälkeen Meirelles ilmoitti lopettavansa elokuvien teon. Hän kuitenkin pyörsi päätöksensä, kun hänelle tuli tilaisuus ohjata aiemmin havittelemansa Saramagon romaani. _Blindness_-elokuvasovitusta (2008)seurasi elokuva _360_(2011). Sen jälkeen Meirelles palasi tv-sarjojen pariin, mutta on ohjaaja tehnyt niiden jälkeenkin uusia aluevaltauksia. Uuden kokeileminen on aina viehättänyt Meirellesiä. Hän on ohjannut muun muassa _Les Pêcheurs de Perles_ -oopperateoksen vuonna 2015 ja Rio de Janeiron olympialaisten avajaisshow’n vuonna 2016. Tällä hetkellä ohjaajalla on monta projektia käynnissä, muun muassa ilmastokriisiä käsittelevä sarja BBC:lle, tiededokumentti sekä Netflixin tuottama elokuva _The Pope_. # Iracema

Brazil, West Germany, and France co-produced feature film

![Image 1](https://gbaike-image.cdn.bcebos.com/f31fbe096b63f6246b60247d8112fcf81a4c510f050d/f31fbe096b63f6246b60247d8112fcf81a4c510f050d_3_4?x-bce-process=image/format,f_auto)

Iracema is a 1974 Brazilian, West German, and French co-produced drama film co-directed by Jorge Bodanzky and Orlando Senna, who also co-wrote the screenplay, collaborating with writer Hermanno Penna to complete the narrative structure. The film tells the road journey of an indigenous woman, Iracema, who leaves the Amazon rainforest for the city. It blends fictional narrative with pseudo-documentary techniques, using an ecological critique perspective to depict the destruction of the natural environment and human relationships by capitalism.

1

The film employs the "new cinema" aesthetic style that followed Brazil's Cinema Novo, featuring both non-professional and professional actors. It had its world premiere at the Taormina Film Festival in Italy in July 1975, was released in Swedish theaters on February 20 of the following year, the French-language version was released in France on June 2, 1976, and it was released in the United States on May 25, 1982. The main cast includes Paulo César Pereio and Edna de Cássia, the latter making her screen debut in the role of the female lead Iracema.

Plot Introduction

The film Iracema, originally titled Iracema - Uma Transa Amazônica (English: Iracema: An Amazonian Transaction), also known as Iracema, tells the road journey of a young Indigenous woman, Iracema, who leaves her Amazonian village for the city, and presents the cultural conflict between urban and rural areas through the road movie format.

The film was produced by Orlando Senna. Cinematography was handled by Jorge Bodanzky. The music was composed by Jorge Bodanzky and Achim Tappen. Art direction was overseen by Orlando Senna. Editing was completed by Jorge Bodanzky and Eva Grundmann. Sound was handled by Achim Tappen.

5

Behind the Scenes / Production

The entire film was shot on 16mm film, combining naturalistic lighting with handheld cinematography to create a distinct visual documentary style. The scene design encompasses the Amazon Rainforest, interstate highways, and emerging industrial zones, enhancing regional authenticity through on-location shooting. The sound design emphasizes ambient sound recording, paired with Portuguese dialogue to construct regional cultural characteristics.

5

The film was completed in 1974.

6

Promotion and Release

The film was a co-production between República Federativa do Brasil, West Germany, and France. It had its world premiere at the Taormina Film Festival in Italy in July 1975. It was released in Sweden cinemas on February 20 of the following year, becoming the first representative work of Cinema Novo to be publicly screened in the Nordic region. It was released in France on June 2, 1976. The film was released in the The United States of America on May 25, 1982. A restored version was re-released in Rzeczpospolita Polska on June 20, 2007.

2

Film Characteristics

The film employs the Cinema Novo style of Brazil, blending fictional and documentary techniques, incorporating a road-trip plot, and, from an ecologically avant-garde perspective, reveals the reality that trees, animals, and people had already suffered from exploitative capitalism 50 years ago.

3

Artistic Evaluation

Film critics regard the film as pioneering the "eco-critical film" genre, and its narrative strategy of blending fiction and documentary is referred to as "Amazonian neorealism." The seven-minute aerial shot of the rainforest in the film has become an important resource for later studies of Amazonian ecological imagery from the 1970s. In 2003, the Brazilian Film Archive designated it as part of the "National Image Heritage" for permanent preservation.

Paul Sparks is an American actor. He is known for his role as Mickey Doyle in the HBO period drama series Boardwalk Empire and for his Primetime Emmy Award-nominated role as Thomas Yates in the Netflix political drama series House of Cards. He has also appeared in the films Deception (2008), Afterschool (2008), The Missing Person (2008), Mud (2012), Parkland (2013), and Stealing Cars (2015). ×

# Paul Sparks

Highest Rated: 100%  Hands That Bind (2021)

Lowest Rated: 10%  Deception (2008)

Birthday: Oct 16, 1971

Birthplace: Lawton, Oklahoma, USA

American actor Paul Sparks is most widely recognized as the imposing Mickey Doyle on the period drama "Boardwalk Empire" (HBO, 2010-14). After beginning his screen career with a few one-off TV-show appearances, the tall performer was involved in the 2003 Broadway production of the baseball play "Take Me Out." Returning to television in 2005, Sparks was featured on an episode of "Law & Order: Criminal Intent" (NBC, 2001-2011) and later had his first recurring role on the crime drama "Brotherhood" (Showtime, 2006-08). He subsequently focused on film productions, turning up in small parts in the 2008 independent dramas "Synecdoche, New York" and "Rachel Getting Married." In 2010, Sparks was cast as Doyle on "Boardwalk Empire," marking a major step forward in his career. The following year, he had a small part in the HBO production of "Mildred Pierce," reinforcing his effectiveness in dramas set in the past and positioning him as an actor just warming up to roles that fit his talent.

# Paul Sparks

Highest Rated: 100%  Hands That Bind (2021)

Lowest Rated: 10%  Deception (2008)

Birthday: Oct 16, 1971

Birthplace: Lawton, Oklahoma, USA

American actor Paul Sparks is most widely recognized as the imposing Mickey Doyle on the period drama "Boardwalk Empire" (HBO, 2010-14). After beginning his screen career with a few one-off TV-show appearances, the tall performer was involved in the 2003 Broadway production of the baseball play "Take Me Out." Returning to television in 2005, Sparks was featured on an episode of "Law & Order: Criminal Intent" (NBC, 2001-2011) and later had his first recurring role on the crime drama "Brotherhood" (Showtime, 2006-08). He subsequently focused on film productions, turning up in small parts in the 2008 independent dramas "Synecdoche, New York" and "Rachel Getting Married." In 2010, Sparks was cast as Doyle on "Boardwalk Empire," marking a major step forward in his career. The following year, he had a small part in the HBO production of "Mildred Pierce," reinforcing his effectiveness in dramas set in the past and positioning him as an actor just warming up to roles that fit his talent.

Paul Sparks is an American actor. He is known for his role as Mickey Doyle in the HBO period drama series Boardwalk Empire and for his Primetime Emmy Award-nominated role as Thomas Yates in the Netflix political drama series House of Cards. He has also appeared in the films Deception (2008), Afterschool (2008), The Missing Person (2008), Mud (2012), Parkland (2013), and Stealing Cars (2015). ×

### Biography

Paul Sparks is an American actor. He is known for his role as Mickey Doyle in the HBO period drama series Boardwalk Empire and for his Primetime Emmy Award-nominated role as Thomas Yates in the Netflix political drama series House of Cards. He has also appeared in the films Deception (2008), Afterschool (2008), The Missing Person (2008), Mud (2012), Parkland (2013), and Stealing Cars (2015).

#### Your Privacy

When you visit any website, it may store or retrieve information on your browser, mostly in the form of cookies. This information might be about you, your preferences, or your device, and is mostly used to make the site work as you expect. The information does not usually identify you directly, but it can give you a more personalized web experience. Because we respect your right to privacy, you can choose not to allow some types of cookies. Click on the different category headings to learn more and change our default settings. Blocking some types of cookies may impact your experience of the site and the services we are able to offer. 

[More information](https://cookiepedia.co.uk/giving-consent-to-cookies)

#### Strictly Necessary Cookies

Always Active

These cookies are necessary for the website to function and cannot be switched off in our systems. They also help us to remember prior selections you have made, such as setting your privacy preferences, such as setting your privacy preferences, logging in or filling in forms. You can set your browser to block or alert you about these cookies, but some parts of the site will not then work.

#### Performance Cookies

- [x] Performance Cookies 

These cookies allow us to count visits and traffic sources so we can measure and improve the performance of our site. They help us to know which pages are the most and least popular and see how visitors move around the site. If you do not allow these cookies, we will have less information to help us improve the site’s functionality.

#### Functional Cookies

- [x] Functional Cookies 

These cookies enable the website to provide enhanced functionality and personalization, such as remembering language settings and customer service chat history. If you do not allow these cookies, then some or all of these services may not function properly.

#### Social Media Cookies

- [x] Social Media Cookies 

These cookies are set by a range of social media services that we have added to the site to enable you to share our content with your friends and networks. They are capable of tracking your browser across other sites and building up a profile of your interests. This may impact the content and messages you see on other websites you visit. If you do not allow these cookies you may not be able to use or see these sharing tools.

#### Targeting Cookies

- [x] Targeting Cookies 

These cookies may be set through our site by our advertising partners. They may be used by those companies to build a profile of your interests and show you relevant adverts on this and other sites. If you do not allow these cookies, you will still see advertising, but it will not be targeted to your specific interests.

#### November 22, 1963, 12:38 pm - A trauma patient is rushed to Parkland Memorial Hospital in Dallas. His name is President John F.Kennedy.

November 22nd, 1963 was a day that changed the world forever — when young American President John F. Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas, Texas. This film follows, almost in real time, a handful of individuals forced to make split-second decisions after an event that would change their lives and forever alter the world’s landscape.

proud to be 1 of 562 people to have seen Trust Me and to have watched the entire directorial catalog of Clark Gregg (two movies). i really liked most of this super indie feature. howard, the main character played by gregg, is such a noble underdog and has a great arc. for an industry piece, the inside baseball stuff never gets too cringe, which is important, but the ending does zag quite a bit. its maybe 2-3 scenes and a better finish away from being a super solid sophomore film from gregg. glad i watched it tho :)

[Review by **Matt**](https://letterboxd.com/mattmahogany/film/trust-me/ "Read Matt’s review")

Borders on brilliant for the first hour where writer/director/lead Clark Gregg (him from those superhero films the kids love) channels his inner Ari Gold, giving us a really well acted drama of an agent trying to help both a prodigious young star and his own reputation.

It sadly takes a nosedive into melodrama and cliche in its final act though, and while Sam Rockwell and Alison Janney's support is frustratingly underused I couldn't help but think how much better the whole thing would've been if Clark had stuck with the more sensible - and enjoyable - first sixty or so minutes.

A tight script and really crisp dialog stand out in Gregg's second feature film. A slinky, noir-inspired score by Kilian is also welcome. Everyone delivers fine performances, and Gregg and Rockwell are great in their scenes together, and Sharbino and Sparks do especially well, too. The film also provides a biting and unflattering look at the business behind making movies, and casting them specifically. It feels very personal to Gregg, watching along, and you can tell a very focused attention was given to its production. More of Gregg in starring roles, please.

Clark Gregg's Trust Me is a good little film that sucks you in with some great comedy and good little cameos and before you know it the drama and heart at the centre of it has sucked you in ready to gut punch you with its ending. Gregg's Hollywood agent is such a lovable loser that you can't help but empathise with him and that is a true skill demonstrated by Gregg as both writer and actor. His direction leaves something to be desired however but not in any major ways, somebody else may have taken their time to develop the dramatic moments further for example but in true Hollywood stories about Hollywood style it's told at a frenetic pace that leaves no room for wonder or allows for pauses for breath.

Definitely not a widely known film, and one of Clark Gregg’s two directorial efforts. He also wrote the film.

Gregg, who I know best as Agent Phil Coulson from the MCU, stars as Howard Holloway, a struggling agent in Hollywood who is hoping to land a young actress as a client and take him back to the spotlight.

The film has a ton of high profile actors in it, like Sam Rockwell, Allison Janney, and William H. Macy to name a few. It’s a decent enough look at the job of a lower end talent agent which is not a subject I’ve seen covered too much.

I don’t think the film entirely sticks the last act and particularly the ending, but as a low-budget outing it’s a good watch.

Clark Gregg goes proto-neo-noir for his sophomore directorial effort. Those two ladies are the true north for Howard Holloway and everyone else is due south. Gregg has an interesting eye as a director, capturing the rushed world of Hollywood wheeling and dealing as well as the relaxed “real life” experiences around it. Everyone else, skip it See more Apr 4, 2021 I don't know why I am just finding this movie in 2021. What a fantastic treasure to discover. This off-center romance was well acted, well written, and well paced. The music and set design could be considered another character. Incredibly, we never learn the name of the female main character, but her fear of living outside her well managed world is deftly and delicately portrayed. It is clear she wants more from the world, and in Wes, I hope she finds it. The intimate conversations edged close to being uncomfortable, as they should, but the love story effortlessly rebounds the discomfort, and makes it okay to squirm a little with them on their journey. Although only one of them has relegated themselves to a life in the bunker, they both seem to yearn for the same thing. I can say definitively, this movie left me wanting to know more about them, but it is quite alright that I don't. [Review by **BilboBallin**](link_74)[1](link_74)

proud to be 1 of 562 people to have seen Trust Me and to have watched the entire directorial catalog of Clark Gregg (two movies). i really liked most of this super indie feature. howard, the main character played by gregg, is such a noble underdog and has a great arc. for an industry piece, the inside baseball stuff never gets too cringe, which is important, but the ending does zag quite a bit. its maybe 2-3 scenes and a better finish away from being a super solid sophomore film from gregg. glad i watched it tho :)

[![Image 12: Matt](https://a.ltrbxd.com/resized/avatar/upload/7/1/7/5/1/6/shard/avtr-0-80-0-80-crop.jpg?v=9a0ca3bf11)](https://letterboxd.com/mattmahogany/ [link_75])

[Review by **Matt**](link_76)

Borders on brilliant for the first hour where writer/director/lead Clark Gregg (him from those superhero films the kids love) channels his inner Ari Gold, giving us a really well acted drama of an agent trying to help both a prodigious young star and his own reputation.

It sadly takes a nosedive into melodrama and cliche in its final act though, and while Sam Rockwell and Alison Janney's support is frustratingly underused I couldn't help but think how much better the whole thing would've been if Clark had stuck with the more sensible - and enjoyable - first sixty or so minutes.

[Review by **David Hatfield**](link_82)

> _"Did you ever think some deep down place that you were really something else?"_

A tight script and really crisp dialog stand out in Gregg's second feature film. A slinky, noir-inspired score by Kilian is also welcome. Everyone delivers fine performances, and Gregg and Rockwell are great in their scenes together, and Sharbino and Sparks do especially well, too. The film also provides a biting and unflattering look at the business behind making movies, and casting them specifically. It feels very personal to Gregg, watching along, and you can tell a very focused attention was given to its production. More of Gregg in starring roles, please.

I salute Clark Gregg for going a fantastic job, for doing the main three things you can do in a movie. It just lacked a little bit of what I wanted.

[Review by **bbbgtoby**](link_88)

Clark Gregg's Trust Me is a good little film that sucks you in with some great comedy and good little cameos and before you know it the drama and heart at the centre of it has sucked you in ready to gut punch you with its ending. Gregg's Hollywood agent is such a lovable loser that you can't help but empathise with him and that is a true skill demonstrated by Gregg as both writer and actor. His direction leaves something to be desired however but not in any major ways, somebody else may have taken their time to develop the dramatic moments further for example but in true Hollywood stories about Hollywood style it's told at a frenetic pace that leaves no room for wonder or allows for pauses for breath.

[![Image 19: Lockerus](https://a.ltrbxd.com/resized/avatar/upload/7/1/4/0/0/8/shard/avtr-0-80-0-80-crop.jpg?v=3899cabfea)](https://letterboxd.com/lockerus/ [link_89])

[Review by **Lockerus**](link_90)

Definitely not a widely known film, and one of Clark Gregg’s two directorial efforts. He also wrote the film.

Gregg, who I know best as Agent Phil Coulson from the MCU, stars as Howard Holloway, a struggling agent in Hollywood who is hoping to land a young actress as a client and take him back to the spotlight.

The film has a ton of high profile actors in it, like Sam Rockwell, Allison Janney, and William H. Macy to name a few. It’s a decent enough look at the job of a lower end talent agent which is not a subject I’ve seen covered too much.

I don’t think the film entirely sticks the last act and particularly the ending, but as a low-budget outing it’s a good watch.

[![Image 20: Michael Vazquez](https://a.ltrbxd.com/resized/avatar/upload/3/8/9/2/3/shard/avtr-0-80-0-80-crop.jpg?v=6430777331)](https://letterboxd.com/michael11391/ [link_91])

[Review by **Michael Vazquez**](link_92)

It’s not very comedic nor intriguing enough. A couple of actors are underused from the supporting side. But I give Clark Gregg the benefit of the doubt for trying. He went for it and I appreciated that.

[Review by **Chris**](link_94)

Interesting movie directed by Clark Gregg with a really good cast. Sweet story, but the last few minutes were weird as fuck.

Given that the opening shot shows the heroine on the toilet, what a nice surprise to find that this is a pure love story, told with elegance and simplicity on a low budget. A mannered, occasionally mesmerizing romance that frequently cops to its own artificiality. Go to Full Review  Mat Bradley-Tschirgi  Battleship Pretension Dec 8, 2020 Sparrows Dance is a unique romantic comedy in that it's asking the viewer to follow around the romantic apartment bound exploits of a pair of withdrawn loners. Go to Full Review  Stephen Saito  Moveable Fest Dec 17, 2018 The real beauty of "Sparrows Dance" is seeing all the artifice of its movie trappings fall away, a construction that Buschel asks the audience to confront directly in a slow dance scene Go to Full Review  Jared Mobarak  The Film Stage Jun 28, 2016

B+

Sparrows Dance unfolds like a play with its emotion projected through cadence, carefully written words, and an excitingly raw series of expressive body language. Go to Full Review  Read all reviews

It is clear she wants more from the world, and in Wes, I hope she finds it. The intimate conversations edged close to being uncomfortable, as they should, but the love story effortlessly rebounds the discomfort, and makes it okay to squirm a little with them on their journey. ### Synopsis

#### November 22, 1963, 12:38 pm - A trauma patient is rushed to Parkland Memorial Hospital in Dallas. His name is President John F.Kennedy.

November 22nd, 1963 was a day that changed the world forever — when young American President John F. Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas, Texas. This film follows, almost in real time, a handful of individuals forced to make split-second decisions after an event that would change their lives and forever alter the world’s landscape.

### Synopsis

#### November 22, 1963, 12:38 pm - A trauma patient is rushed to Parkland Memorial Hospital in Dallas. His name is President John F.Kennedy.

November 22nd, 1963 was a day that changed the world forever — when young American President John F. Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas, Texas. This film follows, almost in real time, a handful of individuals forced to make split-second decisions after an event that would change their lives and forever alter the world’s landscape.

Peter Landesman(born 3 January 1965) is an American screenwriter, film director, producer, journalist, novelist and painter. He wrote a number of cover stories for The New York Times Magazine,The New Yorker,The Atlantic Monthly, and others, including investigations into global arms trafficking, sex trafficking, refugee trafficking, the Rwandan genocide, and the creation and smuggling of forged and stolen art and antiquities. He also reported on the conflicts in Kosovo,Rwanda, Pakistan and Afghanistan post-9/11.

As a filmmaker, he wrote and directed the biographical films Parkland(2013),Concussion (2015) and Mark Felt: The Man Who Brought Down the White House(2017). ×

### Synopsis

#### November 22, 1963, 12:38 pm - A trauma patient is rushed to Parkland Memorial Hospital in Dallas. His name is President John F.Kennedy.

November 22nd, 1963 was a day that changed the world forever — when young American President John F. Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas, Texas. This film follows, almost in real time, a handful of individuals forced to make split-second decisions after an event that would change their lives and forever alter the world’s landscape.

##### Written by [GenerationofSwine](https://www.themoviedb.org/u/GenerationofSwine/reviews) on January 12, 2023

I can see why people don't like this.

It is the singular most depressing movie I've ever seen.

It's not like JFK where it pushes a theory. It just focuses on the death of the president and it's done in such a way that's designed to bring you to tears again and again.

I'm probably never going to watch this again, it's a little too much for me. But, if you are looking for a film that is going to invoke a visceral emotional response in the audience, than Parkland is the movie for you.

Robert Clark Gregg Jr. (born April 2, 1962) is an American actor, director, and screenwriter. He is best known for portraying Phil Coulson in films and television series set in the Marvel Cinematic Universe from 2008 to 2021. Gregg also voiced Coulson in the animated television series Ultimate Spider-Man (2012–2017) and the video games Lego Marvel Super Heroes (2013), Marvel Heroes (2013), and Lego Marvel's Avengers (2016).

Gregg is also known for his role as FBI Special Agent Mike Casper on the NBC political drama series The West Wing (2001–2004) and as Richard, the ex-husband of Christine Campbell, in the CBS sitcom The New Adventures of Old Christine (2006–2010).

He wrote the horror film What Lies Beneath (2000)and wrote and directed the black comedy Choke (2008) and the comedy-drama Trust Me (2013). He appeared in the films The Adventures of Sebastian Cole (1998), One Hour Photo (2002), We Were Soldiers (2002), In Good Company (2004), When a Stranger Calls (2006), 500 Days of Summer (2009), Much Ado About Nothing (2012), The To Do List (2013), Labour Day (2013), Live by Night (2016), and Being the Ricardos (2021). ×

proud to be 1 of 562 people to have seen Trust Me and to have watched the entire directorial catalog of Clark Gregg (two movies). i really liked most of this super indie feature. howard, the main character played by gregg, is such a noble underdog and has a great arc. for an industry piece, the inside baseball stuff never gets too cringe, which is important, but the ending does zag quite a bit. its maybe 2-3 scenes and a better finish away from being a super solid sophomore film from gregg. glad i watched it tho :)

[Review by **Matt**](https://letterboxd.com/mattmahogany/film/trust-me/ "Read Matt’s review")

Borders on brilliant for the first hour where writer/director/lead Clark Gregg (him from those superhero films the kids love) channels his inner Ari Gold, giving us a really well acted drama of an agent trying to help both a prodigious young star and his own reputation.

It sadly takes a nosedive into melodrama and cliche in its final act though, and while Sam Rockwell and Alison Janney's support is frustratingly underused I couldn't help but think how much better the whole thing would've been if Clark had stuck with the more sensible - and enjoyable - first sixty or so minutes.

> _"Did you ever think some deep down place that you were really something else?"_

A tight script and really crisp dialog stand out in Gregg's second feature film. A slinky, noir-inspired score by Kilian is also welcome. Everyone delivers fine performances, and Gregg and Rockwell are great in their scenes together, and Sharbino and Sparks do especially well, too. The film also provides a biting and unflattering look at the business behind making movies, and casting them specifically. It feels very personal to Gregg, watching along, and you can tell a very focused attention was given to its production. More of Gregg in starring roles, please.

[Review by **Sarah Collins**](https://letterboxd.com/sarahcollins/film/trust-me/ "Read Sarah Collins’s review")

I rate it three stars because it was a good try, but it didn't intrigue me all the most really. It had a stunning cast which had a lot of mixed actors that do shine in the best of places, but just not enough for me to make me love their characters. I salute Clark Gregg for going a fantastic job, for doing the main three things you can do in a movie. It just lacked a little bit of what I wanted.
