**Rachel Hannah Weisz** ([/v aɪ s/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English");[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-2) born 7 March 1970)[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-birthplace-9) is a British actress. Known for her roles in [independent films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_films "Independent films") and [blockbusters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blockbuster_(entertainment) "Blockbuster (entertainment)"), she has received [several awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_awards_and_nominations_received_by_Rachel_Weisz "List of awards and nominations received by Rachel Weisz"), including an [Academy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award "Academy Award"), a [British Academy Film Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Academy_Film_Award "British Academy Film Award"), a [Golden Globe Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award "Golden Globe Award"), a [Screen Actors Guild Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screen_Actors_Guild_Award "Screen Actors Guild Award"), and a [Laurence Olivier Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurence_Olivier_Award "Laurence Olivier Award").

Weisz began acting in stage and television productions in the early 1990s, and made her film debut in _[Death Machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death\_Machine "Death Machine")_ (1994). She won a [Critics' Circle Theatre Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critics'_Circle_Theatre_Award "Critics' Circle Theatre Award") for her role in the 1994 revival of [Noël Coward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No%C3%ABl_Coward "Noël Coward")'s play _[Design for Living](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Design\_for\_Living "Design for Living")_, and went on to appear in the 1999 [Donmar Warehouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donmar_Warehouse "Donmar Warehouse") production of [Tennessee Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee_Williams "Tennessee Williams")' drama _[Suddenly Last Summer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suddenly\_Last\_Summer "Suddenly Last Summer")_. Her film breakthrough came with her starring role as [Evelyn Carnahan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evelyn_Carnahan "Evelyn Carnahan") in the Hollywood action films _[The Mummy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Mummy\_(1999\_film) "The Mummy (1999 film)")_ (1999) and _[The Mummy Returns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Mummy\_Returns "The Mummy Returns")_ (2001).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-hollywood_debut-10) Weisz went on to star in several films of the 2000s, including _[Enemy at the Gates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enemy\_at\_the\_Gates "Enemy at the Gates")_ (2001), _[About a Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/About\_a\_Boy\_(film) "About a Boy (film)")_ (2002), _[Runaway Jury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runaway\_Jury "Runaway Jury")_ (2003), _[Constantine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantine\_(film) "Constantine (film)")_ (2005), _[The Fountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Fountain "The Fountain")_ (2006), _[Definitely, Maybe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Definitely,\_Maybe "Definitely, Maybe")_ (2008), _[The Lovely Bones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Lovely\_Bones\_(film) "The Lovely Bones (film)")_ (2009) and _[The Whistleblower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Whistleblower "The Whistleblower")_ (2010).

For her performance as an activist in the 2005 thriller _[The Constant Gardener](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Constant\_Gardener\_(film) "The Constant Gardener (film)")_, she won the [Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Supporting_Actress "Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress"), and for playing [Blanche DuBois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blanche_DuBois "Blanche DuBois") in a 2009 revival of _[A Streetcar Named Desire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Streetcar\_Named\_Desire "A Streetcar Named Desire")_, she won the [Laurence Olivier Award for Best Actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurence_Olivier_Award_for_Best_Actress "Laurence Olivier Award for Best Actress"). In the 2010s, Weisz continued to star in big-budget films such as the action film _[The Bourne Legacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Bourne\_Legacy\_(film) "The Bourne Legacy (film)")_ (2012) and the fantasy film _[Oz the Great and Powerful](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oz\_the\_Great\_and\_Powerful "Oz the Great and Powerful")_ (2013) and achieved critical acclaim for her performances in the independent films _[The Deep Blue Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Deep\_Blue\_Sea\_(2011\_film) "The Deep Blue Sea (2011 film)")_ (2011), _[Denial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denial\_(2016\_film) "Denial (2016 film)")_ (2016), and _[The Favourite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Favourite\_(2018\_film) "The Favourite (2018 film)")_ (2018). For her portrayal of [Sarah Churchill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Churchill,_Duchess_of_Marlborough "Sarah Churchill, Duchess of Marlborough") in _The Favourite_, she won the [BAFTA Award for Best Actress in a Supporting Role](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Actress_in_a_Supporting_Role "BAFTA Award for Best Actress in a Supporting Role") and received a second Academy Award nomination.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-11) Weisz portrayed [Melina Vostokoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melina_Vostokoff_(Marvel_Cinematic_Universe) "Melina Vostokoff (Marvel Cinematic Universe)") in the [Marvel Cinematic Universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvel_Cinematic_Universe "Marvel Cinematic Universe") film _[Black Widow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black\_Widow\_(2021\_film) "Black Widow (2021 film)")_ (2021) and starred as twin obstetricians in the thriller miniseries _[Dead Ringers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead\_Ringers\_(miniseries) "Dead Ringers (miniseries)")_ (2023).

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rachel_Weisz&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Weisz was born on 7 March 1970 in [Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster "Westminster"), [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), and grew up in [Hampstead Garden Suburb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hampstead_Garden_Suburb "Hampstead Garden Suburb").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-12) In 1938, before [WW2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WW2 "WW2"), her parents as children had come to the UK to escape the [Nazis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazis "Nazis").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-13)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-14)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-15)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-16) Her father, George Weisz, was a [Hungarian Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Jewish "Hungarian Jewish") mechanical engineer and inventor known for pioneering a type of [ventilator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ventilator "Ventilator").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-17)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-18)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-19) Her mother, Edith Ruth ([née](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_name#Maiden_and_married_names "Birth name") Teich),[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-20) was a teacher, and later a psychotherapist, originally from [Vienna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna "Vienna"), Austria.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-thisislondon-21)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-22) Her maternal grandfather's ancestry was [Austrian Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austrian_Jewish "Austrian Jewish"); her maternal grandmother was [Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic "Catholic") and of Italian ancestry.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-23)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-24)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-25)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-26)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-27) The scholar and [social activist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_activist "Social activist")[James Parkes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Parkes_(priest) "James Parkes (priest)") helped her mother's family to leave Austria for England.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-People-Denial-2016-28) Weisz's mother was raised in the Catholic church and formally [converted to Judaism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Converted_to_Judaism "Converted to Judaism") upon marrying Weisz's father.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-theguardian.com-29)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-naie-30) Weisz's maternal grandfather was Alexander Teich, a Jewish activist who had been a secretary of the [World Union of Jewish Students](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Union_of_Jewish_Students "World Union of Jewish Students").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-llev-31)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-rasl-32)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-mrp-33)

Her younger sister [Minnie Weisz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnie_Weisz "Minnie Weisz") is a [visual artist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fine-art_photography "Fine-art photography").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-34) Weisz's parents valued the arts; they encouraged their children to form opinions of their own by engaging their participation in family debates.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-talk-35) Weisz left [North London Collegiate School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_London_Collegiate_School "North London Collegiate School") and attended [Benenden School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benenden_School "Benenden School") for one year, completing her [A-levels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A-level "A-level") at [St Paul's Girls School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Paul's_Girls_School "St Paul's Girls School").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-Yahoo-36)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-37)

Known for being an "[English rose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_rose_(epithet) "English rose (epithet)")",[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-38)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-39)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-HelloMagazine-40)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-theguardian.com-29) Weisz began modelling at the age of 14.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-41) In 1984, she gained public attention when she turned down an offer to star in _[King David](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King\_David\_(film) "King David (film)")_ with [Richard Gere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Gere "Richard Gere").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-Yahoo-36)

In 1988, Weisz went up to [Trinity Hall, Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_Hall,_Cambridge "Trinity Hall, Cambridge"), taking a [2:1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2:1 "2:1") in [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_literary_studies "English literary studies"). At Trinity Hall, she was a contemporary of [Sacha Baron Cohen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacha_Baron_Cohen "Sacha Baron Cohen"), [Alexander Armstrong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Armstrong "Alexander Armstrong"), [Emily Maitlis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emily_Maitlis "Emily Maitlis"), [Sue Perkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Perkins "Sue Perkins"), [Mel Giedroyc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel_Giedroyc "Mel Giedroyc"), [Richard Osman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Osman "Richard Osman") and [Ben Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Miller "Ben Miller") (whom she dated briefly).[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-42) She appeared in student plays, co-founding an all-female student drama group _Cambridge Talking Tongues_.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-43) The group won a _Guardian_ Student Drama Award at the 1991 [Edinburgh Festival Fringe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh_Festival_Fringe "Edinburgh Festival Fringe") for an improvised two-woman–show piece written by Weisz herself called _Slight Possession_,[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-ncg-44) directed by David Farr.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-45)

Weisz then trained under master clown [Philippe Gaulier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippe_Gaulier "Philippe Gaulier") at [École Philippe Gaulier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89cole_Philippe_Gaulier "École Philippe Gaulier").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-46)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-47)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rachel_Weisz&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### 1990s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rachel_Weisz&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1990s")]

In 1992, Weisz appeared in the television film _Advocates II_, followed by roles in the _[Inspector Morse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inspector\_Morse\_(TV\_series) "Inspector Morse (TV series)")_ episode "[Twilight of the Gods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twilight_of_the_Gods_(Inspector_Morse) "Twilight of the Gods (Inspector Morse)")", and the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC")'s steamy period drama _[Scarlet and Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scarlet\_and\_Black\_(TV\_series) "Scarlet and Black (TV series)")_, alongside [Ewan McGregor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ewan_McGregor "Ewan McGregor").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-MSNF-48)_Dirty Something_, a BBC Screen Two, hour-long television film made in 1992, was Weisz's first film.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-49)

Weisz's breakthrough role on the stage was that of Gilda in [Sean Mathias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Mathias "Sean Mathias")'s 1994 revival of [Noël Coward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No%C3%ABl_Coward "Noël Coward")'s _[Design for Living](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Design\_for\_Living "Design for Living")_ at the [Gielgud Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gielgud_Theatre "Gielgud Theatre"),[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-esu-50)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-wen-51) for which she received the London Critics' Circle Award for the most promising newcomer.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-52)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-53) Her portrayal was described as "wonderful" by a contemporary review.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-54)

Weisz started her film career with a minor role in the 1994 film _[Death Machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death\_Machine "Death Machine")_;[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-MSNF-48) her first major role came in the 1996 film _[Chain Reaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chain\_Reaction\_(1996\_film) "Chain Reaction (1996 film)")_.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-55) The film received mostly negative reviews–it holds a 16% rating on [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes")[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-56) and was a minor financial success.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-57) She next appeared as Miranda Fox in _[Stealing Beauty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stealing\_Beauty "Stealing Beauty")_, directed by [Bernardo Bertolucci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernardo_Bertolucci "Bernardo Bertolucci"),[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-58) where she was first labelled an "English rose".[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-HelloMagazine-40)

Weisz found roles in the 1997 American drama _[Swept from the Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swept\_from\_the\_Sea "Swept from the Sea")_,[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-59) the 1998 British television comedy-drama _[My Summer with Des](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My\_Summer\_with\_Des "My Summer with Des")_, [Michael Winterbottom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Winterbottom "Michael Winterbottom")'s crime film _[I Want You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I\_Want\_You\_(1998\_film) "I Want You (1998 film)")_,[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-indmagaz-60) and [David Leland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Leland "David Leland")'s _[The Land Girls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Land\_Girls "The Land Girls")_, based on [Angela Huth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angela_Huth "Angela Huth")'s book of the same name.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-61)

In 1999, Weisz played Greta in the historical film _[Sunshine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunshine\_(1999\_film) "Sunshine (1999 film)")_.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-62) The same year, her international breakthrough came with the 1999 adventure film _[The Mummy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Mummy\_(1999\_film) "The Mummy (1999 film)")_, in which she played the female lead opposite [Brendan Fraser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brendan_Fraser "Brendan Fraser"). Her character, Evelyn Carnahan, is an English [Egyptologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egyptologist "Egyptologist"),[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-63) who undertakes an expedition to the fictional ancient Egyptian city of Hamunaptra to discover an ancient book. _[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety\_(magazine) "Variety (magazine)")_ criticised the direction of the film, writing: "(the actors) have been directed to broad, undisciplined performances [...] Buffoonery hardly seems like Weisz's natural domain, as the actress strains for comic effects that she can't achieve".[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-64) She followed this up with the sequel _[The Mummy Returns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Mummy\_Returns "The Mummy Returns")_ in 2001, which grossed an estimated $433 million worldwide,[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-65) (equivalent to $787 million in 2025 dollars)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-inflation-US-66) higher than the original's $260 million[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-67) (equal to $502 million in 2025 dollars).[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-inflation-US-66)

Also in 1999, she played the role of Catherine in the [Donmar Warehouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donmar_Warehouse "Donmar Warehouse") production of [Tennessee Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee_Williams "Tennessee Williams")' _[Suddenly Last Summer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suddenly\_Last\_Summer "Suddenly Last Summer")_,[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-autogenerated1-68)_What's on Stage_ called her "captivating", stating that she brought "a degree of credibility to a difficult part".[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-69) In 2001, Weisz appeared in [Neil LaBute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_LaBute "Neil LaBute")'s _[The Shape of Things](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Shape\_of\_Things "The Shape of Things")_ at the [Almeida Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almeida_Theatre "Almeida Theatre"), then temporarily located in London's [King's Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King's_Cross,_London "King's Cross, London"), for which she received a [Theatre World Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_World_Award "Theatre World Award").[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-shape-70)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-71) CurtainUp called her "a sophisticated, independent artist" with "great stage presence".[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-72)

### 2000s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rachel_Weisz&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 2000s")]

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rachel_Weisz&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Personal life")]

In 2001, Weisz began dating filmmaker and producer [Darren Aronofsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darren_Aronofsky "Darren Aronofsky"). They met backstage at London's [Almeida Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almeida_Theatre "Almeida Theatre"), where she was starring in _The Shape of Things_. Weisz moved to New York City with Aronofsky the following year;[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-shape-70) in 2005, they were engaged. Their son was born in May 2006 in New York City.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-usatoday-134)[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-135) The couple resided in the [East Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Village,_Manhattan "East Village, Manhattan") in [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan"). _Mohel_[Philip Sherman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Sherman_(rabbi) "Philip Sherman (rabbi)") performed their son's [brit milah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brit_milah "Brit milah") ([bris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bris "Bris")).[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-136) In November 2010, Weisz and Aronofsky announced that they had been apart for months but remained close friends and were committed to bringing up their son together in New York.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-peoplesplit-137)

Weisz and the English actor [Daniel Craig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Craig "Daniel Craig") were friends for many years and worked together on the 2011 film _[Dream House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dream\_House\_(2011\_film) "Dream House (2011 film)")_. They began dating in December 2010 and married on 22 June 2011 in a private New York ceremony, with four guests in attendance, including Weisz's son and Craig's daughter.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-138) On 1 September 2018, it was reported that they had their first child together, a daughter, completing their family of 5.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-139)

Weisz has been featured on the covers of magazines such as _[Vogue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vogue\_(magazine) "Vogue (magazine)")_.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-140) She served as a [muse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artistic_inspiration "Artistic inspiration") to the fashion designer [Narciso Rodriguez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narciso_Rodriguez "Narciso Rodriguez").[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-141) Weisz learned [karate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karate "Karate") for her role in _[The Brothers Bloom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Brothers\_Bloom "The Brothers Bloom")_.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-142) A British citizen by birth, Weisz became a [naturalised American citizen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citizenship_of_the_United_States "Citizenship of the United States") in 2011.[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-:0-143)

Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress

The 2026 recipient: Amy Madigan

Awarded for	Best Performance by an Actress in a Supporting Role
Country	United States
Presented by	Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences (AMPAS)
First award	March 4, 1937; 89 years ago (for films released in 1936)
Most recent winner	Amy Madigan, Weapons (2025)
Most awards	Dianne Wiest and Shelley Winters (2)
Most nominations	Thelma Ritter (6)
Website	oscars.org

The Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress is an award presented annually by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences (AMPAS). It has been awarded since the 9th Academy Awards to an actress who has delivered an outstanding performance in a supporting role in a film released that year. The award is traditionally presented by the previous year's Best Supporting Actor winner. However, in recent years, it has shifted towards being presented by previous years' Best Supporting Actress winners instead. In lieu of the traditional Oscar statuette, supporting acting recipients were given plaques up until the 16th Academy Awards,[1] when statuettes were awarded to each category instead.[2]

The Best Supporting Actress award has been presented a total of 90 times, to 88 actresses. The first winner was Gale Sondergaard for her role in Anthony Adverse (1936). The most recent winner is Amy Madigan for her role as Aunt Gladys in Weapons (2025).[3] The record for most wins is two, held jointly by Dianne Wiest and Shelley Winters. Each other recipient has only won once, in this category. Thelma Ritter has received the most nominations in the category, with six, followed closely by Amy Adams with five, although neither has ever won—yet, in the latter's instance. Hattie McDaniel, whom the Academy sat in the back of the room, made history in 1940 when she became the first person of color to win an Oscar in any category, for her performance as Mammy in Gone with the Wind (1939).[4]

Tatum O'Neal remains the youngest person to win a competitive acting Oscar at 10 years old, for her role in Paper Moon (1973). With five minutes and two seconds of screentime (the majority in one scene), Beatrice Straight's performance in Network (1976) holds the record for the shortest to win an Oscar.[5] The 40-year gap between Madigan's nomination for Weapons and her previous one for Twice in a Lifetime (1985) set the record for longest gap between Oscar nominations for an actress.[6]

Winners and nomineesedit

In the following table, the years are listed as per Academy convention, and generally correspond to the year of film release in Los Angeles County; the ceremonies are always held the following year.[8] For the first five ceremonies, the eligibility period spanned twelve months, from August 1 to July 31.[9] For the 6th ceremony held in 1934, the extended eligibility period lasted from August 1, 1932, to December 31, 1933.[9] Since the 7th ceremony held in 1935, the period of eligibility became the full previous calendar year from January 1 to December 31.[9]

**The Golden Globe Award for Best Director – Motion Picture** is a [Golden Globe Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Awards "Golden Globe Awards") that was first presented annually by the [Hollywood Foreign Press Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood_Foreign_Press_Association "Hollywood Foreign Press Association"), an organization composed of journalists who cover the United States [film industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_industry "Film industry") for publications based outside [North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America "North America"), [since 1943](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Golden_Globe_Awards "1st Golden Globe Awards") until [2023](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/80th_Golden_Globe_Awards "80th Golden Globe Awards").

Having won all four of his nominations, [Elia Kazan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elia_Kazan "Elia Kazan") has been honored most often in this category. [Clint Eastwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clint_Eastwood "Clint Eastwood"), [Miloš Forman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milo%C5%A1_Forman "Miloš Forman"), [David Lean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Lean "David Lean"), [Martin Scorsese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Scorsese "Martin Scorsese"), [Steven Spielberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Spielberg "Steven Spielberg"), and [Oliver Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Stone "Oliver Stone") tie for second place with three wins each. [Steven Spielberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Spielberg "Steven Spielberg") has had the most nominations (fourteen). [Barbra Streisand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbra_Streisand "Barbra Streisand"), [Chloé Zhao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chlo%C3%A9_Zhao "Chloé Zhao") and [Jane Campion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Campion "Jane Campion") are the only women to have won the award.

Receiving the award [in 1984](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/41st_Golden_Globe_Awards "41st Golden Globe Awards") for _[Yentl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yentl\_(film) "Yentl (film)")_, Barbra Streisand became the first woman to win the Golden Globe for Best Director.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Director#cite_note-1)

She remained the only woman to win a Golden Globe for directing for 37 years until Chloé Zhao won the award for _[Nomadland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nomadland "Nomadland")_ in [2021](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/78th_Golden_Globe_Awards "78th Golden Globe Awards") and became the second woman and the first Asian woman to do so.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Director#cite_note-BBC_News-2)

In the following lists, the first names, listed in **bold** type against a blue background, are the winners, and the following names are the remaining nominees. The years given are those in which the films under consideration were released, not the year of the ceremony, which takes place in January of the following year.

_**Amistad**_ is a 1997 American [historical drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_drama "Historical drama") film directed by [Steven Spielberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Spielberg "Steven Spielberg") and written by [David Franzoni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Franzoni "David Franzoni"), based on the events in 1839 aboard the Spanish slave ship _[La Amistad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_Amistad "La Amistad")_, during which [Mende tribesmen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mende_people "Mende people") abducted for the slave trade managed to gain control of their captors' ship off the coast of [Cuba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuba "Cuba"), and the international [legal battle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_v._The_Amistad "United States v. The Amistad") that followed their capture by the _[Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington\_(1837) "Washington (1837)")_, a [U.S. revenue cutter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Revenue_Cutter_Service "United States Revenue Cutter Service"). The case was ultimately [resolved by the U.S. Supreme Court in 1841](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_v._The_Amistad "United States v. The Amistad").

[Morgan Freeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgan_Freeman "Morgan Freeman"), [Anthony Hopkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Hopkins "Anthony Hopkins"), and [Matthew McConaughey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_McConaughey "Matthew McConaughey") star, along with [Djimon Hounsou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Djimon_Hounsou "Djimon Hounsou") in his breakout role as [Cinqué](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Cinqu%C3%A9 "Joseph Cinqué"); [Pete Postlethwaite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite "Pete Postlethwaite"), [Nigel Hawthorne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigel_Hawthorne "Nigel Hawthorne") and [Chiwetel Ejiofor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiwetel_Ejiofor "Chiwetel Ejiofor") appear in supporting roles.

_Amistad_ was released by [DreamWorks Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DreamWorks_Pictures "DreamWorks Pictures") on December 10, 1997. The film received largely positive critical reviews and grossed $58.3 million worldwide against a $39 million budget.

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amistad_(film)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

The [schooner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schooner "Schooner")_La Amistad_ is transporting black slaves off the coast of the [Spanish colony of Cuba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captaincy_General_of_Cuba "Captaincy General of Cuba") in 1839. A captive, [Cinqué](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Cinqu%C3%A9 "Joseph Cinqué"), leads an uprising against the crew, most of whom are killed. Two navigators, Pedro Montes and José Ruiz, are spared on condition they help sail the ship to Africa. The Spaniards betray them and instead sail into U.S. waters, where the ship is stopped by the [U.S. revenue cutter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Revenue_Cutter_Service "United States Revenue Cutter Service")_[Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington\_(1837) "Washington (1837)")_, and the mutineers are arrested.

A complicated legal battle ensues over the slaves. United States Attorney [William S. Holabird](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_S._Holabird "William S. Holabird") brings charges of piracy and murder against them. Those charges are dismissed in a criminal case because the killings occurred outside United States territorial waters.

A civil case then follows, with the Amistad Africans being claimed as property by Montes and Ruiz, and as [salvage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_salvage "Marine salvage") by two officers from the _Washington_. The Spanish government of [Queen Isabella II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabella_II_of_Spain "Isabella II of Spain")[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-2) intervenes in support of Montes and Ruiz, under the Treaty of 1795, also known as Pinckney's Treaty. To avoid a diplomatic incident, President [Martin Van Buren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren "Martin Van Buren") directs his [Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State")[John Forsyth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Forsyth_(politician) "John Forsyth (politician)") to support the Spanish claim. Meanwhile, abolitionist [Lewis Tappan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_Tappan "Lewis Tappan") and his black associate Theodore Joadson (a former slave) resolve to help the captives. They approach the brilliant lawyer, former U.S. president and serving [U.S. representative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives")[John Quincy Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams "John Quincy Adams"), but he is reluctant to get involved. They instead hire the young and eccentric attorney [Roger Sherman Baldwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Sherman_Baldwin "Roger Sherman Baldwin").

Baldwin, unable to converse directly with his clients due to the language barrier, suspects that the slaves are not Cubans but Africans who have been kidnapped and transported illegally as part of the banned [transatlantic slave trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transatlantic_slave_trade "Transatlantic slave trade"). He and Joadson search _La Amistad_ and find documents which prove that the captives were kidnapped from [Sierra Leone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierra_Leone "Sierra Leone") and transported across the Atlantic aboard the Portuguese slave ship _[Tecora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tecora "Tecora")_ before being transferred to _La Amistad_ in [Havana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Havana "Havana"). The judge is impressed and signals his intention to dismiss the U.S. and Spanish governments' case and release the captives.

To preclude this possibility, Van Buren replaces the judge with a younger man, Coglin, who he believes will be easier to manipulate. Joadson seeks advice from Adams, who tells him that court cases are usually won by the side with the best 'story'. Baldwin and Joadson recruit [freedman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedman "Freedman")[James Covey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Covey "James Covey") as a translator, enabling Cinqué to testify directly before the court. He describes how he was kidnapped from his home, and the horrors of the [Middle Passage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Passage "Middle Passage"). Baldwin calls Captain [Charles Fitzgerald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Fitzgerald "Charles Fitzgerald") of the [Royal Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy "Royal Navy")'s [West Africa Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Africa_Squadron "West Africa Squadron") to corroborate Cinqué's testimony. He speculates that the captives were taken aboard the _Tecora_ at the notorious [slave fort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slave_fort "Slave fort")[Lomboko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lomboko "Lomboko"). Under cross-examination, Fitzgerald admits that there is no direct evidence of Lomboko's existence. As tension rises, Cinqué abruptly stands and demands, "Give us, us free!". Moved by Cinqué's emotion, Judge Coglin rules that the Africans are to be released, and that Montes and Ruiz are to be arrested and charged with illegal slave-trading.

Under pressure from Senator [John C. Calhoun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_C._Calhoun "John C. Calhoun") of [South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Carolina "South Carolina"), who represents the slave-holding interests of the [American South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antebellum_South "Antebellum South"), Van Buren appeals the case to the [Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States"). Baldwin and Joadson visit Adams again, and after meeting Cinqué he agrees to represent the Africans before the Supreme Court. Adams' impassioned and eloquent speech convinces the court to [confirm the judgement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_v._The_Amistad "United States v. The Amistad") and release the Africans.

Lomboko is stormed by [Royal Marines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Marines "Royal Marines") led by Fitzgerald, and the slaves held there are freed. Fitzgerald orders the ship's cannon to destroy the fortress, and dictates a sardonic letter to Forsyth saying that he was correct — the infamous slave fort does not (now) exist.

Van Buren is discredited by his failure to prevent the release of the Africans, and loses [the 1840 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1840_United_States_presidential_election "1840 United States presidential election") to [William Henry Harrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Henry_Harrison "William Henry Harrison"). The Spanish government continues to press its claim for compensation up until the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War").

The captions say that Cinqué returns to Africa, but is unable to reunite with his family due to civil war in Sierra Leone.

### Casting

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amistad_(film)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Casting")]

In casting the role of Joseph Cinqué, Spielberg had strict requirements that the actor must have an impressive physical appearance, be able to command authority and be of West African descent. The actor who secured the role would also need to learn the [Mende](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mende_language "Mende language") accent spoken by Cinqué.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-tbg_12dec97-3)[Cuba Gooding Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuba_Gooding_Jr. "Cuba Gooding Jr.") was offered the role but turned it down and later regretted it.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-4)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-5)[Dustin Hoffman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dustin_Hoffman "Dustin Hoffman") was offered a role but turned it down,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-6)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-7) while [Will Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Will_Smith "Will Smith") and musician [Seal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seal_(musician) "Seal (musician)") both tried to secure the part. Despite open auditions being held in London, Paris and [Sierra Leone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierra_Leone "Sierra Leone"), the role remained unfilled with just nine weeks before filming was due to start. Spielberg was prepared to delay production by up to two years if he could not find the right actor.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-sfe_14dec97-8) After considering over 150 actors, Spielberg watched the audition tape of relatively unknown actor [Djimon Hounsou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Djimon_Hounsou "Djimon Hounsou") reading a speech from the film's script. After Hounsou read the speech in English and further learned it in Mende, Spielberg was impressed enough to cast him in the role of Cinqué.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-9) Hounsou auditioned with the hope of landing just a small role[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-sfe_14dec97-8) and said he was not aware of the story before securing the role. He read numerous books on the rebellion and subsequent trial to acquaint himself with events portrayed in the film.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-tbg_12dec97-3)

Morgan Freeman was selected for the role of Theodore Joadson on a first-come basis; Joadson was a fictional character in the film representing the composite of African American abolitionists in the 19th century. The actor and film director [Spike Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spike_Lee "Spike Lee") was reportedly offered the role but declined it.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-10) Freeman had been offered the role of Ensign [James Covey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Covey "James Covey"), but he chose to play Joadson instead after he realized that Covey was too young for him. [Chiwetel Ejiofor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiwetel_Ejiofor "Chiwetel Ejiofor") made his film debut as Covey, having auditioned for it while playing Othello at the [Royal National Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Theatre "Royal National Theatre") in London while he was still a student at the [London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Academy_of_Music_and_Dramatic_Art "London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-11)

Retired [U.S. Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Supreme_Court "U.S. Supreme Court") Justice [Harry Blackmun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Blackmun "Harry Blackmun") made a [cameo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cameo_appearance "Cameo appearance") appearance in the film as Justice [Joseph Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Story "Joseph Story"). Blackmun was honored to appear in the movie, acknowledging it was a "significant film about our nation's struggle with slavery".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-12)

## Production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amistad_(film)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Production")]

[Djimon Hounsou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Djimon_Hounsou "Djimon Hounsou") had just 10 days to learn the Mende language for his role as Joseph Cinqué; despite both Mende and Hounsou's native [Gun language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gun_language "Gun language")[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-13) being from West Africa, there were few similarities. Hounsou struggled to learn all his lines in Mende and resorted to [phonetically](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phonetic "Phonetic") reciting some of them, except for the most important scenes where he made sure to understand every word spoken. Hounsou expressed that being restrained in real chains and [shackles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shackle "Shackle") during filming was among the most challenging aspects of the movie, causing him to contemplate quitting on the first day.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-tbg_12dec97-3)

### Filming

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amistad_(film)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Filming")]

Filming locations included [Mystic Seaport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mystic_Seaport "Mystic Seaport"), which doubled as [New Haven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Haven "New Haven"). Film crews spent four days there and employed around 300 extras[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-hc_3dec97-14) Numerous scenes were filmed in [Newport, Rhode Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport,_Rhode_Island "Newport, Rhode Island"). Many courthouse scenes were shot in the [Old Colony House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_House "Old Colony House"), while the prison scenes were shot within [Fort Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Adams "Fort Adams").

During the scene where the characters Joseph Cinqué and [John Quincy Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams "John Quincy Adams") meet for the first time, actors Hounsou and [Anthony Hopkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Hopkins "Anthony Hopkins") "struggled through take after take, trying not to cry" and had to be continually told by [Steven Spielberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Spielberg "Steven Spielberg") to hold back the tears as it wasn't appropriate for that moment in the scene. Hopkins reportedly wept once the scene was completed.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-sfe_14dec97-8)

### Post-production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amistad_(film)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Post-production")]

The entire film was completed in 51 days and cost around $39 million (~$85.6 million in 2024).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-hc_3dec97-14)

Prior to release, a legal battle ensued between Spielberg's [DreamWorks Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DreamWorks_Pictures "DreamWorks Pictures") and novelist [Barbara Chase-Riboud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Chase-Riboud "Barbara Chase-Riboud"); the latter claiming that specific details from her 1989 novel _Echo of Lions_ were lifted for the screenplay. Chase-Riboud filed a $10 million lawsuit of copyright infringement.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-15)

## Historical accuracy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amistad_(film)&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Historical accuracy")]

Professor Howard Jones's 1987 book _[Mutiny on the Amistad: The Saga of a Slave Revolt and Its Impact on American Abolition, Law, and Diplomacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutiny\_on\_the\_Amistad:\_The\_Saga\_of\_a\_Slave\_Revolt\_and\_Its\_Impact\_on\_American\_Abolition,\_Law,\_and\_Diplomacy "Mutiny on the Amistad: The Saga of a Slave Revolt and Its Impact on American Abolition, Law, and Diplomacy")_ was cited by the producers as one of numerous sources used for research during the script's development.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-17)

Many academics, including [Columbia University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University "Columbia University") professor [Eric Foner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Foner "Eric Foner"), have criticized _Amistad_ for the misleading characterization of the _Amistad_ case as a "turning point" in American views on slavery, writing that:

> In fact, the _Amistad_ case revolved around the Atlantic slave trade — by 1840 outlawed by international treaty — and had nothing whatsoever to do with slavery as a domestic institution. Incongruous as it may seem, it was perfectly possible in the nineteenth century to condemn the importation of slaves from Africa while simultaneously defending slavery and the flourishing slave trade within the United States... _Amistad_’s problems go far deeper than such anachronisms as President Martin Van Buren campaigning for re-election on a whistle-stop train tour (in 1840, candidates did not campaign), or people constantly talking about the impending [Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War"), which lay 20 years in the future.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-foner-18)

[Elmer P. Martin Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elmer_P._Martin_Jr. "Elmer P. Martin Jr.") argued that the film missed an opportunity to mention contemporary events like the [_Creole_ case](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creole_case "Creole case"), a similar slave revolt on an American ship in 1841. Martin noted that some antebellum abolitionists such as [Frederick Douglass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Douglass "Frederick Douglass") found it "strange and perverse" that some of the defenders of the _Amistad_ slaves were willing to excuse the "similar traffic carried on with the same motives and purposes" in American waters.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-19)

Some critics, like historian [Eric McKitrick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_McKitrick "Eric McKitrick"), felt that the fictional character of Joadson, as portrayed by Morgan Freeman, softened the film's portrayal of contemporary American race relations: "No such person of the bearing and dignity depicted by Mr. Freeman would have been allowed to exist in the America of 1840." However, [Richard S. Newman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_S._Newman "Richard S. Newman") drew a connection between Joadson and Black reformers like [James Forten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Forten "James Forten"), an early abolitionist who influenced white reformers like Tappan and [William Lloyd Garrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Lloyd_Garrison "William Lloyd Garrison").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-20)

## Reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amistad_(film)&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Reception")]

### Critical response

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amistad_(film)&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Critical response")]

_Amistad_ received mainly positive reviews. On [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes"), the film has an approval rating of 78% based on reviews from 68 critics, with an average score of 7.0/10. Its consensus reads: "Heartfelt without resorting to preachiness, _Amistad_ tells an important story with engaging sensitivity and absorbing skill."[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-21)[Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic") calculated an average score of 63 out of 100 based on 23 reviews, indicating "generally favorable" reviews.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-22) Audiences polled by [CinemaScore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CinemaScore "CinemaScore") gave the film an average grade of "A−" on an A+ to F scale.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-23)

Susan Wloszczyna of _[USA Today](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USA\_Today "USA Today")_ summed up the feelings of many reviewers when she wrote, "as Spielberg vehicles go, _Amistad_ — part mystery, action thriller, courtroom drama, even culture-clash comedy — lands between the disturbing lyricism of _[Schindler's List](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schindler's\_List "Schindler's List")_ and the storybook artificiality of _[The Color Purple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Color\_Purple\_(1985\_film) "The Color Purple (1985 film)")_."[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-24)[Roger Ebert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Ebert "Roger Ebert") awarded the film three out of four stars, writing:

> _Amistad,_ like Spielberg's _Schindler's List,_ is [...] about the ways good men try to work realistically within an evil system to spare a few of its victims. [...] _Schindler's List_ works better as narrative because it is about a risky deception, while _Amistad_ is about the search for a truth that, if found, will be small consolation to the millions of existing slaves. As a result, the movie doesn't have the emotional charge of Spielberg's earlier film — or of _The Color Purple,_ which moved me to tears. [...] What is most valuable about _Amistad_ is the way it provides faces and names for its African characters, whom the movies so often make into faceless victims.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-25)

In 2014, the movie was one of several discussed by Noah Berlatsky in _[The Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Atlantic "The Atlantic")_ in an article concerning [white savior narratives in film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_savior_narrative_in_film "White savior narrative in film"), calling it "sanctimonious drivel."[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-berlatsky-26)

Morgan Freeman is very proud of the movie, having said, "I loved the film. I really did. I had a moment of err, during the killings. I thought that was a little over-wrought. But [Spielberg] wanted to make a point and I understood that."[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-27)

### Box office

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amistad_(film)&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Box office")]

The film debuted at No. 3 on Wednesday, December 10, 1997. It earned $44,229,441 at the box office in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-28)

### Other cultural significance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amistad_(film)&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Other cultural significance")]

The United States Department of State and the [Instituto Cubano del Arte e Industria Cinematográficos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instituto_Cubano_del_Arte_e_Industria_Cinematogr%C3%A1ficos "Instituto Cubano del Arte e Industria Cinematográficos") (ICAIC) collaborated in 1998 to screen _Amistad_ as part of an effort to increase "cultural diplomacy" built around shared national histories of racial struggles in the United States and Cuba.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-:1-30)

## Home media

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amistad_(film)&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Home media")]

[DreamWorks Home Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DreamWorks_Home_Entertainment "DreamWorks Home Entertainment") released the film on VHS in 1998, and then on DVD the following year. On August 17, 1999, it received a LaserDisc release in the United States.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-31) It was also released on LaserDisc in Japan on October 22, 1999.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-32) In February 2006, [Viacom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viacom_(2005%E2%80%932019) "Viacom (2005–2019)") (now known as [Paramount Skydance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount_Skydance "Paramount Skydance")) acquired the rights to _Amistad_ and all other live-action films DreamWorks had released between 1997 and 2005, following its billion-dollar acquisition of the studio's live-action film and television library.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-33)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-34)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-35) On May 6, 2014, [Paramount Home Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount_Home_Entertainment "Paramount Home Entertainment") released the film on Blu-ray.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad_(film)#cite_note-36)

_**Dark Water**_ is a 2005 American [supernatural horror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supernatural_horror "Supernatural horror") film directed by [Walter Salles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Salles "Walter Salles") and written by [Rafael Yglesias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rafael_Yglesias "Rafael Yglesias"). It is a [remake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remake "Remake") of the [2002 Japanese film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_Water_(2002_film) "Dark Water (2002 film)") based on the short story "[Floating Water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_Water_(book) "Dark Water (book)")" by [Koji Suzuki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koji_Suzuki_(writer) "Koji Suzuki (writer)"), who also wrote the [_Ring_ trilogy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(Suzuki_novel) "Ring (Suzuki novel)"). The film stars [Jennifer Connelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jennifer_Connelly "Jennifer Connelly"), [Tim Roth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Roth "Tim Roth"), [John C. Reilly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_C._Reilly "John C. Reilly"), [Pete Postlethwaite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite "Pete Postlethwaite"), [Perla Haney-Jardine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perla_Haney-Jardine "Perla Haney-Jardine"), [Dougray Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dougray_Scott "Dougray Scott") and [Ariel Gade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ariel_Gade "Ariel Gade").

_Dark Water_ was released on July 8, 2005, and grossed $49.5 million worldwide.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_Water_(2005_film)#cite_note-BoxOfficeMojo-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_Water_(2005_film)#cite_note-numbers-3) It is a co-production between the United States and Japan.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_Water_(2005_film)#cite_note-afi-1)

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dark_Water_(2005_film)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

Dahlia battles her ex-husband Kyle on shared custody conditions of their five-year-old daughter, Ceci. Kyle wants Ceci to live closer to his apartment in [Jersey City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jersey_City "Jersey City"), where there is a nearby school and rents are affordable. Dahlia instead chooses a dilapidated complex, with no other children, on [Roosevelt Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roosevelt_Island "Roosevelt Island")–despite Ceci being able to access the dangerous and unprotected rooftop and its [water tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rooftop_water_tower "Rooftop water tower"). After they move in, the bedroom ceiling leaks dark water. Dahlia finds the apartment above flooded and a family portrait of the former tenants, the Rimsky family: a mother, father, and a girl who is Ceci's age. She complains to the manager and to the superintendent, Veeck, about the water, but they do nothing. Paranoid, she complains to her lawyer, Platzer, that Kyle paid people to damage the plumbing.

Dahlia is haunted by ghostly visions and a recurring nightmare in which Mrs. Rimsky threatens to harm Ceci if Dahlia talks to the police. Ceci's teacher is troubled by her "imaginary friend", Natasha, and Dahlia catches Ceci talking to Natasha as well. In the bathroom, Ceci passes out as dark water gushes from the toilets and sinks.

That night, Dahlia sees water spilling from the water tower. Inside, she finds Natasha's body and calls the police. Veeck is arrested, as he was aware of the body, which was why he refused to fix the complex's plumbing problems. Veeck admits that the Rimskys paid him to keep quiet about their wilful neglect of Natasha. Left to fend for herself, Natasha fell into the water and drowned, becoming a vengeful ghost who is jealous of Ceci.

Dahlia finally decides that perhaps the situation is unsafe for Ceci, and will move closer to Kyle. Dahlia is packing and Ceci is taking a bath when Natasha visits Dahlia, begging her not to leave. Natasha attempts to drown Ceci until Dahlia promises to be her mother, at which point, Natasha drowns Dahlia by flooding the bathroom; they walk the hall together as ghosts.

Ceci moves in with Kyle, who is now given full custody of Ceci. Three weeks later, they pick up the last of her belongings from the old apartment. Dahlia's ghost temporarily traps Ceci in the elevator, telling her she will always be with her. The elevator door opens, and Kyle takes Ceci to his home.

## Reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dark_Water_(2005_film)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Reception")]

### Box office

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dark_Water_(2005_film)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Box office")]

_Dark Water_ played in 2,657 theaters with a complete average run of 3.2 weeks. The film made $10 million, which is 39% of the movie's total gross, on its opening weekend. It went on to make $25.5 million in the US[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_Water_(2005_film)#cite_note-numbers-3) and $24 million[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_Water_(2005_film)#cite_note-numbers-3) in the international box office, adding up to a worldwide box office total of $49.5 million.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_Water_(2005_film)#cite_note-5)

### Critical response

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dark_Water_(2005_film)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Critical response")]

_Dark Water_ holds a 47% approval rating at [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes") based on 154 reviews and an average score of 5.54/10. The site's critics' consensus reads: "All the atmospherics in _Dark Water_ can't make up for the lack of genuine scares."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_Water_(2005_film)#cite_note-6)[Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), which uses a [weighted average](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weighted_arithmetic_mean "Weighted arithmetic mean"), assigned the film a score of 52 out of 100, based on 35 critics, indicating "mixed or average" reviews.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_Water_(2005_film)#cite_note-Metacritic-7) Audiences polled by [CinemaScore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CinemaScore "CinemaScore") gave the film an average grade of "D−" on an A+ to F scale.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_Water_(2005_film)#cite_note-8)

William Thomas described the film in _[Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire\_(film\_magazine) "Empire (film magazine)")_ as "interesting and unsettling, but never terrifying. Best viewed as a family drama-come-Tale Of The Unexpected rather than a full-on horror".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_Water_(2005_film)#cite_note-9) For _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling\_Stone "Rolling Stone")_, [Peter Travers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Travers "Peter Travers") wrote, "A classy ghost story is just the ticket in a summer of crass jolts... Screenwriter Rafael Yglesias ([Fearless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fearless_(1993_film) "Fearless (1993 film)")) stays alert to the psychological fears that underpin the supernatural doings in the apartment upstairs. Connelly digs deep into the role of a woman with issues of abandonment and rage that slowly reveal their roots. In a movie with more subtext than _[Rosemary’s Baby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosemary's\_Baby\_(film) "Rosemary's Baby (film)")_, nearly everyone, including Tim Roth as Dahlia’s lawyer, harbors secrets. Salles unleashes a torrent of suspense for one purpose: to plumb the violence of the mind."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_Water_(2005_film)#cite_note-10)

[Todd McCarthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Todd_McCarthy "Todd McCarthy") of _[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety\_(magazine) "Variety (magazine)")_ called it "well-crafted but thoroughly unsuspenseful" and said it "is dripping with clammy, claustrophobic atmosphere, but ultimately reveals itself as just another mildewed, child-centric ghost story of little import or resonance."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_Water_(2005_film)#cite_note-11) From _[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Washington\_Post "The Washington Post")_, [Ann Hornaday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ann_Hornaday "Ann Hornaday") described the film as a "tasteful but unremitting bummer and yet one more case of an Oscar-winning actress proving that she can still do the kinds of disposable movies big awards are supposedly meant to banish from your résume forever."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_Water_(2005_film)#cite_note-12) For _[Slant Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slant\_Magazine "Slant Magazine")_ Nick Schager wrote that the film improves on the source material characterizations, while over explaining the supernatural events. He concluded by saying, "this slick adaptation is also a moldy, third-generation retread of _The Ring_."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_Water_(2005_film)#cite_note-13)
