## Production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Children_of_Men&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Production")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/Alfonso_Cuaron_-_2006_-_Children_of_Men_%28Mexico_premiere%29.jpg/250px-Alfonso_Cuaron_-_2006_-_Children_of_Men_%28Mexico_premiere%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alfonso_Cuaron_-_2006_-_Children_of_Men_(Mexico_premiere).jpg)

Director [Alfonso Cuarón](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Cuar%C3%B3n "Alfonso Cuarón") (pictured at the film's premiere in Mexico City, 2006) did not read the novel the film is based on, only a summary.

The option for the book was acquired by [Beacon Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beacon_Pictures "Beacon Pictures") in 1997.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-BeaconPix-26) The adaptation of the [P. D. James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P._D._James "P. D. James") novel was originally written by [Paul Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Chart "Paul Chart"), and later rewritten by [Mark Fergus and Hawk Ostby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Fergus_and_Hawk_Ostby "Mark Fergus and Hawk Ostby"). The studio brought director [Alfonso Cuarón](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Cuar%C3%B3n "Alfonso Cuarón") on board in 2001.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-27) Cuarón and screenwriter Timothy J. Sexton began rewriting the script after the director completed _[Y tu mamá también](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Y\_tu\_mam%C3%A1\_tambi%C3%A9n "Y tu mamá también")_. Afraid he would "start second guessing things",[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-Moviehole-23) Cuarón chose not to read P. D. James' novel, opting to have Sexton read the book while Cuarón himself read an abridged version.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-Cinematical-18)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-Filmmaker-28) Cuarón did not immediately begin production, instead directing _[Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry\_Potter\_and\_the\_Prisoner\_of\_Azkaban\_(film) "Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (film)")_. During this period, David Arata rewrote the screenplay and delivered the draft which secured [Clive Owen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_Owen "Clive Owen") and sent the film into [pre-production](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-production "Pre-production"). The director's work experience in the United Kingdom exposed him to the "social dynamics of the British psyche", giving him insight into the depiction of "British reality".[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-29) Cuarón used the film _[The Battle of Algiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Battle\_of\_Algiers\_(film) "The Battle of Algiers (film)")_ as a model for social reconstruction in preparation for production, presenting the film to Clive Owen as an example of his vision for _Children of Men_. In order to create a philosophical and social framework for the film, the director read literature by [Slavoj Žižek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavoj_%C5%BDi%C5%BEek "Slavoj Žižek"), as well as similar works.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-time_out-30) The 1927 film _[Sunrise: A Song of Two Humans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunrise:\_A\_Song\_of\_Two\_Humans "Sunrise: A Song of Two Humans")_ was also influential.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-HollywoodElsewhere-31)

### Location

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Children_of_Men&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Location")]

_[A Clockwork Orange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Clockwork\_Orange\_(film) "A Clockwork Orange (film)")_ was one of the inspirations for the futuristic, yet battered patina of 2027 London.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-HollywoodElsewhere-31)_Children of Men_ was the second film Cuarón made in London, with the director portraying the city using single, wide shots.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-Variety_Nightmare-32) While Cuarón was preparing the film, the [London bombings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7_July_2005_London_bombings "7 July 2005 London bombings") occurred, but the director did not consider moving the production. "It would have been impossible to shoot anywhere but London, because of the very obvious way the locations were incorporated into the film", Cuarón told _Variety_. "For example, the shot of [Fleet Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fleet_Street "Fleet Street") looking towards St. Paul's would have been impossible to shoot anywhere else."[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-Variety_Nightmare-32) Due to these circumstances, the opening terrorist attack scene on Fleet Street was shot a month and a half after the London bombing.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-time_out-30)

Cuarón chose to shoot some scenes in [East London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_London "East London"), a location he considered "a place without glamour". The set locations were dressed to make them appear even more run-down; Cuarón says he told the crew "'Let's make it more Mexican'. In other words, we'd look at a location and then say: yes, but in Mexico there would be this and this. It was about making the place look run-down. It was about poverty."[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-time_out-30) He also made use of London's most popular sites, shooting in locations like [Trafalgar Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trafalgar_Square "Trafalgar Square") and [Battersea Power Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battersea_Power_Station "Battersea Power Station"). The power station scene (whose conversion into an art archive is a reference to the [Tate Modern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate_Modern "Tate Modern")), has been compared to [Antonioni's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelangelo_Antonioni "Michelangelo Antonioni")_[Red Desert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red\_Desert\_(film) "Red Desert (film)")_.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-33) Cuarón added a [pig balloon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pink_Floyd_pigs "Pink Floyd pigs") to the scene as homage to [Pink Floyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pink_Floyd "Pink Floyd")'s _[Animals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animals\_(Pink\_Floyd\_album) "Animals (Pink Floyd album)")_.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-34) Other art works visible in this scene include [Michelangelo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelangelo "Michelangelo")'s _[David](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David\_(Michelangelo) "David (Michelangelo)")_,[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-America-35)[Picasso's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pablo_Picasso "Pablo Picasso")_[Guernica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guernica\_(painting) "Guernica (painting)")_,[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-36) and [Banksy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banksy "Banksy")'s _[Kissing Coppers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kissing\_Coppers "Kissing Coppers")_.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-FilmComment-37) London visual effects companies Double Negative and Framestore worked directly with Cuarón from script to post production, developing effects and creating "environments and shots that wouldn't otherwise be possible".[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-Variety_Nightmare-32)

[The Historic Dockyard in Chatham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chatham_Dockyard "Chatham Dockyard") was used to film the scene in the empty activist safehouse.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-38)

[The Shard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shard "The Shard") tower was digitally added to London's skyline based on early architectural drawings as when the film was made the skyscraper had not yet been built but would have been by the time of the film's setting.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-Shard-39)

### Style and design

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Children_of_Men&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Style and design")]

"In most sci-fi epics, special effects substitute for story. Here they seamlessly advance it", observes Colin Covert of _Star Tribune_.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-40) Billboards were designed to balance a contemporary and futuristic appearance as well as easily visualizing what else was occurring in the rest of the world at the time, and cars were made to resemble modern ones at first glance, although a closer look made them seem unfamiliar.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-41) Cuarón informed the art department that the film was the "anti-_[Blade Runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blade\_Runner "Blade Runner")_",[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-42) rejecting technologically advanced proposals and downplaying the science fiction elements of the 2027 setting. The director focused on images reflecting the contemporary period.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-44)

References to the [2012 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Summer_Olympics "2012 Summer Olympics") were included in the film as London had been announced as the host city in July 2005, a few months before filming took place.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-45)

### Single-shot sequences

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Children_of_Men&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Single-shot sequences")]

_Children of Men_ used several lengthy [single-shot sequences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_take "Long take") in which extremely complex actions take place. The longest of these include a shot in which Kee gives birth (3m19s); an ambush on a country road (4m7s); and a scene in which Theo is captured by the Fishes, escapes, and runs down a street and through a building in the middle of a raging battle (6m18s).[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-46) These sequences were extremely difficult to film, although the effect of continuity is sometimes an illusion, aided by [computer-generated imagery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer-generated_imagery "Computer-generated imagery") (CGI) effects and the use of 'seamless cuts' to enhance the [long takes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_take "Long take").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-VFX-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-48)

Cuarón had experimented with long takes in _[Great Expectations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great\_Expectations\_(1998\_film) "Great Expectations (1998 film)")_, _[Y tu mamá también](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Y\_tu\_mam%C3%A1\_tambi%C3%A9n "Y tu mamá también")_, and _[Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry\_Potter\_and\_the\_Prisoner\_of\_Azkaban\_(film) "Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (film)")_. His style is influenced by the Swiss film _[Jonah Who Will Be 25 in the Year 2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah\_Who\_Will\_Be\_25\_in\_the\_Year\_2000 "Jonah Who Will Be 25 in the Year 2000")_, one of his favourites. He said "I was studying cinema when I first saw [_Jonah_], and interested in the [French New Wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_New_Wave "French New Wave"). _Jonah_ was so unflashy compared with those films. The camera keeps a certain distance and there are relatively few close-ups. It's elegant and flowing, constantly tracking, but very slowly and not calling attention to itself."[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-49)

The creation of the single-shot sequences was a challenging, time-consuming process that sparked concerns from the studio. It took fourteen days to prepare for the single shot in which Clive Owen's character searches a building under attack and five hours every time they wanted to reshoot it. In the middle of one shot, blood splattered onto the lens, and cinematographer [Emmanuel Lubezki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmanuel_Lubezki "Emmanuel Lubezki") convinced the director to leave it in. According to Owen, "Right in the thick of it are me and the camera operator because we're doing this very complicated, very specific dance which, when we come to shoot, we have to make feel completely random."[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-50)

Cuarón's initial idea for maintaining [continuity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuity_(fiction) "Continuity (fiction)") during the roadside ambush scene was dismissed by production experts as an "impossible shot to do". Fresh from the visual effects-laden _Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban_, Cuarón suggested using computer-generated imagery to film the scene. Lubezki refused to allow it, reminding the director that they had intended to make a film akin to a "raw [documentary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Documentary_film "Documentary film")". Instead, a special camera rig invented by [Gary Thieltges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Thieltges "Gary Thieltges") of Doggicam Systems was employed, allowing Cuarón to develop the scene as one extended shot.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-ChicagoTribune-24)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-51) A vehicle was modified to enable seats to tilt and lower actors out of the way of the camera, and the windshield was designed to tilt out of the way to allow camera movement in and out through the front windscreen. A crew of four, including the director of photography and camera operator, rode on the roof.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-52)

However, the commonly reported statement that the action scenes are continuous shots[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-53) is not entirely true. Visual effects supervisor Frazer Churchill explains that the effects team had to "combine several takes to create impossibly long shots", where their job was to "create the illusion of a continuous camera move". Once the team was able to create a "seamless blend", they would move on to the next shot. These techniques were important for three continuous shots: the coffee shop explosion in the opening shot, the car ambush, and the battlefield scene. The coffee shop scene was composed of "two different takes shot over two consecutive days"; the car ambush was shot in "six sections and at four different locations over one week and required five seamless digital transitions"; and the battlefield scene "was captured in five separate takes over two locations". Churchill and the [Double Negative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_Negative_(VFX) "Double Negative (VFX)") team created over 160 of these types of effects for the film.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-54) In an interview with _Variety_, Cuarón acknowledged this nature of the "single-shot" action sequences: "Maybe I'm spilling a big secret, but sometimes it's more than what it looks like. The important thing is how you blend everything and how you keep the perception of a fluid choreography through all of these different pieces."[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-Debruge-19)

[Tim Webber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Webber "Tim Webber") of VFX house [Framestore CFC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Framestore_CFC "Framestore CFC") was responsible for the three-and-a-half-minute single take of Kee giving birth, helping to choreograph and create the CG effects of the childbirth.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-Variety_Nightmare-32) Cuarón had originally intended to use an [animatronic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animatronic "Animatronic") baby as Kee's child with the exception of the childbirth scene. In the end, two takes were shot, with the second take concealing Clare-Hope Ashitey's legs, replacing them with prosthetic legs. Cuarón was pleased with the results of the effect, and returned to previous shots of the baby in animatronic form, replacing them with Framestore's [computer-generated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer-generated_imagery "Computer-generated imagery") baby.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-VFX-47)

### Sound

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Children_of_Men&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Sound")]

See also: [Children of Men (soundtracks)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men_(soundtracks) "Children of Men (soundtracks)")

Cuarón used a combination of rock, pop, electronic music, hip-hop and classical music for the film's soundtrack.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-LATimes-55) Ambient sounds of traffic, barking dogs, and advertisements follow the character of Theo through London, East Sussex and Kent, producing what _[Los Angeles Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los\_Angeles\_Times "Los Angeles Times")_ writer Kevin Crust called an "urban audio rumble".[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-LATimes-55) Crust considered that the music comments indirectly on the barren world of _Children of Men_: [Deep Purple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_Purple "Deep Purple")'s version of "[Hush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hush_(Billy_Joe_Royal_song) "Hush (Billy Joe Royal song)")" playing from Jasper's car radio becomes a "sly lullaby for a world without babies" while [King Crimson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Crimson "King Crimson")'s "[The Court of the Crimson King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Court_of_the_Crimson_King "The Court of the Crimson King")" make a similar allusion with their lyrics, "three lullabies in an ancient tongue".[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-LATimes-55)

Amongst a genre-spanning selection of [electronic music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_music "Electronic music"), a remix of [Aphex Twin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aphex_Twin "Aphex Twin")'s "Omgyjya Switch 7", which includes the 'Male Thijs Loud Scream' audio sample by Thanvannispen[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-56) can be heard during an early scene in Jasper's house. During a conversation between the two men, [Radiohead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiohead "Radiohead")'s "[Life in a Glasshouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_in_a_Glasshouse "Life in a Glasshouse")" plays in the background. A number of [dubstep](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubstep "Dubstep") tracks, including "Anti-War Dub" by [Digital Mystikz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_Mystikz "Digital Mystikz"), as well as tracks by [Kode9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kode9 "Kode9")& The Space Ape, [Pinch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinch_(dubstep_musician) "Pinch (dubstep musician)") and [Pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Martin_(British_musician) "Kevin Martin (British musician)") are also featured.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-57)

For the Bexhill scenes during the film's second half, Cuarón makes use of silence and cacophonous [sound effects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_effect "Sound effect") such as the firing of automatic weapons and loudspeakers directing the movement of refugees.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-LATimes-55) Classical music by [George Frideric Handel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Frideric_Handel "George Frideric Handel"), [Gustav Mahler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustav_Mahler "Gustav Mahler"), [Dmitri Shostakovich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dmitri_Shostakovich "Dmitri Shostakovich") and [Krzysztof Penderecki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krzysztof_Penderecki "Krzysztof Penderecki")'s "[Threnody to the Victims of Hiroshima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Threnody_to_the_Victims_of_Hiroshima "Threnody to the Victims of Hiroshima")" complements the chaos of the refugee camp.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-LATimes-55) Throughout the film, [John Tavener](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Tavener "John Tavener")'s _Fragments of a Prayer_ is used as a spiritual motif.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-LATimes-55)

## Themes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Children_of_Men&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Themes")]

### Hope and faith

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Children_of_Men&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Hope and faith")]

_Children of Men_ explores the themes of [hope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope "Hope") and [faith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith "Faith")[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-58) in the face of overwhelming futility and despair.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-USATODAY-59)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-HollywoodElsewhere-31) The film's source, [P. D. James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P._D._James "P. D. James")' novel _[The Children of Men](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Children\_of\_Men "The Children of Men")_ (1992), describes what happens when society is unable to reproduce, using male infertility to explain this problem.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-Independent1-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-61) In the novel, it is made clear that hope depends on future generations. James writes "It was reasonable to struggle, to suffer, perhaps even to die, for a more just, a more compassionate society, but not in a world with no future where, all too soon, the very words 'justice', 'compassion', 'society', 'struggle', 'evil', would be unheard echoes on an empty air."[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-62)

The film does not explain the cause of the infertility, although environmental destruction and divine punishment are considered.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-HollywoodElsewhere-31)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-:1-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-64) Cuarón has attributed this unanswered question (and others in the film) to his dislike for the purely expository film: "There's a kind of cinema I detest, which is a cinema that is about exposition and explanations... It's become now what I call a medium for lazy readers... Cinema is a hostage of narrative. And I'm very good at narrative as a hostage of cinema."[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-:0-65) Cuarón's disdain for [back-story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back-story "Back-story") and exposition led him to use the concept of infertility as a "metaphor for the fading sense of hope".[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-:0-65)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-:1-63) The "almost mythical" Human Project is turned into a "metaphor for the possibility of the evolution of the human spirit, the evolution of human understanding".[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-Tomatoes1-66) Cuarón believed that explaining things such as the cause of the infertility and the Human Project would create a "pure science-fiction movie", removing focus from the story as a metaphor for hope.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-iwgblog-67)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-:1-63) Without dictating how the audience should feel by the end of the film, Cuarón encourages viewers to come to their own conclusions about the sense of hope depicted in the final scenes: "We wanted the end to be a glimpse of a possibility of hope, for the audience to invest their own sense of hope into that ending. So if you're a hopeful person you'll see a lot of hope, and if you're a bleak person you'll see a complete hopelessness at the end."[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-Filmmaker-28)

### Religion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Children_of_Men&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Religion")]

Richard Blake, writing for [Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church") magazine _[America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/America\_(magazine) "America (magazine)")_, suggested that like [Virgil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgil "Virgil")'s _[Aeneid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeneid "Aeneid")_, [Dante](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dante_Alighieri "Dante Alighieri")'s _[The Divine Comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Divine\_Comedy "The Divine Comedy")_, and [Chaucer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffrey_Chaucer "Geoffrey Chaucer")'s _[The Canterbury Tales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Canterbury\_Tales "The Canterbury Tales")_, the crux of the journey in _Children of Men_ lies in what is uncovered along the path rather than the terminus itself.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-America-35)

According to Cuarón, the title of P. D. James' book (_[The Children of Men](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Children\_of\_Men "The Children of Men")_) is an allegory derived from a [passage of scripture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psalm_90 "Psalm 90") in the Bible.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-68) ([Psalm 90 (89):3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psalm_90 "Psalm 90") of the [King James Version](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_James_Version "King James Version"): "Thou turnest man to destruction; and sayest, Return, ye children of men") James refers to her story as a "Christian fable"[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-Independent1-60) while Cuarón describes it as "almost like a look at Christianity": "I didn't want to shy away from the spiritual archetypes", Cuarón told _[Filmmaker Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filmmaker\_Magazine "Filmmaker Magazine")_. "But I wasn't interested in dealing with [dogma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dogma "Dogma")."[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-Filmmaker-28)

> Ms. James's nativity story is, in Mr. Cuarón's version, set against the image of a prisoner in an orange smock with a black bag on his head, arms stretched out as if on a cross.

—[Manohla Dargis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manohla_Dargis "Manohla Dargis"), [[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-69)

This divergence from the original was criticised by some, including Anthony Sacramone of _[First Things](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First\_Things "First Things")_, who called the film "an act of vandalism", noting the irony of how Cuarón had removed religion from P.D. James' fable, in which morally sterile [nihilism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nihilism "Nihilism") is overcome by [Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity").[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-70)

The film has been noted for its use of [Christian symbolism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_symbolism "Christian symbolism"); for example, British terrorists named "[Fishes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ichthys "Ichthys")" protect the rights of refugees.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-71) Opening on [Christmas Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christmas_Day "Christmas Day") in the United States, critics compared the characters of Theo and Kee with Joseph and Mary,[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-72) calling the film a "modern-day [Nativity story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nativity_story "Nativity story")".[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-Slate-73) Kee's pregnancy is revealed to Theo in a barn, alluding to the manger of the [Nativity scene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nativity_scene "Nativity scene"); when Theo asks Kee who the father of the baby is she jokingly states she is a virgin; and when other characters discover Kee and her baby, they respond with "[Jesus Christ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thou_shalt_not_take_the_name_of_the_Lord_thy_God_in_vain#In_Christianity "Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain")" or the [sign of the cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sign_of_the_cross "Sign of the cross").[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-74)

To highlight these spiritual themes, Cuarón commissioned a 15-minute piece by British composer [John Tavener](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Tavener "John Tavener"), a member of the [Eastern Orthodox Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Orthodox_Church "Eastern Orthodox Church") whose work resonates with the themes of "motherhood, birth, rebirth, and redemption in the eyes of God". Calling his score a "musical and spiritual reaction to Alfonso's film", snippets of Tavener's "Fragments of a Prayer" contain lyrics in Latin, German, and Sanskrit sung by mezzo-soprano [Sarah Connolly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Connolly "Sarah Connolly"). Words like "mata" (mother), "pahi mam" (protect me), "avatara" (saviour), and "alleluia" appear throughout the film.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-75)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-76)

In the [closing credits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closing_credits "Closing credits"), the [Sanskrit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanskrit "Sanskrit") words "Shantih Shantih Shantih" appear as end titles.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-77)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-78) Writer and [film critic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_critic "Film critic") Laura Eldred of the [University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_North_Carolina_at_Chapel_Hill "University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill") observes that _Children of Men_ is "full of tidbits that call out to the educated viewer". During a visit to his house by Theo and Kee, Jasper says "Shanti, shanti, shanti". Eldred notes that the "shanti" used in the film is also found at the end of an [Upanishad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upanishad "Upanishad") and in the final line of [T. S. Eliot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._S._Eliot "T. S. Eliot")'s poem _[The Waste Land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Waste\_Land "The Waste Land")_, a work Eldred describes as "devoted to contemplating a world emptied of fertility: a world on its last, teetering legs". "Shanti" is also a common beginning and ending to all Hindu prayers, and means "peace", referencing the invocation of divine intervention and rebirth through an end to violence.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-79)

### Contemporary references

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Children_of_Men&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Contemporary references")]

_Children of Men_ takes an unconventional approach to the modern [action film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_film "Action film"), using a documentary, newsreel style.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-80) Film critics Michael Rowin, Jason Guerrasio and Ethan Alter observe the film's underlying touchstone of immigration. For Alter and other critics, the structural support and impetus for the contemporary references rests upon the visual nature of the film's [exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposition_(plot_device) "Exposition (plot device)"), occurring in the form of imagery as opposed to conventional dialogue.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-FJI-81) Other popular images appear, such as a sign over the refugee camp reading "Homeland Security".[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-82) The similarity between the hellish, [cinéma vérité](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cin%C3%A9ma_v%C3%A9rit%C3%A9 "Cinéma vérité") stylised battle scenes of the film and current news and documentary coverage of the [Iraq War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_War "Iraq War"), is noted by film critic [Manohla Dargis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manohla_Dargis "Manohla Dargis"), describing Cuarón's fictional landscapes as "war zones of extraordinary plausibility".[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-NYT1-83)

In the film, refugees are "hunted down like cockroaches", rounded up and put into roofless cages open to the elements and camps, and even shot, leading film critics like Chris Smith and Claudia Puig to observe symbolic "overtones" and images of the [Holocaust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holocaust "Holocaust").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-USATODAY-59)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-84) This is reinforced in the scene where an elderly refugee woman speaking German is seen detained in a cage,[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-FilmComment-37) and in the scene where government agents strip and assault refugees the song "Arbeit Macht Frei" by [The Libertines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Libertines "The Libertines"), from _[Arbeit macht frei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arbeit\_macht\_frei "Arbeit macht frei")_, plays in the background.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-85) "The visual allusions to the Nazi round-ups are unnerving", writes Richard A. Blake. "It shows what people can become when the government orchestrates their fears for its own advantage."[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-America-35)

Cuarón explains how he uses imagery in his fictional and futuristic events to allude to real, contemporary or historical incidents and beliefs,

> They exit the Russian apartments, and the next shot you see is this woman wailing, holding the body of her son in her arms. This was a reference to a real photograph of a woman holding the body of her son in the Balkans, crying with the corpse of her son. It's very obvious that when the photographer captured that photograph, he was referencing [La Pietà](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piet%C3%A0_(Michelangelo) "Pietà (Michelangelo)"), the Michelangelo sculpture of Mary holding the corpse of Jesus. So: We have a reference to something that really happened, in the Balkans, which is itself a reference to the Michelangelo sculpture. At the same time, we use the sculpture of [David](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_(Michelangelo) "David (Michelangelo)") early on, which is also by Michelangelo, and we have of course the whole reference to the [Nativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nativity_of_Jesus "Nativity of Jesus"). And so everything was referencing and cross-referencing, as much as we could.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-Cinematical-18)

## Release

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Children_of_Men&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Release")]

### Box office

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Children_of_Men&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Box office")]

_Children of Men_ had its [world premiere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_premiere "Film premiere") at the [63rd Venice International Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/63rd_Venice_International_Film_Festival "63rd Venice International Film Festival") on 3 September 2006.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-86) On 22 September 2006, the film debuted at number 1 in the United Kingdom with $2.4 million in 368 screens.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-bom-87) It debuted in a limited release of 16 theaters in the United States on 22 December 2006, expanding to more than 1,200 theaters on 5 January 2007.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-88)As of 6 February 2008[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Children_of_Men&action=edit), _Children of Men_ had grossed $69,612,678 worldwide, with $35,552,383 of the revenue generated in the United States.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-89)

### Home media

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Children_of_Men&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Home media")]

The HD-DVD and DVD were released in Europe on 15 January 2007[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-90) and in the United States on 27 March 2007. Extras include a half-hour documentary by director Alfonso Cuarón, entitled _The Possibility of Hope_ (2007), which explores the intersection between the film's themes and reality with a critical analysis by eminent scholars: the Slovenian sociologist and philosopher [Slavoj Žižek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavoj_%C5%BDi%C5%BEek "Slavoj Žižek"), anti-globalization activist [Naomi Klein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naomi_Klein "Naomi Klein"), environmentalist futurist [James Lovelock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Lovelock "James Lovelock"), sociologist [Saskia Sassen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saskia_Sassen "Saskia Sassen"), [human geographer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_geography "Human geography") Fabrizio Eva, cultural theorist [Tzvetan Todorov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tzvetan_Todorov "Tzvetan Todorov"), and philosopher and economist [John N. Gray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_N._Gray "John N. Gray"). "Under Attack" features a demonstration of the innovative techniques required for the car chase and battle scenes; in "Theo & Julian", Clive Owen and Julianne Moore discuss their characters; "Futuristic Design" opens the door on the production design and look of the film; "Visual Effects" shows how the digital baby was created. Deleted scenes are included.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-91) The film was released on [Blu-ray Disc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blu-ray_Disc "Blu-ray Disc") in the United States on 26 May 2009.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-92)

## Reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Children_of_Men&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Reception")]

### Critical response

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Children_of_Men&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Critical response")]

_Children of Men_ received critical acclaim; on the review aggregator website [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes"), the film received a 92% approval rating based on 252 reviews from critics. The site's critical consensus states: "_Children of Men_ works on every level: as a violent chase thriller, a fantastical cautionary tale, and a sophisticated human drama about societies struggling to live."[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-93) On [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), the film has a score of 84 out of 100, based on 38 reviews, indicating "universal acclaim".[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-94) Audiences polled by [CinemaScore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CinemaScore "CinemaScore") gave the film an average grade "B−" on an A+ to F scale.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-95)

[Roger Ebert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Ebert "Roger Ebert") of the _[Chicago Sun-Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago\_Sun-Times "Chicago Sun-Times")_ gave the film four stars out of four, writing, "Cuarón fulfills the promise of futuristic fiction; characters do not wear strange costumes or visit the moon, and the cities are not plastic hallucinations, but look just like today, except tired and shabby. Here is certainly a world ending not with a bang but a whimper, and the film serves as a cautionary warning."[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-96)[Dana Stevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dana_Stevens_(critic) "Dana Stevens (critic)") of _[Slate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slate\_(magazine) "Slate (magazine)")_ called it "the herald of another blessed event: the arrival of a great director by the name of Alfonso Cuarón". Stevens hailed the film's extended car chase and battle scenes as "two of the most virtuoso single-shot chase sequences I've ever seen".[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-Slate-73)[Manohla Dargis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manohla_Dargis "Manohla Dargis") of _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ called the film a "superbly directed political thriller", raining accolades on the long chase scenes.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-NYT1-83) "Easily one of the best films of the year" said Ethan Alter of _Film Journal International_, with scenes that "dazzle you with their technical complexity and visual virtuosity".[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-FJI-81) Jonathan Romney of _[The Independent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Independent "The Independent")_ praised the accuracy of Cuarón's portrait of the United Kingdom, but he criticized some of the film's futuristic scenes as "run-of-the-mill future fantasy".[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-FilmComment-37)_[Film Comment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film\_Comment "Film Comment")_'s critics' poll of the best films of 2006 ranked the film number 19, while the 2006 readers' poll ranked it number two.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-97) On their list of the best movies of 2006, _[The A.V. Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_A.V.\_Club "The A.V. Club")_, the _[San Francisco Chronicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San\_Francisco\_Chronicle "San Francisco Chronicle")_, _Slate_, and _[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Washington\_Post "The Washington Post")_ placed the film at number one.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-Top10_Lists-98)_[Entertainment Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment\_Weekly "Entertainment Weekly")_ ranked the film seventh on its end-of-the-decade top 10 list, saying, "Alfonso Cuarón's dystopian 2006 film reminded us that adrenaline-juicing action sequences can work best when the future looks just as grimy as today".[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-EWDECADE-99)

[Peter Travers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Travers "Peter Travers") of _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling\_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ ranked it number two on his list of best films of the decade, writing:

> I thought director Alfonso Cuarón's film of P.D. James' futuristic political-fable novel was good when it opened in 2006. After repeated viewings, I know _Children of Men_ is indisputably great... No movie this decade was more redolent of sorrowful beauty and exhilarating action. You don't just watch the car ambush scene (pure camera wizardry)—you live inside it. That's Cuarón's magic: He makes you believe."[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-100)

According to Metacritic's analysis of the films most often noted on the best-of-the-decade lists, _Children of Men_ is the 11th greatest film of the 2000s.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-101)

In the book _501 Must-See Movies_, Rob Hill lauds the movie for its dystopian portrayal of the future and its adept exploration of contemporary issues. Hill highlights the film's societal stagnation and the magnetizing effect of Britain on immigrants and terrorists, emphasizing the director's intelligence in weaving speculative narratives with real-world reflections. He applauds Cuarón's skill in creating a cinematic mirror that resonates with audiences by addressing pressing political and social concerns, all within a compelling dystopian framework.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-102)

In the wake of the [European migrant crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_migrant_crisis "European migrant crisis") since 2015, the [British withdrawal from the European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brexit "Brexit") of the late 2010s, [the first presidency of Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_presidency_of_Donald_Trump "First presidency of Donald Trump") (2017–2021), and the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic") beginning in 2020, all of which involved divisive debates about immigration and increasing border enforcement, several commentators reappraised the film's importance, with many calling it "prescient".[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men#cite_note-115)

_**The Congress**_ ([French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _Le Congrès_, [Hebrew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew_language "Hebrew language"): כנס העתידנים) is a 2013 English-language live-action/animated [science-fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction_film "Science fiction film") drama film written and directed by [Ari Folman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ari_Folman "Ari Folman"), loosely based on [Stanisław Lem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanis%C5%82aw_Lem "Stanisław Lem")'s 1971 Polish science-fiction novel _[The Futurological Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Futurological\_Congress "The Futurological Congress")_. It stars [Robin Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Wright "Robin Wright") as a fictionalized version of herself who agrees to have a film studio use a [digital clone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_clone "Digital clone") of her in any film they want.

The film premiered at the [2013 Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Cannes_Film_Festival "2013 Cannes Film Festival") on 15 May 2013.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Congress_(2013_film)#cite_note-Cannes_2013-8) Independent film distributor [Drafthouse Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drafthouse_Films "Drafthouse Films") announced, along with Films We Like In Toronto, their co-acquisition of the North American rights to the film and a US theatrical and VOD/digital release planned for 2014.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Congress_(2013_film)#cite_note-Drafthouse-9)

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Congress_(2013_film)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

[Robin Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Wright "Robin Wright") is an aging actress whose career suffered because of her erratic behavior and reputation for being fickle and unreliable. Her son, Aaron, suffers from [Usher syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Usher_syndrome "Usher syndrome"), which is slowly destroying his sight and hearing. Aided by Dr. Barker, Robin barely manages to stave off the worst effects of Aaron's decline, although his condition is sliding into its terminal stage.

Robin's longtime agent, Al, takes her to meet Jeff Green, the CEO of Miramount Studios, a film studio that offers to buy her likeness and digitize her into a computer-animated version of herself. Realizing that she may be unable to find future work with the emergence of this new technology, Robin agrees to do it for a hefty sum of money. The contract also requires that she never act again. After her body is digitally scanned, the studio can make films starring her, using only [computer-generated characters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtual_actor "Virtual actor").

Twenty years later, Robin travels to Abrahama City, where she will speak at the "Futurological Congress", Miramount's entertainment conference. Abrahama City is an animated, surreal [utopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utopia "Utopia") that is created from figments of people's [imaginations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imagination "Imagination"), where anyone can become an animated [avatar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avatar_(computing) "Avatar (computing)") of themselves but must use [hallucinogenic drugs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hallucinogen "Hallucinogen") to enter a mutable [illusory state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illusion "Illusion"). In the decades since she was scanned, Robin's virtual persona has become the star of a popular film franchise, _Rebel Robot Robin_, making her and Tom Cruise the only remaining movie stars. While discussing her new contract with Jeff, Robin learns that Miramount developed a new technology that will allow anyone to devour her or possibly [transform themselves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shapeshifting "Shapeshifting") into her with the hallucinogen. Robin agrees to the deal, but has a crisis of conscience, believing that no one should be turned into a product.

When asked to speak to the public at the Congress, Robin publicly voices her contrary views, upsetting everyone there before being taken by security guards. The Congress is then interrupted by rebels opposed to the technology industry. They seemingly assassinate the head of the Congress. During the attack, Robin is rescued by Dylan Truliner, who was Miramount's lead animator for her films. They escape, but she is soon captured by "Miramount Police". Robin is seemingly executed by Jeff as a punishment for rebelling against Miramount and the Congress. Robin is shown on a hospital bed while doctors discuss her case. One doctor reveals that Robin's execution was her hallucinating, that her rescuers were from Miramount. The doctors decide that Robin has become so intoxicated by the hallucinogen that she must be frozen until a treatment for her condition can be found.

Twenty years later, Robin is revived while still hallucinating an animated world. She reunites with Dylan, who says that the hallucinogenic technology is now widespread. People can take on whatever form they wish through it and as a result many negative aspects of humanity no longer exist. Dylan and Robin fall in love and take a journey through a colorful imaginary world. However, Robin is still desperate to return to the real world and be with Aaron. The only way to do that is by using a capsule that blocks all hallucinogenic effects. It is, in the animated world, equivalent to a suicide capsule. Dylan negotiated for one as part of his forced retirement package from Miramount, and he gives it to Robin.

Re-entering the real world, Robin finds herself in a [dystopian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dystopia "Dystopia") environment. A tiny elite hovers over ruined cities in large [airships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airship "Airship"). Most people have left for an existence in the animated world. Aaron did it only six months earlier when his condition left him virtually blind and deaf and he had given up hope of Robin's return. Because Aaron likely created a new identity for himself in the animated world, there is no way for anyone to find him.

Dr. Barker gives Robin an inhalation ampoule that will allow her to return to the animated world, though as her experiences have changed, her hallucinations will as well, and she will never be able to re-enter the same world she had left. Taking the drug, Robin sees Aaron's entire life flash before her eyes. She eventually discovers Aaron in the middle of an animated desert.

## Relation to _The Futurological Congress_ by Stanisław Lem

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Congress_(2013_film)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Relation to The Futurological Congress by Stanisław Lem")]

While some elements of the film were added by Ari Folman, others were based on the science-fiction novel _The Futurological Congress_ by Stanisław Lem. Similarly, to Lem's [Ijon Tichy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ijon_Tichy "Ijon Tichy"), the actress is split between delusional and real mental states. In an early interview about the film, Folman said,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Congress_(2013_film)#cite_note-11)

> "There is certainly nothing based on Lem in the first part of the movie. The second part is definitely different, but I used Lem's _The Futurological Congress_ more as a source of inspiration, rather than the basis of the screenplay."

Later, at the official website of the film in an interview, Folman says that the idea to put Lem's work to film came to him during his film school. He describes how he reconsidered Lem's allegory of [communist dictatorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist_state "Communist state") into a more current setting, namely, the dictatorship in the [entertainment industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment_industry "Entertainment industry"), and expresses his belief that he preserved the spirit of the book despite going far away from it.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Congress_(2013_film)#cite_note-12)

## Production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Congress_(2013_film)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Production")]

The animation was created by Bridgit Folman Films Gang, based in Israel, who worked on the script for 19 years.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Congress_(2013_film)#cite_note-polygon-13) Folman supervised six animation studios worldwide ("studio 352" in Luxemburg, "walking the dog" in Belgium, "bitteschoen" in Berlin, "studio Rakete" in Hamburg, "Studio Orange" in Poland, and "[Snipple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snipple_Animation "Snipple Animation")" in the Philippines). As in _[Waltz with Bashir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waltz\_with\_Bashir "Waltz with Bashir")_, Folman worked with [David Polonsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Polonsky "David Polonsky") as the artistic director and [Yoni Goodman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoni_Goodman "Yoni Goodman") as the animation director. Principal live-action filming was done in the United States and Germany from February to March 2011.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Congress_(2013_film)#cite_note-Film_Detail-10)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Congress_(2013_film)#cite_note-Robin_Wright-14) Folman began working on the film in 2008,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Congress_(2013_film)#cite_note-Slashfilm-15) securing additional financing in 2011 from French bank Coficine-Natixis.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Congress_(2013_film)#cite_note-16) The film was completed and released in 2013.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Congress_(2013_film)#cite_note-Cannes_2013-8)

## Music

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Congress_(2013_film)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Music")]

[Max Richter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Richter "Max Richter"), who had previously worked with Folman in _Waltz with Bashir_, created the soundtrack of _The Congress_.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Congress_(2013_film)#cite_note-17) Many of the songs are composed by Richter himself, but the soundtrack also includes the Andante movement from [Franz Schubert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franz_Schubert "Franz Schubert")'s _[Piano Trio No. 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano\_Trio\_No.\_2\_(Schubert) "Piano Trio No. 2 (Schubert)")_, [Frédéric Chopin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Chopin "Frédéric Chopin")'s _[Nocturne Op.27-1 in C# minor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nocturne\_in\_C-sharp\_Minor,\_Op.\_27,\_No.\_1 "Nocturne in C-sharp Minor, Op. 27, No. 1")_, "[Forever Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forever_Young_(Bob_Dylan_song) "Forever Young (Bob Dylan song)")" from [Bob Dylan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Dylan "Bob Dylan"), and [Leonard Cohen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Cohen "Leonard Cohen")'s ["If It Be Your Will"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Various_Positions "Various Positions"). These last two songs were covered by Robin Wright.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Congress_(2013_film)#cite_note-18)

[Milan Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milan_Entertainment "Milan Entertainment"), Inc. launched the soundtrack (in digital format) on 2 July 2013.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Congress_(2013_film)#cite_note-19)

## Reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Congress_(2013_film)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Reception")]

_The Congress_ received positive reviews. On [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes"), it has a 73% approval rating, based on reviews from 109 critics, with an average rating of 6.70/10. The website's critical consensus states: "_The Congress_ rises on the strength of Robin Wright's powerful performance, with enough ambitious storytelling and technical thrills to overcome its somewhat messy structure."[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Congress_(2013_film)#cite_note-20) On [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), the film has a 63/100 rating based on reviews from 31 critics, signifying "generally favorable reviews".[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Congress_(2013_film)#cite_note-21)

Keith Uhlich of _[The A.V. Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_A.V.\_Club "The A.V. Club")_ named _The Congress_ the sixth-best film of 2014, tying it with the re-release of _[Level Five](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Level\_Five\_(film) "Level Five (film)")_.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Congress_(2013_film)#cite_note-22)

In 2013, _The Congress_ won the Best Animated Feature Film Award at the [26th European Film Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/26th_European_Film_Awards "26th European Film Awards").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Congress_(2013_film)#cite_note-23)

Scout Tafoya gave the movie 3 1⁄2 stars in a 2014 review at RogerEbert.com, saying: "'The Congress' is a roll call of the orgiastic pleasures and bountiful comforts that art provides, and, a reminder of what waits for us when we leave the theater."[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Congress_(2013_film)#cite_note-24)

## Awards

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Congress_(2013_film)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Awards")]

The movie won the [26th European Film Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/26th_European_Film_Awards "26th European Film Awards") for the best animated feature film in 2013, as well as the Directors' Fortnight in the [Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannes_Film_Festival "Cannes Film Festival"). That same year, it won the [Sitges Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sitges_Film_Festival "Sitges Film Festival")'s Critics Award, too. In 2013, it was also nominated for Best Animation Film in the Gijon Film Festival.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Congress_(2013_film)#cite_note-25)

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Congress_(2013_film)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Legacy")]

The film found renewed relevance a decade later, during the [2023 SAG-AFTRA strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_SAG-AFTRA_strike "2023 SAG-AFTRA strike"). Several writers noted similarities between the movie and real life events, where SAG-AFTRA organizers claimed that the film studios had put forward an artificial intelligence proposal that would permit them to scan actors' bodies in exchange for a day's compensation and retain the rights to their image in perpetuity. Caryn James writing for the BBC in 2023 found the plot of _The Congress_ to be "eerily prescient".[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Congress_(2013_film)#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Congress_(2013_film)#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Congress_(2013_film)#cite_note-28)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Congress_(2013_film)#cite_note-polygon-13)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Congress_(2013_film)#cite_note-29)

The third season of the American [horror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horror_fiction "Horror fiction")[anthology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthology_series "Anthology series") television series _[American Horror Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American\_Horror\_Story "American Horror Story")_, subtitled _**Coven**_, is set in 2013 [New Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans "New Orleans") and follows a [coven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coven "Coven") of [witches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Witches "Witches") descended from [Salem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salem,_Massachusetts "Salem, Massachusetts") as they fight for survival and features flashbacks to the [Salem witch trials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salem_witch_trials "Salem witch trials") in 1692, as well as the 1830s, 1910s, 1960s, 1970s, and 1990s. The [ensemble cast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ensemble_cast "Ensemble cast") includes [Sarah Paulson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Paulson "Sarah Paulson"), [Taissa Farmiga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taissa_Farmiga "Taissa Farmiga"), [Frances Conroy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frances_Conroy "Frances Conroy"), [Evan Peters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evan_Peters "Evan Peters"), [Lily Rabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lily_Rabe "Lily Rabe"), [Emma Roberts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Roberts "Emma Roberts"), [Denis O'Hare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denis_O'Hare "Denis O'Hare"), [Kathy Bates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathy_Bates "Kathy Bates"), and [Jessica Lange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessica_Lange "Jessica Lange"), with all returning from previous seasons, except Roberts and Bates. The season marks the first to not feature cast mainstays [Dylan McDermott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dylan_McDermott "Dylan McDermott") and [Zachary Quinto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zachary_Quinto "Zachary Quinto").

Created by [Ryan Murphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryan_Murphy_(producer) "Ryan Murphy (producer)") and [Brad Falchuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brad_Falchuk "Brad Falchuk") for the [cable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cable_television_in_the_United_States "Cable television in the United States") network [FX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FX_(TV_channel) "FX (TV channel)"), the series is produced by [20th Century Fox Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20th_Century_Fox_Television "20th Century Fox Television"). _Coven_ was broadcast between October 9, 2013, to January 29, 2014, consisting of 13 episodes. Like its predecessors, the season was met with both positive reviews and strong ratings, with the premiere attracting a series high of 5.54 million viewers, which, at the time, was the most viewed episode of the series. The season garnered seventeen [Primetime Emmy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/66th_Primetime_Emmy_Awards "66th Primetime Emmy Awards") nominations, including [Outstanding Miniseries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primetime_Emmy_Award_for_Outstanding_Limited_Series "Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Limited Series"). It received nominations for Lange, Paulson, Bassett, Conroy, and Bates at the [66th Primetime Emmy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/66th_Primetime_Emmy_Awards "66th Primetime Emmy Awards"), with Lange and Bates winning their respective categories. In addition, _Coven_ was nominated for [Best Miniseries or TV Film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Miniseries_or_Television_Film "Golden Globe Award for Best Miniseries or Television Film") at the [Golden Globe Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/71st_Golden_Globe_Awards "71st Golden Globe Awards").

| Teenager Zoe Benson discovers she is a witch after accidentally giving her boyfriend a fatal brain aneurysm during sex. She is sent to Miss Robichaux's Academy, a school for witches in New Orleans, where she meets headmistress Cordelia Foxx and fellow students Madison Montgomery, a spoiled teenage actress who can move objects with her mind, Nan, a [clairvoyant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clairvoyant "Clairvoyant"), and Queenie, a human [voodoo doll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voodoo_doll "Voodoo doll"). After young witch Misty Day is burned at the stake, Fiona Goode, the current Supreme and Cordelia's estranged mother, arrives to ensure their safety. At a [fraternity party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_fraternities_and_sororities "College fraternities and sororities"), Zoe bonds with Kyle Spencer, while Madison is drugged and [gang-raped](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gang-rape "Gang-rape") by Kyle's fraternity brothers, including Brener. The boys flee on a bus, which Madison telekinetically overturns. Fiona takes the girls on a field trip and tells them about the history of witches in New Orleans. Nan leads them to a tour of the mansion of Madame [Delphine LaLaurie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delphine_LaLaurie "Delphine LaLaurie"), who in 1834 tortured slave Bastien for having sex with her daughter, leading voodoo priestess and Bastien's lover [Marie Laveau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Laveau "Marie Laveau") to poison LaLaurie. At a hospital, Zoe learns that Kyle died and rapes an unconscious Brener, killing him. Fiona has a still-living LaLaurie dug up. |

Meanwhile, Zoe and Madison decide to cast a resurrection spell in order to bring Kyle, one of several fraternity members that Madison murdered, back to life. When Kyle reanimates as a scared, angry monster, Zoe must seek help from a reclusive [necromancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Necromancer "Necromancer"), Misty Day. Cordelia and her husband Hank have trouble conceiving a child, so he convinces her to perform a fertility ritual, to which they proceed. |

| In 1971, a young Fiona kills the current Supreme, Anna-Leigh Leighton, by slitting her throat. In 2013, Madison and Nan take a liking to the new next-door neighbor, Luke Ramsey, but clash with his overly religious mother Joan. After an encounter with the Ramseys, Madison manifests a previously unknown [pyrokinesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrokinesis "Pyrokinesis"). Zoe returns Kyle to his mother, Alicia, unaware that she abuses him sexually. When Alicia tries to molest Kyle again, he bludgeons her to death with a trophy. Cordelia discovers she can never get pregnant and begs Marie Laveau to perform a voodoo fertility ritual on her, but Laveau refuses to help the daughter of her sworn enemy. Fiona turns Madame LaLaurie into the maid of the academy. When Bastien appears outside the academy in his [Minotaur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minotaur "Minotaur") form, Queenie offers herself to him before he grabs her by the mouth.
