## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Danny_Huston&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Huston was born May 14, 1962, in [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome"), Italy. He is the son of director and actor [John Huston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Huston "John Huston") and actress Zoe Sallis.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Huston#cite_note-13) Huston was in Italy directing _[The Bible: In the Beginning...](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Bible:\_In\_the\_Beginning... "The Bible: In the Beginning...")_, in which Sallis played [Hagar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagar "Hagar"). Through his father, he is the half-brother of [Anjelica Huston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anjelica_Huston "Anjelica Huston") and [Tony Huston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Huston "Tony Huston"). He has two adoptive siblings, Pablo Huston and [Allegra Huston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegra_Huston "Allegra Huston"). He is the uncle of [Jack Huston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Huston "Jack Huston") and grandson of [Walter Huston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Huston "Walter Huston"). He is of Canadian, Welsh, Scots-Irish, Scottish and [Anglo-Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Indian "Anglo-Indian") descent.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Huston#cite_note-bostonglobe-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Huston#cite_note-oea-15)

He spent much of his early life in the United Kingdom and Ireland, and maintains British citizenship through his mother.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Huston#cite_note-16) He worked as an assistant to his father during the production of [_Under the Volcano_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Under_the_Volcano_(1984_film) "Under the Volcano (1984 film)") (1984) and was a second unit director on [_The Dead_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dead_(1987_film) "The Dead (1987 film)") (1987). Huston is a graduate of [London Film School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Film_School "London Film School").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Huston#cite_note-17)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Danny_Huston&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Huston made his acting debut at the age of 12 in the [George Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Kennedy "George Kennedy")-starring thriller film [_The "Human" Factor_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_%22Human%22_Factor_(1975_film) "The \"Human\" Factor (1975 film)") (1975).

In 1988, Huston directed _[Mr. North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr.\_North "Mr. North")_, which was an adaptation of [Thornton Wilder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thornton_Wilder "Thornton Wilder")'s _Theophilus North_. The film was produced by his father, who died before its completion.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Huston#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Huston#cite_note-19) In 1995, Huston played Bartender #2 in _[Leaving Las Vegas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leaving\_Las\_Vegas "Leaving Las Vegas")_ and directed the film _[The Maddening](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Maddening "The Maddening")_.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Huston#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Huston#cite_note-21)

Huston was nominated for Best Male Performance at the Independent Spirit Awards in 2003 for his performance in the independent film _[Ivans Xtc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivans\_Xtc "Ivans Xtc")_.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Huston#cite_note-:0-1)

Huston appeared in [Martin Scorsese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Scorsese "Martin Scorsese")'s _[The Aviator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Aviator\_(2004\_film) "The Aviator (2004 film)")_. The ensemble cast was nominated for a 2004 SAG Award.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Huston#cite_note-:1-2) In 2006, Huston received the Golden Satellite Award for Best Supporting Actor for his performance as Sandy Woodrow in Fernando Meirelles' _[The Constant Gardener](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Constant\_Gardener\_(film) "The Constant Gardener (film)")_. Huston starred in the Australian western _[The Proposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Proposition\_(2005\_film) "The Proposition (2005 film)")_.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Huston#cite_note-22)

Huston starred in _Alpha Male_ and Oliver Parker's _[Fade to Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fade\_to\_Black\_(2006\_film) "Fade to Black (2006 film)")_, in which he played [Orson Welles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orson_Welles "Orson Welles").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Huston#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Huston#cite_note-24) He starred in _[The Kreutzer Sonata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Kreutzer\_Sonata\_(2008\_film) "The Kreutzer Sonata (2008 film)")_, which premiered at the 2008 Edinburgh International Film Festival.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Huston#cite_note-25)

His other film credits include _[Birth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth\_(2004\_film) "Birth (2004 film)")_, _[Silver City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver\_City\_(2004\_film) "Silver City (2004 film)")_, _[Marie Antoinette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie\_Antoinette\_(2006\_film) "Marie Antoinette (2006 film)")_, _[The Number 23](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Number\_23 "The Number 23")_, _[The Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Kingdom\_(2007\_film) "The Kingdom (2007 film)")_, _[How to Lose Friends & Alienate People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/How\_to\_Lose\_Friends\_&\_Alienate\_People\_(film) "How to Lose Friends & Alienate People (film)")_, and _[30 Days of Night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/30\_Days\_of\_Night\_(film) "30 Days of Night (film)")_. He portrayed [Samuel Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Adams "Samuel Adams") in the award-winning [HBO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HBO "HBO") miniseries _[John Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John\_Adams\_(miniseries) "John Adams (miniseries)")_ and [Colonel William Stryker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonel_William_Stryker "Colonel William Stryker") in _[X-Men Origins: Wolverine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-Men\_Origins:\_Wolverine "X-Men Origins: Wolverine")_, a prequel to the [original trilogy of _X-Men_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-Men_(film_series)#X-Men_original_trilogy_(2000%E2%80%932006) "X-Men (film series)") films.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Huston#cite_note-:6-26)

Huston has been featured in _[Boogie Woogie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boogie\_Woogie\_(film) "Boogie Woogie (film)")_, _[The Warrior's Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Warrior's\_Way "The Warrior's Way")_, _[Edge of Darkness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edge\_of\_Darkness\_(2010\_film) "Edge of Darkness (2010 film)")_, _[Clash of the Titans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash\_of\_the\_Titans\_(2010\_film) "Clash of the Titans (2010 film)")_, _[Robin Hood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin\_Hood\_(2010\_film) "Robin Hood (2010 film)")_, _[You Don't Know Jack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You\_Don't\_Know\_Jack\_(film) "You Don't Know Jack (film)")_, and _[Medallion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medallion\_(film) "Medallion (film)")_.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Huston#cite_note-:6-26)

Huston played gangster Ben "The Butcher" Diamond on [Mitch Glazer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitch_Glazer "Mitch Glazer")'s _[Magic City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magic\_City\_(TV\_series) "Magic City (TV series)")_, for which he was nominated for the [Golden Globe Award for Best Supporting Actor – Series, Miniseries or Television Film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Supporting_Actor_%E2%80%93_Series,_Miniseries_or_Television_Film "Golden Globe Award for Best Supporting Actor – Series, Miniseries or Television Film") in 2013.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Huston#cite_note-27) He portrayed [The Axeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Axeman_(American_Horror_Story) "The Axeman (American Horror Story)") in the [FX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FX_(TV_channel) "FX (TV channel)") thriller series _[American Horror Story: Coven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American\_Horror\_Story:\_Coven "American Horror Story: Coven")_ and Massimo Dolcefino in _[American Horror Story: Freak Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American\_Horror\_Story:\_Freak\_Show "American Horror Story: Freak Show")_.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Huston#cite_note-:3-11) Huston starred as [General Erich Ludendorff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erich_Ludendorff "Erich Ludendorff") in the 2017 film _[Wonder Woman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wonder\_Woman\_(2017\_film) "Wonder Woman (2017 film)")_ and as Wade Jennings in _[Angel Has Fallen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angel\_Has\_Fallen "Angel Has Fallen")_.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Huston#cite_note-:4-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Huston#cite_note-:5-10)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Danny_Huston&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Personal life")]

From 1989 to 1993, Huston was married to actress [Virginia Madsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Madsen "Virginia Madsen"). In 2001, he married Katie Jane Evans with whom he has a daughter.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Huston#cite_note-:7-28) Huston and Evans separated in 2006. Evans died by suicide in October 2008 before the divorce was finalized.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Huston#cite_note-29)

## About The Film

R | Aug 31, 2005 | Thriller, Drama | 2hr 9min

Nominated for four Academy Awards®, The Constant Gardener stars Ralph Fiennes and Academy Award® winner for Best Supporting Actress Rachel Weisz. In this gripping suspense-thriller, a diplomat on the hunt for his wife's murderer uncovers a treacherous conspiracy that will destroy millions of innocent people - unless he can reveal its sinister roots. From the best-selling spy novel by John le Carre comes this edge-of-your-seat story of murder, deception and revenge that critics are calling "a hair-raising thriller with an unforgettable finale" (Karen Durbin, Elle).

Starring Ralph Fiennes, Rachel Weisz, Danny Huston, Bill Nighy, Pete Postlethwaite, Richard McCabe, Donald Sumpter, Juliet Aubrey, Hubert Kounde, Archie Panjabi, Gerard McSorley, Sidede Onyulo, Anneke Kim Sarnau

Directed By Fernando Meirelles

Written By Jeffrey Caine, John le Carre

Produced By Simon Channing Williams

**Peter William Postlethwaite** (7 February 1946 – 2 January 2011) was an English [character actor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Character_actor "Character actor").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-1) After various stage[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-theatricalia-2) and minor television appearances, Postlethwaite's first major success arose through the film _[Distant Voices, Still Lives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distant\_Voices,\_Still\_Lives "Distant Voices, Still Lives")_ (1988), directed by [Terence Davies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terence_Davies "Terence Davies"). He had a breakthrough in Hollywood when he portrayed David in _[Alien 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alien\_3 "Alien 3")_ (1992), and his international reputation was further solidified when he was nominated for the [Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Supporting_Actor "Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor") for his role as Giuseppe Conlon, father of [Gerry Conlon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerry_Conlon "Gerry Conlon"), in _[In the Name of the Father](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In\_the\_Name\_of\_the\_Father\_(film) "In the Name of the Father (film)")_ (1993).

Following this role, he portrayed the mysterious lawyer Mr. Kobayashi in _[The Usual Suspects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Usual\_Suspects "The Usual Suspects")_ and went on to appear in a wide variety of films, including _[James and the Giant Peach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James\_and\_the\_Giant\_Peach\_(film) "James and the Giant Peach (film)")_, _[Dragonheart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dragonheart "Dragonheart")_, _[Romeo + Juliet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romeo\_+\_Juliet "Romeo + Juliet")_, _[Brassed Off](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brassed\_Off "Brassed Off")_, _[The Lost World: Jurassic Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Lost\_World:\_Jurassic\_Park "The Lost World: Jurassic Park")_, _[Amistad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad\_(film) "Amistad (film)")_, _[The Shipping News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Shipping\_News\_(film) "The Shipping News (film)")_, _[Dark Water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark\_Water\_(2005\_film) "Dark Water (2005 film)")_, _[The Constant Gardener](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Constant\_Gardener\_(film) "The Constant Gardener (film)")_, and _[Inception](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inception "Inception")_. On television, Postlethwaite played [Sergeant Obadiah Hakeswill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obadiah_Hakeswill "Obadiah Hakeswill") on _[Sharpe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharpe\_(TV\_series) "Sharpe (TV series)")_. On stage, he was a member of the [Royal Shakespeare Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Shakespeare_Company "Royal Shakespeare Company") from 1981 to 1987.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-theatricalia-2)

Director [Steven Spielberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Spielberg "Steven Spielberg") once called him "the best actor in the world".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-A_face_we_won't_forget-3) He was made an [Officer of the Order of the British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Officer_of_the_Order_of_the_British_Empire "Officer of the Order of the British Empire") in the [2004 New Year Honours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_New_Year_Honours "2004 New Year Honours") list. Less than one month after his death, he was nominated for the [BAFTA Award for Best Actor in a Supporting Role](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Actor_in_a_Supporting_Role "BAFTA Award for Best Actor in a Supporting Role") for his performance as gangster Fergie Colm in _[The Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Town\_(2010\_film) "The Town (2010 film)")_ (2010).

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pete_Postlethwaite&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Peter William Postlethwaite was born into a working-class [Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic "Catholic") family at 101 Norris Street[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-4) in [Warrington, Lancashire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warrington,_Lancashire "Warrington, Lancashire") on 7 February 1946,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-6) the son of Mary Geraldine (née Lawless; 1913–2000) and [cooper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooper_(profession) "Cooper (profession)"), wood machinist, and school caretaker William Postlethwaite (1913–1988).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-telegraph-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-8) He had an older brother named Michael (1944–2006) and two older sisters, Patricia and Anne. He would later portray [Irish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_people "Irish people") characters on multiple occasions, leading some to mistakenly believe that he was of Irish descent.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-9)

Postlethwaite attended St Benedict's RC Junior School and a [seminary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seminary "Seminary"), then joined [West Park Grammar School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_La_Salle_School,_St_Helens#Grammar_schools "De La Salle School, St Helens") in [St Helens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Helens,_Merseyside "St Helens, Merseyside"), where he enjoyed sports including [rugby union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_union "Rugby union"). He spent an extra year re-sitting some of his [O-levels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GCE_Ordinary_Level "GCE Ordinary Level"), and then took four [A-levels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GCE_Advanced_Level "GCE Advanced Level") in English, history, geography, and French.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-autobiography-10) Before his acting career, he trained as a teacher at [St Mary's College, Strawberry Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Mary's_University,_Twickenham "St Mary's University, Twickenham") where his chosen subjects were physical education and drama (where he became the first male drama teacher).[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] He initially trained to be a Catholic priest,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-11) but later settled on a career in acting. He trained as an actor at the [Bristol Old Vic Theatre School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Old_Vic_Theatre_School "Bristol Old Vic Theatre School") in 1970.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-12)

He was a veteran of the [Royal Shakespeare Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Shakespeare_Company "Royal Shakespeare Company") and other acting companies. On 13 January 1981, he took the leading role in a [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC") TV [black comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_comedy "Black comedy") by [Alan Bleasdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Bleasdale "Alan Bleasdale"), _The Muscle Market_, which was a spin-off from _[Boys from the Blackstuff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boys\_from\_the\_Blackstuff "Boys from the Blackstuff")_; it was part of the _Play for Today_ series.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

After other early appearances in small parts for television programmes such as _[The Professionals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Professionals\_(TV\_series) "The Professionals (TV series)")_ and as Jack _"Oily_" Wragg in the _[Minder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minder\_(TV\_series) "Minder (TV series)")_ episode _Back In Good Old England,_[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-13) Postlethwaite's first film success came with the film _[Distant Voices, Still Lives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distant\_Voices,\_Still\_Lives "Distant Voices, Still Lives")_ in 1988. He received an [Academy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award "Academy Award") nomination for his role in _[In the Name of the Father](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In\_the\_Name\_of\_the\_Father "In the Name of the Father")_ in 1993. He is well known for his role as mysterious lawyer Mr. Kobayashi in _[The Usual Suspects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Usual\_Suspects "The Usual Suspects")_. He made appearances in several other successful films, including _[Alien 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alien\_3 "Alien 3")_, _[Amistad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amistad\_(film) "Amistad (film)")_, _[Brassed Off](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brassed\_Off "Brassed Off")_, _[The Shipping News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Shipping\_News\_(film) "The Shipping News (film)")_, _[The Constant Gardener](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Constant\_Gardener\_(film) "The Constant Gardener (film)")_, _[Inception](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inception "Inception")_, _[James and the Giant Peach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James\_and\_the\_Giant\_Peach\_(film) "James and the Giant Peach (film)")_ and as Friar Lawrence in Baz Luhrmann's _[Romeo + Juliet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romeo\_+\_Juliet "Romeo + Juliet")_. [_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pete_Postlethwaite&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Early in his career, Postlethwaite was advised to adopt a new surname for his acting work by his first agent and by peers who quipped that his name "would never be put up in [lights outside theatres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marquee_(structure) "Marquee (structure)") because they couldn't afford the electricity". He rejected the advice.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-Postlethwaitename-14) He started his career at the [Everyman Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everyman_Theatre,_Liverpool "Everyman Theatre, Liverpool") in [Liverpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool "Liverpool"), where his colleagues included [Bill Nighy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Nighy "Bill Nighy"), [Jonathan Pryce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Pryce "Jonathan Pryce"), [Antony Sher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antony_Sher "Antony Sher"), [Matthew Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Kelly "Matthew Kelly"), and [Julie Walters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julie_Walters "Julie Walters"), having an intimate relationship with the latter during the mid-to-late 1970s.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-wheatley1-15)

In 2003, he toured [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia") and [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand "New Zealand") in a 90-minute one-man play, _Scaramouche Jones_, in which he played a clown trying to find out who he is before he dies at midnight, receiving a nomination for the [TMA Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TMA_Award "TMA Award") for Best Actor and winning the [Theatregoers' Choice Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatregoers'_Choice_Award "Theatregoers' Choice Award") for Best Solo Performance.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-16) This was directed by Rupert Goold, who would also direct his [Lear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Lear "King Lear") in 2008, in which Postlethwaite played every character. As well as Australia, the play toured Canada, New Zealand and the UK to great acclaim.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-wheatley1-15)

In _[The Art of Discworld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Art\_of\_Discworld "The Art of Discworld")_ (2004), [Terry Pratchett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terry_Pratchett "Terry Pratchett") wrote that he had always imagined [Sam Vimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Vimes "Sam Vimes") as "a younger, slightly bulkier version of Pete Postlethwaite".[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-17)

[Steven Spielberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Spielberg "Steven Spielberg"), who directed Postlethwaite in 1997's _[The Lost World: Jurassic Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Lost\_World:\_Jurassic\_Park "The Lost World: Jurassic Park")_, called him "the best actor in the world".[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-Observer-18) Postlethwaite quipped: "I'm sure what Spielberg actually said was, 'The thing about Pete is that he thinks he's the best actor in the world.'"[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-19) Postlethwaite next starred in a Liverpool stage production of _King Lear_ in 2008 at the Everyman Theatre, Liverpool, and at the Young Vic, London. He appeared in the [climate change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change "Climate change")-themed film _[The Age of Stupid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Age\_of\_Stupid "The Age of Stupid")_, which premiered in March 2009.

One of his more notable roles was [Sergeant Obadiah Hakeswill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obadiah_Hakeswill "Obadiah Hakeswill") in ITV's _[Sharpe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharpe\_(TV\_series) "Sharpe (TV series)")_ series. The actor said this was one of his favourite roles and that he and fellow actor [Sean Bean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Bean "Sean Bean") played well off each other because of their mutual love and respect. [Bernard Cornwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Cornwell "Bernard Cornwell"), the author and creator of the _Sharpe_ series, specifically wrote Hakeswill's character in later novels to reflect Postlethwaite's performance as the character in the TV series. Postlethwaite co-starred with Bean in _[When Saturday Comes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/When\_Saturday\_Comes\_(film) "When Saturday Comes (film)")_. [_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Terminally ill, Postlethwaite made a return to Hollywood in three 2010 films, first as Spyros in _[Clash of the Titans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash\_of\_the\_Titans\_(2010\_film) "Clash of the Titans (2010 film)")_. He next appeared in the blockbuster hit _[Inception](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inception "Inception")_ as Maurice Fischer, an industrialist who is slowly dying. Lastly, his performance in _[The Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Town\_(2010\_film) "The Town (2010 film)")_ as florist and crime boss Fergus "Fergie" Colm was well received by critics, which would earn him a posthumous nomination for [BAFTA Award for Best Actor in a Supporting Role](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Actor_in_a_Supporting_Role "BAFTA Award for Best Actor in a Supporting Role"), and making several publications' lists of Oscar predictions for Best Supporting Actor.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-22) His final appearance on screen was in [Nick Hamm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Hamm "Nick Hamm")'s film _[Killing Bono](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killing\_Bono "Killing Bono")_, based on the memoir of Neil McCormick. The role was written specially for Postlethwaite to accommodate his illness.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-23) The film was released on 1 April 2011. He was scheduled to be in the BBC series _[Exile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exile\_(TV\_series) "Exile (TV series)")_, but had to pull out due to his declining health and was replaced by [Jim Broadbent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Broadbent "Jim Broadbent").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-24)

## Activism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pete_Postlethwaite&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Activism")]

Postlethwaite appeared as a taxi driver in a [political broadcast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party_political_broadcast "Party political broadcast") for the [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK) "Labour Party (UK)") during the [1997 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_United_Kingdom_general_election "1997 United Kingdom general election"),[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-25) and marched in London against the [Iraq War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_War "Iraq War") in 2003.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-26)

In his later years, Postlethwaite was vocal in calling for action on [climate change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change "Climate change"), and installed a [wind turbine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind_turbine "Wind turbine") in his garden; he wrote in _[The Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Sun\_(United\_Kingdom) "The Sun (United Kingdom)")_, "The stakes [of climate change] are very, very high. They're through the roof. How could we willingly know that we're going into extinction ... and let it happen?"[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-28) At the UK premiere of _The Age of Stupid_ in 2009, he told then-[Secretary of State for Energy and Climate Change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_Energy_and_Climate_Change "Secretary of State for Energy and Climate Change")[Ed Miliband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Miliband "Ed Miliband") that he would return his [OBE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Officer_of_the_Most_Excellent_Order_of_the_British_Empire "Officer of the Most Excellent Order of the British Empire") and vote for any party other than Labour if the [Kingsnorth coal-fired power station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingsnorth_power_station#Proposed_replacement "Kingsnorth power station") was given the go-ahead by the Labour government.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-29)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pete_Postlethwaite&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Postlethwaite lived in [West Itchenor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Itchenor "West Itchenor") before moving near [Bishop's Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop's_Castle "Bishop's Castle"). He was a lifelong supporter of [Liverpool F.C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_F.C. "Liverpool F.C.").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-30) He began a relationship with former [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC") producer Jacqueline Morrish in 1987, and they were married in 2003 at [St Nicholas' Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Nicholas_Church,_West_Itchenor "St Nicholas Church, West Itchenor") in West Itchenor. They had a son, actor [Billy Postlethwaite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Postlethwaite "Billy Postlethwaite") (born in 1989),[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-wheatley1-15) and a daughter (born in 1996).

## Health issues and death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pete_Postlethwaite&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Health issues and death")]

Postlethwaite was diagnosed with [testicular cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Testicular_cancer "Testicular cancer") in 1990, and [had his right testicle removed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inguinal_orchiectomy "Inguinal orchiectomy").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-31)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-Observer-18) A life-long smoker since he was 10,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-telegraph-7) he said during a 2009 interview with _[Scotland on Sunday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland\_on\_Sunday "Scotland on Sunday")_, "We've got to hope the next generation will do things differently. I'm sure that in 20 years' time the kids will say: 'Can you believe that people actually used to smoke – put these funny little things in their mouths, lit them and sucked all that crap into their lungs?"[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-Smith-32)

Postlethwaite was diagnosed with [pancreatic cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pancreatic_cancer "Pancreatic cancer") in March 2009,[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-33) and continued acting for the next year and a half, showing clear signs of weight loss during his final performances.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-34) On 2 January 2011, at the age of 64, he died at the [Royal Shrewsbury Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Shrewsbury_Hospital "Royal Shrewsbury Hospital") in [Shrewsbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shrewsbury "Shrewsbury").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-37)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-A_face_we_won't_forget-3) In his final two years, he worked on his memoir _A Spectacle of Dust_ with writer [Andy Richardson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Richardson_(writer) "Andy Richardson (writer)"), which was published in June 2011.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-autobiography-10)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Postlethwaite#cite_note-book-38)

## Awards

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pete_Postlethwaite&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Awards")]

Postlethwaite was made an [Officer of the Order of the British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Officer_of_the_Order_of_the_British_Empire "Officer of the Order of the British Empire") in the 2004 New Year Honours list and received an Honorary Fellowship in recognition of outstanding contribution to the dramatic arts by [Liverpool John Moores University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_John_Moores_University "Liverpool John Moores University") in 2005 and an honorary degree from the [University of Liverpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Liverpool "University of Liverpool") in 2006. He received an [Academy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award "Academy Award") nomination for his role _[In the Name of the Father](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In\_the\_Name\_of\_the\_Father "In the Name of the Father")_ and was posthumously nominated for a [BAFTA Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Award "BAFTA Award") for his performance in _[The Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Town\_(2010\_film) "The Town (2010 film)")_.

# Screenwriter Jeffrey Caine On _The Constant Gardener_’s 15th Anniversary

How John le Carré’s corporate thriller became a cinematic classic

[](https://facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.focusfeatures.com%2Farticle%2F15th-anniversary_interview_jeffrey-caine)[](https://twitter.com/share?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.focusfeatures.com%2Farticle%2F15th-anniversary_interview_jeffrey-caine)

Aug 31, 2020

When[Fernando Meirelles](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0576987/?ref_=tt_ov_dr)’ adaptation of John le Carré’s [_The Constant Gardener_](http://focusfeatures.com/the_constant_gardener)opened in theaters on August 31, 2005, it proved a revelation. In the film, Justin Quayle ([Ralph Fiennes](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0000146/?ref_=tt_cl_t1)), a soft-spoken British diplomat stationed in Kenya, goes to any length to uncover the truth behind what happened to his wife Tessa ([Rachel Weisz](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0001838/?ref_=tt_cl_t2)) in the African wilderness. Moving from post-colonial garden parties in Nairobi to the European headquarters of multinational pharmaceutical corporations, the film unravels a tale at once profoundly intimate and global in scale. “That it offers passion, betrayal, gorgeous cinematography, social commentary, stellar performances and clever wit puts it in a special category near perfection,” exclaimed [_USA Today_](https://usatoday30.usatoday.com/life/movies/reviews/2005-08-30-constant-gardener_x.htm). In addition to Rachel Weisz winning an Academy Award® for Best Supporting Actress, the film was nominated for Best Film Editing ([Claire Simpson](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0800943/?ref_=ttfc_fc_cr15)), Best Original Score ([Alberto Iglesias](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0407076/?ref_=ttfc_fc_cr13)), and Best Adapted Screenplay ([Jeffrey Caine](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0128997/?ref_=ttfc_fc_wr1)).

For Caine, who had penned the screenplay for the James Bond extravaganza[_GoldenEye_](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0113189/?ref_=nm_flmg_wr_11), _The Constant Gardener_ was more than a thriller. Having lost his own wife in 1995, he knew all too well the love and sorrow at the story's heart. With the _The Constant Gardener_ turning fifteen, we spoke with Caine about writing the acclaimed screenplay that, as [_Rolling Stone_](https://www.rollingstone.com/movies/movie-reviews/the-constant-gardener-118301/) notes, "put a human face on John le Carré’s novel of sex, lies and dirty politics in modern Africa."

**Watch****The Constant Gardener****now on**[**iTunes**](https://itunes.apple.com/us/movie/the-constant-gardener/id309664079)**or at**[**Amazon**](https://www.amazon.com/constant-gardener-ralph-fiennes/dp/b000i9vo76/ref=sr_1_2?dchild=1&keywords=the+constant+gardener&qid=1597711953&sr=8-2)**.**

[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1l1lzzfpWFU)

The official trailer for _The Constant Gardener_.

How did you end up writing the screenplay for _The Constant Gardener_?

I knew [Sarah Golding](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm2241261/?ref_=fn_al_nm_1), the script editor for the production company Potboiler who acquired the rights to the book. Sarah told me I was on the shortlist to adapt the book. She was right to pick me. She knew that I had personal experience of the kind of grief that Justin suffers in the story. She knew I could bring in my personal history and emotion into the writing. Then I had lunch with John le Carré, [Mike Newell](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0001565/?ref_=fn_al_nm_1) (who was set to direct the film at that time) and the film’s producer [Simon Channing Williams](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0151925/?ref_=fn_al_nm_1). I was there to impress le Carré, who being a writer of note had the right to approve whoever adapted his novel. I assume I did, since I was hired.

![Image 9: artcont_1597966113.jpg](https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/blt223a4a92692ca457/blt4748c15ffb734923/68a3809bb3d99beda2d9c38e/4649_artcont_1597966113.jpg?branch=production&width=3840)

_The Constant Gardener_ screenwriter Jeffrey Caine.

In adapting the novel, did you do additional research either into the pharmaceutical industry or the African locations?

Not that much. Interestingly, my physicians, a husband and wife team at the general practice I went to, had spent a year or two in Kenya. They gave me a good sense of the place and the state of medicine there. I acknowledged them in the film's credits. But really most of the research was already there in the novel. Being such an experienced writer, le Carré really knew his stuff.

Your adaptation has been praised for keeping the novel’s non-linear structure. What did you want to change from the novel?

In the book, le Carré has a couple of British cops go to Kenya to investigate the death of Tessa and they give away the game very early in the story. Le Carré did that deliberately. It was his way of saying, "Look. I'm not that interested in the thriller aspect. This is really a polemic against the way British companies exploit Third World countries in testing for drugs. You don't need to worry about how the story plays out. I'm going to tell you all the answers up front." In a movie, you can't do that. When I pitched my adaptation, the first thing I told them I wanted to do was take out the cops.

What was the main focus of the story for you?

My job was to set Justin on the trail of uncovering what happened to Tessa. Once that happens, the film takes off as a thriller and works as a thriller. We originally had an entire sequence in Canada. That was all in the book. We filmed it but never used it. Fernando felt that it slowed the movie down just when it needed to speed up. He was absolutely right about that.

![Image 10: artcont_1597712903.jpg](https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/blt223a4a92692ca457/blt3f54f6a611f609d4/68a3809c8ff3ef03b217d60f/4651_artcont_1597712903.jpg?branch=production&width=3840)

Fernando Meirelles directing Ralph Fiennes on the set of _The Constant Gardener_.

When Meirelles became the director, did it help to have a non-European perspective on the story?

Enormously so. That’s why Simon Channing Williams wanted Fernando to be the director after Newell left the film. Williams felt a Third World perspective would give the film an added texture. While Fernando had made his very successful Brazilian film [_City of God_](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0317248/?ref_=fn_al_tt_1), he didn’t know anything about the traditional old-school-boy world of British diplomacy in the former colonies. It was as foreign to him as was Kenya. But what he did understand was the Third World.

![Image 11: artcont_1597965588.jpg](https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/blt223a4a92692ca457/blt5ac857ebb81eb30a/68a3809bc8a77774617c3b57/4650_artcont_1597965588.jpg?branch=production&width=3840)

Bill Nighy, Ralph Fiennes, and Jeffrey Caine in in _The Constant Gardener_.

How was it working with Meirelles?

It was great. I am not quick to praise directors. I always assume they presume too much and they try to take over your role in writing the script. Fernando never did any of those things. He was a great director to work with. He brought his own wonderful skills and insights to my screenplay. _The Constant Gardener_ would not have been the same film without him.

You also appear in the film. How did that happen?

I have always been an amateur actor. So I asked Williams if I could have a speaking role. He gave me this part as a club doorman. We found a club and the doorman loaned me his jacket. After the scene was filmed, the doorman came up and told me nobody would have known that I was not the real doorman.

Le Carré said, "I have a great affection for _The Constant Gardener_ because it was actually a film and a book which I can truly say did good. It held the pharmaceutical industry to account.” How do you feel about the film?

I don't know how much influence it has had on the pharmaceutical industry, but as a film, I stand by it. I don't always stand by my films. I sometimes feel my scripts are spoiled in production for one reason or another. Here I loved pretty much everything about the picture. I love the way it was done and the atmosphere of it.

![Image 12: artcont_1597771494.jpg](https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/blt223a4a92692ca457/blt5baf8b9b8cfe0f0c/68a3809d8a8882a7ee184d0c/4654_artcont_1597771494.jpg?branch=production&width=3840)

Rachel Wesiz as Tessa in _The Constant Gardener_.

The film was nominated for four Academy Awards®—

And even more at the BAFTAs.

Yes, it got ten BAFTA nominations. How did that make you feel?

That was very pleasing to us. I wish that Fernando had gotten an Oscar® nod and I was surprised that Ralph wasn't nominated. But overall we were very happy.

Do you still hear from people who have just seen the film?

Fifteen years after the event, people still tell me how much they enjoy _The Constant Gardener_. Films can be forgotten very quickly unless they become classics. I am not sure that _The Constant Gardener_ has quite achieved that. But it is on its way. Maybe in another fifteen years. But I’m always delighted to hear people tell me that they have just seen it and how much they like it—even love it.

When a British diplomat's wife -- a socially-conscious lawyer -- turns up dead in Kenya, he sets out to find the truth surrounding her murder. In the process, he finds out that his wife had been compiling data against a multinational drug company that uses helpless Africans as guinea pigs to test a tuberculosis remedy with unfortunately fatal side effects. Therefore, those who may have had the most reason to silence her are closer to home than he ever imagined.

Isherwood
 
all reviews of this user 

An incredibly shot thriller that intelligently grafts an uncompromising indictment of big pharmaceutical companies making millions off of disease-ridden Africa in a basic conspiracy shell. Director Meirelles manages to bring this optic of social issues into focus in such a way that even viewers least familiar with the topic will feel that they just untied the Gordian Knot, and the intelligence officer does not have to have a heart attack even with the (inevitable) simplification of the whole intricate machination. It’s a perfectly balanced blend of compelling content, well-managed form (authentic handheld camerawork), and, as a bonus, the excellent acting tandem of Fiennes and Weisz. After Hotel Rwanda, the developed world received another unflattering postcard signed with "Africa."
(01/05/2007)

Matty
 
all reviews of this user 

Major pharmaceutical companies, overpriced drugs tested on humans, the British government – a complicated cycle in which too much money is being thrown around for any common person to stop it. Really? The rich get richer, the poor get poorer, the poorer get sick, and the sick die. Who cares? No one. Who should care? Everyone. Unlike Syriana, The Constant Gardener isn’t a disjointed work, even though it is also composed of many fragments and can be seen as two films in one. The director’s strongly humanistic leanings lead him to use slightly more extortionate techniques, which unfortunately lose their persuasiveness as their intensity increases. An example of such a scene is the “end of the first film” after Justin’s return to London – was this even necessary? The camerawork, though at times brilliant, seems too agile at other times, when I personally would have welcomed a more restrained approach. It’s a shame that the screenplay wasn’t written in such a way as to give Weisz space to perform throughout the film, rather than mainly just in the first half, as her character, Tessa, enlivens the story in an extraordinary way and provides the strongest motivation to keep fighting. So let’s not just be cautious gardeners, because anyone can change the face of the world. I truly believe that, at least for now, and Meirelles deserves to be praised for that. 85%
(05/10/2007)

lamps
 
all reviews of this user 

I didn't know what to expect from The Constant Gardener, and to be honest, I couldn't figure it out even after the opening thirty minutes, when I felt a bit out of place in the merry-go-round of time blending and almost authentic African passages. But then Meirelles quickly hints at the direction he wants to take, letting the story flow more smoothly, and in the last act he sets up for one of the most impressive human dramas in a long time. On the one hand, a look at a current problem, a portrayal of African misery and the dirtiness of our society, and on the other hand, the love of two people whose steps have led them to a position where they automatically become inconvenient in the eyes of a higher power. And all that is combined so perfectly, with great feeling and, above all, thought, that despite the duller start I was not only absolutely satisfied, but maybe even a little touched. Rachel Weisz is really excellent, maybe one of the best actresses of today, but in my eyes she’s a bit overshadowed by Ralph Fiennes, who again pulls the whole film solely on his shoulders, and at least an Oscar nomination would have been appropriate. I definitely recommend it to anyone who is not indifferent to the current African situation.
(11/02/2012)

A socially critical drama set in the environment of Sub-Saharan Africa, where wealthy countries gladly export their waste and problems. I don't consider the film's motif as excessive, although it is necessary to emphasize that it is not always wise to put pharmaceutical companies in a difficult position. Researching new medicines is damn expensive and uncertain, so, for example, widely spread ideas that companies should distribute their products for free, would lead not so much to a decrease in profit (which the companies would ensure otherwise), but rather to a halt in the development of new medicines. As for bypassing strict security measures in research, patients themselves often have an interest in reducing waiting time and receiving timely help. While Ralph Fiennes is convincing in his role as an acting chameleon and it is truly a joy to watch him at times, Rachel Weisz reaches the limits of her acting abilities and the chemistry between the married couple does not work for me as it should. I also have a problem with the behavior of the film's characters, for example, the final act of resignation and passive waiting for execution somehow doesn't make sense. It's a decent film, but I never considered giving it four stars. In addition to the points mentioned above, the film deserves a more critical edit - at least 15 minutes could easily be sacrificed out of those 130 minutes. Overall impression: 60%.
(01/26/2013)

When a British diplomat's wife -- a socially-conscious lawyer -- turns up dead in Kenya, he sets out to find the truth surrounding her murder. In the process, he finds out that his wife had been compiling data against a multinational drug company that uses helpless Africans as guinea pigs to test a tuberculosis remedy with unfortunately fatal side effects. Therefore, those who may have had the most reason to silence her are closer to home than he ever imagined.

Isherwood
 
all reviews of this user 

An incredibly shot thriller that intelligently grafts an uncompromising indictment of big pharmaceutical companies making millions off of disease-ridden Africa in a basic conspiracy shell. Director Meirelles manages to bring this optic of social issues into focus in such a way that even viewers least familiar with the topic will feel that they just untied the Gordian Knot, and the intelligence officer does not have to have a heart attack even with the (inevitable) simplification of the whole intricate machination. It’s a perfectly balanced blend of compelling content, well-managed form (authentic handheld camerawork), and, as a bonus, the excellent acting tandem of Fiennes and Weisz. After Hotel Rwanda, the developed world received another unflattering postcard signed with "Africa."
(01/05/2007)

Matty
 
all reviews of this user 

Major pharmaceutical companies, overpriced drugs tested on humans, the British government – a complicated cycle in which too much money is being thrown around for any common person to stop it. Really? The rich get richer, the poor get poorer, the poorer get sick, and the sick die. Who cares? No one. Who should care? Everyone. Unlike Syriana, The Constant Gardener isn’t a disjointed work, even though it is also composed of many fragments and can be seen as two films in one. The director’s strongly humanistic leanings lead him to use slightly more extortionate techniques, which unfortunately lose their persuasiveness as their intensity increases. An example of such a scene is the “end of the first film” after Justin’s return to London – was this even necessary? The camerawork, though at times brilliant, seems too agile at other times, when I personally would have welcomed a more restrained approach. It’s a shame that the screenplay wasn’t written in such a way as to give Weisz space to perform throughout the film, rather than mainly just in the first half, as her character, Tessa, enlivens the story in an extraordinary way and provides the strongest motivation to keep fighting. So let’s not just be cautious gardeners, because anyone can change the face of the world. I truly believe that, at least for now, and Meirelles deserves to be praised for that. 85%
(05/10/2007)

lamps
 
all reviews of this user 

I didn't know what to expect from The Constant Gardener, and to be honest, I couldn't figure it out even after the opening thirty minutes, when I felt a bit out of place in the merry-go-round of time blending and almost authentic African passages. But then Meirelles quickly hints at the direction he wants to take, letting the story flow more smoothly, and in the last act he sets up for one of the most impressive human dramas in a long time. On the one hand, a look at a current problem, a portrayal of African misery and the dirtiness of our society, and on the other hand, the love of two people whose steps have led them to a position where they automatically become inconvenient in the eyes of a higher power. And all that is combined so perfectly, with great feeling and, above all, thought, that despite the duller start I was not only absolutely satisfied, but maybe even a little touched. Rachel Weisz is really excellent, maybe one of the best actresses of today, but in my eyes she’s a bit overshadowed by Ralph Fiennes, who again pulls the whole film solely on his shoulders, and at least an Oscar nomination would have been appropriate. I definitely recommend it to anyone who is not indifferent to the current African situation.
(11/02/2012)

A bit of a modern noir film. The man is placed in a role where he wants to solve the death of his wife; he wants to know what happened. The initial idyll turns into a pursuit of truth that may not be particularly kind. The film has interesting moments, and politics are included fairly tolerably, but I just didn't find the film enjoyable. It’s long and lacks tension.
(03/27/2014)

gudaulin
 
all reviews of this user 

A socially critical drama set in the environment of Sub-Saharan Africa, where wealthy countries gladly export their waste and problems. I don't consider the film's motif as excessive, although it is necessary to emphasize that it is not always wise to put pharmaceutical companies in a difficult position. Researching new medicines is damn expensive and uncertain, so, for example, widely spread ideas that companies should distribute their products for free, would lead not so much to a decrease in profit (which the companies would ensure otherwise), but rather to a halt in the development of new medicines. As for bypassing strict security measures in research, patients themselves often have an interest in reducing waiting time and receiving timely help. While Ralph Fiennes is convincing in his role as an acting chameleon and it is truly a joy to watch him at times, Rachel Weisz reaches the limits of her acting abilities and the chemistry between the married couple does not work for me as it should. I also have a problem with the behavior of the film's characters, for example, the final act of resignation and passive waiting for execution somehow doesn't make sense. It's a decent film, but I never considered giving it four stars. In addition to the points mentioned above, the film deserves a more critical edit - at least 15 minutes could easily be sacrificed out of those 130 minutes. Overall impression: 60%.
(01/26/2013)

Jun 5, 2014

[8 Spangle](https://www.metacritic.com/user/Spangle/)

"The Constant Gardener" is a slow burning political thriller that is a little confusing in the first half, but as more and more gets revealed in the second half, things begin to make a lot more sense and the puzzle pieces really begin to come together. Ralph Fiennes and Rachel Weisz are both great in this one, as expected. It is not hard to believe that Weisz won an Oscar for her performance here. The cinematography is also gorgeous as they were able to extract every bit of beauty they could out of their African location. As mentioned, this one is a tad slow, but it never really failed to have my attention. Throughout the film, I was completely hooked as I tried to follow every twist and turn before the big conclusion at the end. The great part about this one is that the second half really does explain much of what we see in the first half. It is a tad confusing, but the answers to any questions we have are ultimately provided and things begin to make a bit more sense. In addition, the film brings a lot of ethical concerns surrounding drug companies and their operations in Africa to the forefront, as you know the plot of this one is not too far-fetched. While the film was very thrilling, it also makes you feel a lot of empathy for those who are exploited in the name of medicine. Ultimately, "The Constant Gardener" is a good film with a strong plot, strong acting, and strong direction.

[7 FilipeNeto](https://www.metacritic.com/user/FilipeNeto/)

When I watched this movie I already had some expectations because I had read good reviews and I knew that it had a strong cast. The story also seemed to be very interesting: a British diplomat trying to discover his wife's murderers discovers a corrupt plot between the British government and the pharmaceutical industry, working in Kenya. Needless to say, I think, I was very pleased with the movie. The plot's main subject is strong, moving and human. Actor's work is very competent. The two central characters are affectionate, romantic and passionate, especially Tessa, who defends her ideas with great conviction. This helps a lot to make them dear to the audience, holding our attention until the end. How much of this is pure fiction is something I kept thinking about later. We know that the pharmaceutical industry generates millions, and this causes me (at least to me) some distrust. Has it ever happened, in recent past, something like what happens in this movie? Is it happening now and we don't know? Even if its not, its always a good reason to think on how some countries and regions are exploited. Going back to the film itself, I liked the way it visually explores African landscapes, with cinematography toasting us with scenes of a very beautiful light and color. The work of Brazilian director Fernando Meirelles (in my opinion, the best Brazilian film director today) is very competent and gives the film a soft aroma of documentary that tastes good, even though its no more than an illusion. Errors or problems? I didn't feel many, but I think it would improve if it had been kept for longer the mystery surrounding the conspiracy. The public soon realizes what's going on and the real reasons behind Tessa's death, and that takes away the interest and logic of her husband's demand.

### Manage Consent Preferences

#### Strictly Necessary Cookies

Always Active

These cookies are necessary for the website to function and cannot be switched off in our systems. They are usually only set in response to actions made by you which amount to a request for services, such as setting your privacy preferences, logging in or filling in forms. You can set your browser to block or alert you about these cookies, but some parts of the site will not then work. These cookies do not store any personally identifiable information.

#### Performance Cookies

Always Active

These cookies allow us to count visits and traffic sources so we can measure and improve the performance of our site. They help us to know which pages are the most and least popular and see how visitors move around the site. All information these cookies collect is aggregated and therefore anonymous. If you do not allow these cookies we will not know when you have visited our site, and will not be able to monitor its performance.

#### Functional Cookies

Always Active

These cookies enable the website to provide enhanced functionality and personalisation. They may be set by us or by third party providers whose services we have added to our pages. If you do not allow these cookies then some or all of these services may not function properly.

#### Targeting Cookies

Always Active

These cookies may be set through our site by our advertising partners. They may be used by those companies to build a profile of your interests and show you relevant adverts on other sites. They do not store directly personal information, but are based on uniquely identifying your browser and internet device. If you do not allow these cookies, you will experience less targeted advertising.

#### Social Media Cookies

Always Active

These cookies are set by a range of social media services that we have added to the site to enable you to share our content with your friends and networks. They are capable of tracking your browser across other sites and building up a profile of your interests. This may impact the content and messages you see on other websites you visit. Once the film did finally start getting rolling, again about 1/3 or 1/2 through, it was great, but harkening back to that first part of the movie, it could be been done much better. A Subjective Distortion of Truth Disguised as Fact That Stumbles Completely Off Course.170923 (1.5)I understand that it is a movie about WikiLeaks, but playing with numbers as if presenting factual truth while remaining utterly subjective is absurd. History is a record written by the victors. A film that goes completely off the rails toward the end. I am deeply disappointed that Benedict Cumberbatch ever accepted this screenplay. Directed by Bill Condon, the 2013 biographical thriller "The Fifth Estate" dramatizes the meteoric rise and subsequent fallout of the whistleblower website WikiLeaks, chronicling the volatile relationship between its enigmatic founder Julian Assange (Benedict Cumberbatch) and his early colleague Daniel Domscheit-Berg (Daniel Brühl). While the film attempts to tackle the pressing ethical dilemmas surrounding information warfare, state secrecy, and digital transparency, its heavily biased perspective, uneven narrative framing, and superficial character development reduce a profound real-world controversy into a frustratingly hollow and muddled melodrama.

### Manage Consent Preferences

#### Strictly Necessary Cookies

Always Active

These cookies are necessary for the website to function and cannot be switched off in our systems. They are usually only set in response to actions made by you which amount to a request for services, such as setting your privacy preferences, logging in or filling in forms. You can set your browser to block or alert you about these cookies, but some parts of the site will not then work. These cookies do not store any personally identifiable information.

#### Performance Cookies

Always Active

These cookies allow us to count visits and traffic sources so we can measure and improve the performance of our site. They help us to know which pages are the most and least popular and see how visitors move around the site. All information these cookies collect is aggregated and therefore anonymous. If you do not allow these cookies we will not know when you have visited our site, and will not be able to monitor its performance.

#### Functional Cookies

Always Active

These cookies enable the website to provide enhanced functionality and personalisation. They may be set by us or by third party providers whose services we have added to our pages. If you do not allow these cookies then some or all of these services may not function properly.

#### Targeting Cookies

Always Active

These cookies may be set through our site by our advertising partners. They may be used by those companies to build a profile of your interests and show you relevant adverts on other sites. They do not store directly personal information, but are based on uniquely identifying your browser and internet device. If you do not allow these cookies, you will experience less targeted advertising.

#### Social Media Cookies

Always Active

These cookies are set by a range of social media services that we have added to the site to enable you to share our content with your friends and networks. They are capable of tracking your browser across other sites and building up a profile of your interests. This may impact the content and messages you see on other websites you visit.
